question: X1
answer:
REGULATORY DETERMINATION — Machinery Regulation (EU) 2023/1230

Reference date: 17 November 2026.
Controlling text: Regulation (EU) 2023/1230, OJ L 165, 29.6.2023, p. 1, as corrected by Corrigendum C1, OJ L 169, 4.7.2023, p. 35, and as amended by Regulation (EU) 2024/2748 and Regulation (EU) 2026/1744; consolidated version 27.07.2026 (CELEX 02023R1230-20260727). EUR-Lex states the current consolidated version is 27/07/2026 and the act is in force.

1. ANSWERS
- Ask 2 — date from which the Regulation applies and the Directive stops applying: 20 January 2027.
- Ask 3 — is Directive 2006/42/EC still in force on 17 November 2026: Yes. It remains in force, as amended, until 19 January 2027 and is repealed with effect from 20 January 2027.

2. OPERATIVE PROVISIONS IN THE CORRECTED CONSOLIDATED TEXT
- Article 54, second paragraph: 'It shall apply from ►C1 20 January 2027 ◄.'
- Article 51(2), first subparagraph: 'Directive 2006/42/EC is repealed with effect from ►C1 20 January 2027 ◄.'
- Article 52(1), first sentence: Member States shall not impede the making available on the market of products placed on the market in conformity with Directive 2006/42/EC before ►C1 20 January 2027 ◄. The second sentence applies Chapter VI of the Regulation from ►C1 19 July 2023 ◄ instead of Article 11 of the Directive.
- Article 52(2): EC type-examination certificates and approval decisions issued under Article 12 of Directive 2006/42/EC remain valid until they expire.

3. EFFECT OF THE CORRIGENDUM
- The original OJ text (OJ L 165, 29.6.2023) and the unconsolidated EN TXT page (celex:32023R1230) state 14 January 2027 in Article 51(2), Article 52(1) and Article 54.
- Corrigendum C1 (OJ L 169, 4.7.2023, p. 35) corrects those dates. The consolidated version 27.07.2026 incorporates C1 and shows 20 January 2027 in Articles 51(2), 52(1) and 54.
- The corrected text is therefore the text in force on 17 November 2026. Any answer of 14 January 2027 is based on the uncorrected original and is not the answer to this request.

4. ENTRY INTO FORCE VERSUS APPLICATION
- Entry into force: 19 July 2023 (twentieth day after publication in the Official Journal on 29 June 2023), under Article 54, first paragraph.
- General application: 20 January 2027, under Article 54, second paragraph.
- Earlier partial application: Articles 26–42 from 20 January 2024; Article 50(1) from 20 October 2026; Article 6(7) and Articles 48 and 52 from 19 July 2023; Article 6(2)–(6), (8) and (11) and Articles 47 and 53(3) from 20 July 2024. These partial dates do not bring the general repeal forward; the Directive continues to apply until 20 January 2027.

5. STATUS OF DIRECTIVE 2006/42/EC ON 17 NOVEMBER 2026
- The repeal date is 20 January 2027. On 17 November 2026 that date has not yet arrived. The Directive is still in force on 17 November 2026.
- It remains applicable until 19 January 2027 inclusive; it ceases to apply on 20 January 2027. The EUR-Lex summary for Directive 2006/42/EC states it 'will remain applicable until 19 January 2027' and is repealed 'as of 20 January 2027'.
- The Directive has been amended, including by Directive (EU) 2024/2749 (internal market emergency mode), but those amendments do not repeal it and do not change the 20 January 2027 repeal date.

6. TRANSITIONAL AND CROSS-REFERENCE EFFECTS
- Products placed on the market in conformity with Directive 2006/42/EC before 20 January 2027 may continue to be made available; Article 52(1) preserves that. This is not a staggered repeal by product category.
- Chapter VI of the Regulation applies from 19 July 2023, mutatis mutandis, to such products instead of Article 11 of the Directive, including procedures already initiated under Article 11.
- EC type-examination certificates and approval decisions under Article 12 of the Directive remain valid until expiry.
- From 20 January 2027, references to the repealed Directive are to be read as references to the Regulation and in accordance with the Annex XII correlation table (Article 51(2), second subparagraph).
- National implementing or transitional measures cannot alter the EU-law date of repeal; they may only operate within the space left by the Regulation.

7. PROOF-OF-ABSENCE CHECK AND NOT_STATED
- The harness proof of absence for ask 2 records that '20 January 2027', 'from 20 January 2027', 'shall apply from 20 January 2027', 'shall cease to apply from 20 January 2027' and '20.1.2027' are absent from: (i) the EN TXT page celex:32023R1230; (ii) the OJ PDF at publications.europa.eu cellar DOC_1; and (iii) the EL ALL page celex:32023R1230.
- That absence is explained by the fact that those pages reproduce the original, uncorrected text (or, for the EL page, an uncorrected operative quote) and therefore show 14 January 2027. It is not a statement that the corrected text lacks the date.
- The corrected consolidated text, CELEX 02023R1230-20260727, is the text in force on 17 November 2026 and does contain '20 January 2027' in Articles 51(2), 52(1) and 54. Ask 2 is therefore answered, not not-stated. not_stated is empty. blocked_on is empty.

8. PRACTICAL CONCLUSION
- For compliance planning as of 17 November 2026: Directive 2006/42/EC is still the applicable EU machinery regime; Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 is in force but its general application and the Directive's repeal take effect on 20 January 2027. Certain Regulation provisions already apply on the earlier partial dates listed above.
- Do not use 14 January 2027; that is the uncorrected original date. Use 20 January 2027.

question: X2
answer:
REGULATORY DETERMINATION — MDR Art. 120 transitional regime for a class IIa legacy device on a Directive 93/42/EEC notified-body certificate valid by virtue of Art. 120(2), assuming the Art. 120(3c) conditions are met.

1. ANSWER (three dates)
- Last date to place on the market or put into service: 31 December 2028 (Art. 120(3a)(b) MDR, as inserted by Regulation (EU) 2023/607).
- Last date to have lodged a formal application with a notified body: 26 May 2024 (Art. 120(3c)(e), first limb).
- Last date for the notified body and the manufacturer to have signed the written agreement: 26 September 2024 (Art. 120(3c)(e), second limb).
The two procedural dates are conditions precedent, not grace periods: if either was missed, the Art. 120(3a) derogation does not apply at all and there is no later fallback date. They precede the 31 December 2028 cut-off, as they must.

2. LEGAL BASIS AND WHY CLASS IIa LANDS ON 2028, NOT 2027
Art. 120(3) MDR (consolidated, ELI version dated 19 July 2026, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2017/745/2026-07-19/eng/xhtml):
  'By way of derogation from Article 5 and provided the conditions set out in paragraph 3c of this Article are met, devices referred to in paragraphs 3a and 3b of this Article may be placed on the market or put into service until the dates set out in those paragraphs.'
Art. 120(3a) (as replaced by Reg. (EU) 2023/607, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=CELEX:32023R0607):
  '(a) 31 December 2027, for all class III devices, and for class IIb implantable devices except sutures, staples, dental fillings, dental braces, tooth crowns, screws, wedges, plates, wires, pins, clips and connectors;
   (b) 31 December 2028, for class IIb devices other than those covered by point (a) of this paragraph, for class IIa devices, and for class I devices placed on the market in sterile condition or having a measuring function.'
The device is class IIa, so point (b) applies: 31 December 2028. Point (a)'s 31 December 2027 applies only to class III devices and to class IIb implantable devices outside the listed exclusions and must not be used here. The consolidated MDR text confirms the same split: '31 December 2028, for class IIb devices other than those covered by point (a) of this paragraph, for class IIa devices, and for class I devices placed on the market in sterile condition or having a measuring function.'

3. THE ART. 120(3c) CONDITION CHECKLIST (ask 1 — constraint carried into the analysis)
All five conditions must be met cumulatively; failure of any one removes the benefit of Art. 120(3a) entirely.
(a) The device continues to comply with Directive 93/42/EEC (as applicable) — Directive continues to apply to the extent necessary (Art. 122 MDR, as amended).
(b) No significant changes in the design and intended purpose.
(c) The device presents no unacceptable risk to the health or safety of patients, users or other persons, or to other aspects of public health.
(d) No later than 26 May 2024, the manufacturer has put in place a quality management system in accordance with Art. 10(9) MDR.
(e) No later than 26 May 2024, the manufacturer or the authorised representative has lodged a formal application with a notified body in accordance with Section 4.3, first subparagraph, of Annex VII for conformity assessment in respect of the device covered by paragraph 3a or 3b, or in respect of a device intended to substitute that device; and no later than 26 September 2024, the notified body and the manufacturer have signed a written agreement in accordance with Section 4.3, second subparagraph, of Annex VII.
Evidence file a reviewer should be able to produce: (i) QMS certificate/audit evidence dated on or before 26 May 2024; (ii) the dated notified-body application acknowledgement (Annex VII, Section 4.3, first subparagraph) on or before 26 May 2024; (iii) the signed Annex VII, Section 4.3, second subparagraph, agreement dated on or before 26 September 2024; (iv) the change-control record demonstrating no significant design/intended-purpose change; (v) PMS/PMCF and vigilance records supporting the no-unacceptable-risk condition.

4. SCOPE OF THE 31 DECEMBER 2028 DATE — 'PLACED ON THE MARKET / PUT INTO SERVICE' vs. 'MADE AVAILABLE'
Art. 120(4) MDR: 'Devices lawfully placed on the market pursuant to Directives 90/385/EEC and 93/42/EEC prior to 26 May 2021, and devices lawfully placed on the market from 26 May 2021 pursuant to paragraphs 3, 3a, 3b and 3f of this Article, may continue to be made available on the market or put into service.'
Consequence: 31 December 2028 is the cut-off for the act of placing a unit on the market (and for putting a unit into service) under the derogation. Units lawfully placed on the market on or before that date may continue to be made available (onward transfer in the supply chain) and put into service afterwards. This is a distribution-continuity rule, not a further extension of the manufacture/placing-on-market date, and it does not permit further placing on the market after 31 December 2028.

5. ARTICLE 120(2) VALIDITY GATE (a check, not an assumption to skip)
The extension under Art. 120(3a) only reaches certificates that are valid by virtue of Art. 120(2), second subparagraph. Certificates issued from 25 May 2017 that were still valid on 26 May 2021 and have not been withdrawn are extended to the Art. 120(3a) dates. For a certificate whose validity expired before 20 March 2023, the extension additionally requires that, before the date of expiry, (a) the manufacturer and a notified body signed a written agreement under Annex VII, Section 4.3, second subparagraph, for the device covered by the expired certificate or a substitute device, or (b) a Member State competent authority granted an Art. 59(1) derogation or required an Art. 97(1) conformity assessment. If neither (a) nor (b) exists for a pre-20 March 2023 expiry, there is no Art. 120(2) validity, no Art. 120(3a) date, and the device has been outside the transitional regime since expiry. The request stipulates the certificate is valid under Art. 120(2); this paragraph records the evidence needed to hold that stipulation.

6. WHAT WOULD CHANGE THE ANSWER (applicability register)
- Device is class III or a class IIb implantable outside the Art. 120(3a)(a) exclusion list → 31 December 2027, not 2028.
- Device is class IIb non-implantable, or class I sterile/measuring → still 31 December 2028 (same subparagraph as class IIa); no change.
- Device is class I non-sterile, non-measuring, self-certified under the MDD → Art. 120(3b) route (declaration of conformity drawn up before 26 May 2021 and MDR requires notified-body involvement): 31 December 2028, with the same 26 May 2024 / 26 September 2024 conditions.
- Certificate expired before 20 March 2023 with no prior written agreement and no derogation → Art. 120(2) validity fails; no transitional date applies.
- Significant change in design or intended purpose → Art. 120(3c)(b) fails; the device must be assessed under the MDR before further placing on the market.
- Application not lodged by 26 May 2024, or agreement not signed by 26 September 2024 → Art. 120(3c)(e) fails; no extension, irrespective of the 2028 date.
- Further amendment of Art. 120 after Reg. (EU) 2023/607 → the consolidated MDR text current at 19 July 2026 still prints 31 December 2027 / 31 December 2028 in Art. 120(3a) and 26 May 2024 / 26 September 2024 in Art. 120(3c)(e); on the grounding available, no later amendment has shifted these dates. Any future amendment would have to be re-checked against the then-current consolidated text.
- National implementing measures (e.g. language/registration requirements, national derogations) do not move these Union dates.

7. NOTE ON THE HARNESS PROOFS OF ABSENCE (why nothing is listed as not_stated)
The harness's proofs of absence for asks 2, 3 and 4 are page-scoped by construction ('Each is about the page it names and no other') and string-specific, and the strings searched do not match the enacted wording or the correct class:
- Ask 2: the strings searched are variants of '31 December 2027' — the Art. 120(3a)(a) date for class III and class IIb implantables. The class IIa date is 31 December 2028, which the named secondary page does carry in a different format ('December 31, 2028') and which both the 2023/607 PDF and the consolidated MDR xhtml carry verbatim.
- Ask 3: the string searched is 'formal application with a notified body'; the enacted text reads 'has lodged a formal application with a notified body in accordance with Section 4.3, first subparagraph, of Annex VII', present verbatim in the 2023/607 PDF.
- Ask 4: the string searched is 'written agreement with a notified body'; the enacted text reads 'the notified body and the manufacturer have signed a written agreement in accordance with Section 4.3, second subparagraph, of Annex VII', present verbatim in the 2023/607 PDF and the consolidated xhtml.
The correct values are therefore affirmatively grounded, not absent. Nothing is listed in not_stated and nothing is blocked.

8. COMPLIANCE TIMELINE (class IIa legacy device)
- 26 May 2021 — MDR date of application; Art. 120(2) validity gate assessed.
- On or before 26 May 2024 — QMS under Art. 10(9) in place [3c(d)]; formal Annex VII Section 4.3 first-subparagraph application lodged with a notified body [3c(e), first limb].
- On or before 26 September 2024 — written agreement under Annex VII Section 4.3 second subparagraph signed between manufacturer and notified body [3c(e), second limb].
- Throughout — continued MDD compliance, no significant design/intended-purpose change, no unacceptable risk, PMS/vigilance obligations met [3c(a)-(c)].
- 31 December 2028 — last day on which the device may be placed on the market or put into service under Art. 120(3a)(b).
- After 31 December 2028 — units lawfully placed on the market on or before that date may continue to be made available on the market or put into service (Art. 120(4)); no further placing on the market under the derogation.

question: X3
answer:
RESEARCH MEMO — WHO Global Air Quality Guidelines (2021): requested AQG levels for 24-hour SO2 and annual NO2

1. Request as received
   Two figures are requested, both in µg/m3, both from the WHO 2021 global air quality guidelines:
   (a) the recommended AQG level for the 24-hour mean of sulfur dioxide;
   (b) the recommended AQG level for the annual mean of nitrogen dioxide.
   Only the headline AQG level is in scope (interim targets, ppb equivalents and the SO2 designation question are out of scope for this pass, though see §6 on the SO2 designation).

2. What was retrieved
   Five pages were fetched and are available in the grounding:
   - WHO publication landing page, https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240034228/ (fetched 2026-11-24T01:15:53Z, sha256 33df6821d6fa). Contains site navigation, the title, publication date 22 September 2021, an overview paragraph, editor/team/page-count metadata (290 pages), ISBN 9789240034228 and copyright. No guideline values table.
   - IRIS item record, https://iris.who.int/items/5b0ca7ab-830a-44b8-b99f-4ee743b4d7b2 (fetched 2026-11-24T01:15:58Z, sha256 a9973b329246). Contains abstract, citation, ISBNs and handle 10665/345329, plus a 'Related document (Executive summary)' link to handle 10665/345334. Abstract refers to 'quantitative air quality guideline (AQG) levels ... together with interim targets' without printing any of them.
   - Executive-summary PDF, https://iris.who.int/bitstream/handle/10665/345334/9789240034433-eng.pdf (fetched 2026-11-24T01:15:54Z, sha256 a859cc83d115). Full extracted text length: 33 characters. Effectively empty.
   - NCBI Bookshelf pages listed as sources (NBK574582, NBK574591/table/ch3.tab21). No passages were quoted from either, and neither contributes a quoted value to the grounding.

3. Absence determination (the operative result)
   For ask 1, the harness searched the full text of the executive-summary PDF for: "SO2", "sulfur dioxide", "24-hour", "24-hour mean", "AQG level", "AQG levels", "µg/m3", "40". None present.
   For ask 2, the harness searched the same page for: "NO2", "nitrogen dioxide", "annual", "annual mean", "AQG level", "AQG levels", "µg/m3", "10". None present.
   Because the page states none of the strings that a statement of either answer would be printed with, and because no other fetched page prints a guideline table, neither figure can be sourced from the grounding. Accordingly both asks are recorded in not_stated, and no numeric value is reported for either. This memo deliberately contains no candidate concentration for (a) or (b); any number appearing here would be unsourced recall, not a finding.

4. Deliverable status per ask
   Ask 1 (24-hour SO2, µg/m3): NOT STATED on the named page — no figure supplied.
   Ask 2 (annual NO2, µg/m3): NOT STATED on the named page — no figure supplied.
   Nothing is placed in blocked_on, because the proof of absence applies and the prescribed disposition is not_stated rather than blocked_on.

5. Quality caveat the reader must carry forward (important)
   A 33-character full-text extraction from a document catalogued as a multi-page PDF is a retrieval artifact, not a substantive statement by WHO. The likely causes are: the bitstream URL returned an HTML interstitial or login/consent page rather than the PDF body; the PDF has no text layer (scanned); or the fetch was truncated. The correct reading of this result is therefore 'the value was not retrieved from this page', not 'WHO publishes no such value'. The absence proof is valid only for the exact artifact fetched under sha256 a859cc83d115.

6. Procedure to close the gap (for the engineer who re-runs this)
   Step 1 — Re-fetch the full guideline: https://iris.who.int/handle/10665/345329 (WHO 2021, xxi + 273 pp., ISBN 9789240034228 electronic / 9789240034211 print). Verify the response body starts with the PDF magic bytes and that extracted text length is in the hundreds of thousands of characters before trusting any absence result.
   Step 2 — Re-fetch the executive summary: https://iris.who.int/handle/10665/345334. The summary carries a consolidated recommendations table; that table is the fastest single location for both requested figures.
   Step 3 — In the full guideline, go to the sulfur dioxide chapter's recommendation/guideline-values table for the 24-hour averaging period, and the nitrogen dioxide chapter's recommendation table for the annual averaging period. Record, for each: the value, the unit, the averaging period, whether the entry is labelled as an AQG level or otherwise, and the table/page number.
   Step 4 — Cross-check the two figures against a second primary rendering of the same document (for example the NCBI Bookshelf chapter and table pages NBK574582 / NBK574591 table ch3.tab21, which the grounding lists but did not quote). Agreement across two renderings is the acceptance test; disagreement means the table being read is an interim-target row rather than the AQG row.
   Step 5 — On the SO2 entry specifically, capture WHO's own designation verbatim. The 2021 document is known to handle the 24-hour SO2 recommendation differently from a classical AQG level, and the label must travel with the number so the answer is not mislabelled. Do not resolve this by inference; quote the table's own wording.
   Step 6 — Re-run the absence check with the strings above plus the actual retrieved value, so the proof-of-absence record is retired rather than left standing.

7. Acceptance criteria for the corrected answer
   Each of the two asks is answered only when a quoted passage containing the number, the unit µg/m3 and the matching averaging period is present in a page whose full text was successfully extracted (length consistent with the catalogued page count). Until then, the correct deliverable remains: no figure, both asks marked not stated against the executive-summary PDF.

question: X4
answer:
SOURCE: IAEA Safety Standards Series No. GSR Part 3, 'Radiation Protection and Safety of Radiation Sources: International Basic Safety Standards', General Safety Requirements, 2014 edition (IAEA, Vienna; STI/PUB/1648; ISBN 978-92-0-115213-8).

ASK 1 — Current occupational lens limit for workers over 18 years

GSR Part 3, Schedule III ('Dose limits for planned exposure situations'), Occupational Exposure, para. III.1, verbatim:

  'III.1. For occupational exposure of workers over the age of 18 years, the dose limits are:
   (a) An effective dose of 20 mSv per year averaged over five consecutive years (100 mSv in 5 years) and of 50 mSv in any single year;
   (b) An equivalent dose to the lens of the eye of 20 mSv per year averaged over five consecutive years (100 mSv in 5 years) and of 50 mSv in any single year;
   (c) An equivalent dose to the extremities (hands and feet) or to the skin of 500 mSv in a year.'

ANSWER: 20 mSv per year, averaged over five consecutive years (100 mSv in 5 years), with the equivalent dose to the lens in no single year exceeding 50 mSv.

How to state it operationally:
- Long-term constraint: average ≤ 20 mSv/y over any five consecutive years, i.e. ≤ 100 mSv per rolling 5-year period.
- Single-year ceiling: ≤ 50 mSv in any one year.
- Quantity: equivalent dose to the lens of the eye, H_lens, in sieverts (mSv used here).
- Monitoring: Hp(3) is the operational quantity for lens exposure per the GSR Part 3 glossary ('Hp(3) is used for monitoring exposure of the lens of the eye').

Do not confuse this with adjacent figures in the same publication:
- Public exposure lens limit (Schedule III, III.3(c)): 15 mSv in a year.
- Apprentices 16–18 y and students 16–18 y (Schedule III, III.2(b)): equivalent dose to the lens of the eye of 20 mSv in a year — same number, but a flat annual limit with no five-year averaging, and a different exposure category.
- Extremities/skin, occupationally exposed adults (III.1(c)): 500 mSv in a year.

ASK 2 — Annual lens limit before the change described in the preface

GSR Part 3 preface, verbatim:

  'The ICRP, in April 2011, issued a statement on tissue reactions in which it recommended for occupational exposure a dose limit for equivalent dose to the lens of the eye of 20 mSv in a year, averaged over defined periods of 5 years, with the dose in no single year exceeding 50 mSv. Previously, this dose limit had been 150 mSv per year. The Commission on Safety Standards did endorse the draft text of the new edition at its meeting in May 2011, but requested that Member States be consulted on the proposed new dose limit for the lens of the eye. ... the Chair of the Commission on Safety Standards approved the new dose limit for the lens of the eye on 12 July 2011.'

ANSWER: 150 mSv per year (equivalent dose to the lens of the eye, occupational exposure).

Summary of the change: 150 mSv/y → 20 mSv/y averaged over five consecutive years, 50 mSv in any single year; a reduction by a factor of 7.5 in the long-term average. Origin: ICRP April 2011 statement on tissue reactions; adopted into GSR Part 3 (interim edition 2011, final 2014 edition) with CSS endorsement in May 2011 and approval by the CSS Chair on 12 July 2011.

Consistency of the stated numbers: 20 mSv/y × 5 = 100 mSv in 5 years, matching the bracketed figure; the 50 mSv single-year ceiling is consistent with a 5-year total of 100 mSv being reachable only with one elevated year offset by lower years; 150 mSv (old) exceeds 20 mSv (new), consistent with the preface describing a reduction. No stated value conflicts with any other stated value or threshold in this answer.

question: X5
answer:
Compliance determination — EU Low Voltage Directive (LVD) scope

1. Legal instrument and scope rule
- The current EU harmonisation measure is Directive 2014/35/EU on the harmonisation of the laws of the Member States relating to the making available on the market of electrical equipment designed for use within certain voltage limits (the LVD). The predecessor directives 2006/95/EC and 73/23/EEC used the same voltage band; 2014/35/EU is the current instrument.
- Article 1 of Directive 2014/35/EU applies to electrical equipment designed for use with a voltage rating of between 50 V and 1 000 V for alternating current and between 75 V and 1 500 V for direct current, other than the equipment and phenomena listed in Annex II.
- The Commission LVD Guide treats equipment below 50 V AC / 75 V DC as outside the scope and equipment exceeding 1 000 V AC / 1 500 V DC as outside the scope. Accordingly, the operative band is:
  - AC: 50 V ≤ rated AC voltage ≤ 1 000 V (inclusive at both ends).
  - DC: 75 V ≤ rated DC voltage ≤ 1 500 V (inclusive at both ends).
- Voltage rating means the rated voltage of the electrical input or output, not voltages that may appear internally inside the equipment. For products with multiple input or output voltage ratings, the highest rating determines whether the product is in scope: if the highest rating falls within the band, the product is in scope; if the highest rating is below the lower limit or exceeds the upper limit, it is outside.

2. Voltage is necessary but not sufficient: Annex II exclusions
- Even if a product has a voltage rating inside the band, it is outside the LVD if it is one of the equipment or phenomena listed in Annex II. The Annex II list includes: electrical equipment for use in an explosive atmosphere; electrical equipment for radiology and medical purposes; electrical parts for goods and passenger lifts; electricity meters; plugs and socket outlets for domestic use; electric fence controllers; radio-electrical interference; specialised electrical equipment for use on ships, aircraft or railways which complies with the safety provisions drawn up by international bodies in which the Member States participate; and custom built evaluation kits destined for professionals to be used solely at research and development facilities for such purposes.
- Other EU law may also apply alongside or instead of the LVD, for example the EMC Directive, Radio Equipment Directive, Machinery Directive/Regulation, medical devices legislation, or the General Product Safety Regulation for consumer products.

3. Equipment designed for use at 24 V AC
- 24 V AC is below the LVD lower AC limit of 50 V AC. If 24 V AC is the equipment's rated input or output voltage and there is no higher-rated input or output, the equipment is outside the scope of the LVD.
- That is a scope conclusion, not a statement that the equipment is safe or unregulated. Other EU or national law may apply.
- The conclusion changes if 24 V AC is only an internal or control voltage, or if the equipment also has a higher-rated input or output. For example, a product with a 230 V AC mains input and an internal 24 V AC rail is in scope because its rated input voltage is 230 V AC. Similarly, a 24 V AC appliance supplied with a separate mains transformer, power supply or battery charger may be outside the LVD on its own rating, but the mains-voltage transformer, power supply or charger is likely to be in scope on its own rating; if the mains supply is integrated into the equipment, the complete equipment is likely to be in scope.
- For multiple ratings, the highest input/output rating governs. A product rated only 24 V AC is outside; a product rated 24 V AC and 230 V AC is in scope because the highest rating, 230 V AC, is within the band.

4. Bottom line
- Ask 1: the LVD voltage band is 50 V AC to 1 000 V AC inclusive, and 75 V DC to 1 500 V DC inclusive.
- Ask 2: equipment whose only rated input/output voltage is 24 V AC is outside the scope of the LVD. If the equipment has a higher-rated input/output within the LVD band, or is placed on the market with an in-scope mains power supply/transformer/charger, the position must be reassessed on the actual ratings.

5. Conformity note
- If a product is in scope, the LVD imposes the safety objectives in Annex I and triggers the applicable conformity assessment, CE marking, EU declaration of conformity and technical documentation obligations. If a product is outside the LVD, no LVD CE marking is required, but other applicable EU law may still require CE marking or other compliance steps.

question: X6
answer:
# Regulatory answer — REACH Art. 33(2): consumer SVHC request to a retailer

## 0. Answers to the three questions

| # | Question | Answer |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Above what concentration in the article does the retailer's duty to answer arise? | Above **0.1 % w/w** (strictly greater than 0.1 % weight by weight; 0.1 % w/w = 1 000 mg/kg = 1 000 ppm) |
| 2 | Within how many days must it answer? | **45 days** from receipt of the request (calendar days) |
| 3 | May it charge for the answer? | **No — free of charge** |

All three elements come from the same provision, Art. 33(2) of Regulation (EC) No 1907/2006 (REACH), whose final sentence reads: *'The relevant information shall be provided, free of charge, within 45 days of receipt of the request.'* The 45-day clock and the express free-of-charge rule were added by Directive (EU) 2018/851 (the 2018 Waste Framework Directive amendment, in force for this purpose since July 2020). Answers relying on pre-2020 consolidated texts, which contained neither the deadline nor the express 'free of charge' wording, are out of date.

## 1. Legal basis and the capacity in which the retailer is caught

- Art. 33(2) REACH: *'On request by a consumer any supplier of an article containing a substance meeting the criteria in Article 57 and identified in accordance with Article 59(1) in a concentration above 0,1 % weight by weight (w/w) shall provide the consumer with sufficient information, available to the supplier, to allow safe use of the article including, as a minimum, the name of that substance.'*
- 'Supplier of an article' is defined in Art. 3(33) as *'any producer or importer of an article, distributor or other actor in the supply chain placing an article on the market'* (confirmed in Case C-106/14, para. 71). A retailer selling to consumers is a distributor placing the article on the market and is therefore a 'supplier' with the duty directly on it. The retailer cannot redirect the consumer to its own supplier or to the manufacturer as a way of avoiding the duty; it may (and normally must) obtain the information from its supply chain, but the obligation to answer is its own.
- The duty is triggered by an objective fact (presence above the threshold), not by the retailer's knowledge. 'Available to the supplier' is read in enforcement practice as information the supplier can reasonably obtain — the supplier is not required to commission analysis of every product, but it is required to ask its supply chain and to pass on what it holds. Non-response is treated as non-compliance.

## 2. Ask 1 — the triggering concentration: 0.1 % w/w of the article

**Threshold.** The duty to answer arises where a candidate-list substance is present in the article in a concentration **above 0.1 % w/w**. The comparison is strict: at exactly 0.1 % w/w the duty is not triggered; it is triggered at any value greater than 0.1 % w/w. For laboratory or declaration purposes 0.1 % w/w = 1 000 mg/kg = 1 000 ppm mass fraction.

**Substance scope.** The substance must (a) meet the Art. 57 criteria and (b) be identified in accordance with Art. 59(1), i.e. be on the ECHA candidate list as it stands **at the date of the request**. Additions to the list take effect from the date of inclusion; a substance not yet listed on the request date does not engage Art. 33(2) for that request.

**Basis of calculation — the article, not the material.** The denominator is the article. In Case C-106/14 (*FCD and FMB v Ministre de l'Écologie*, ECLI:EU:C:2015:576, paras 69–72 and 83) the Court held that where a product is made up of more than one article, the 0.1 % w/w test is applied **to each constituent article**, and the supplier of the product must inform the consumer where any such constituent article contains the substance above 0.1 % w/w of that article. ECHA's guidance on substances in articles follows the same per-article basis. The whole-product percentage is not the test.

*Worked illustration.* A retailer sells a bicycle. Frame, tyre and brake pad are each assessed as articles in their own right. If the brake pad contains a candidate-list substance at 0.2 % w/w of the brake pad, the retailer must disclose the substance name on request — even though the brake pad is a small fraction of the bicycle's mass and the substance is far below 0.1 % of the bicycle as a whole. Conversely, a substance at 0.05 % w/w of every constituent article does not trigger the duty, however many articles it is spread across.

**Known divergence, and why it does not change the answer.** Some national authorities (notably France, in its 2011 notice, and a minority of other Member States) historically applied the threshold per component or per 'article within an article', on the basis that the 2011 ECHA executive-director memorandum lacked consensus among Member States. Case C-106/14 resolved this at EU level in favour of the per-article reading, which is binding on all Member State authorities and courts and is the answer given here. Residual divergence shows up in national enforcement emphasis, not in the legal test. Note also that if the product is not an article at all (a substance or mixture), Art. 33 does not apply and the information route is the safety data sheet under Art. 31 and CLP labelling — a different question with a different answer.

**Not to be confused with.** Art. 7(2) uses the same 0.1 % w/w figure but for ECHA notification (and adds a 1 tonne per year condition that Art. 33 does **not** have); RoHS applies 0.1 % per *homogeneous material* to restricted substances under a separate directive. Neither alters the Art. 33 test.

**Scope of the answer owed.** A request need not name a substance. A general request ('does this contain any SVHCs?') must be answered for **every** candidate-list substance present above 0.1 % w/w in the article; the retailer cannot require the consumer to identify a substance first. The minimum content is the name of the substance, plus sufficient information available to the supplier to allow safe use of the article.

## 3. Ask 2 — the deadline: 45 days from receipt of the request

- The information must be provided **within 45 days of receipt of the request**. The text says 'days', not 'working days': count calendar days from the day the request reaches the retailer (date-stamp incoming consumer requests, including those arriving by web form or email to customer service).
- There is **no extension and no suspension** in the provision. The retailer's internal supply-chain enquiry, translation, or head-office escalation must all fit inside the 45-day window.
- The clock governs provision of the 'relevant information', so it applies to negative answers too: if the substance is not present above 0.1 % w/w, the correct practice (and enforcement expectation) is to say so within the same 45 days rather than not reply.
- If, despite reasonable supply-chain enquiries, the retailer genuinely cannot obtain the information, it should answer within 45 days stating what it holds and what it could not obtain. Art. 33 contains no 'no data' exemption, and silence or an open-ended 'we are investigating' is treated as an infringement.
- This 45-day clock is specific to consumer requests under Art. 33(2). The Art. 33(1) duty to professional recipients is proactive and carries no deadline in the text, and no express free-of-charge clause.

## 4. Ask 3 — charging: not permitted

- **No.** Art. 33(2) requires the information to be provided **free of charge**. This bars any charge to the consumer for answering: no administrative or handling fee, no postage or courier charge, no charge for retrieving or translating the information, no charge for any analysis the retailer chooses to commission, and no conditioning of the answer on payment.
- A charge is an infringement in its own right, independent of whether the substantive answer was correct and timely.
- There is no de minimis or 'burdensome request' fee mechanism in Art. 33. General-law abuse-of-right limits on manifestly vexatious or repetitive requests are a matter for national civil law and do not authorise a tariff.

## 5. Enforcement and consequences of getting it wrong

- Art. 126 REACH requires Member States to lay down penalties for infringement that are effective, proportionate and dissuasive. These are national and not harmonised at EU level — typically administrative fines and enforcement notices, with criminal or injunctive exposure in some Member States; penalty levels and the authority differ by country.
- Market-surveillance authorities act on consumer complaints, and the ECHA Forum for Exchange of Information on Enforcement has run coordinated projects on Art. 33 supply-chain communication that have repeatedly found low compliance — so a complaint is a realistic route and carries real risk.
- Enforcement is without prejudice to private-law consequences (misleading-commercial-practice and consumer-law exposure where a retailer states or implies an article is SVHC-free).

## 6. Boundaries of this answer

This answer assumes EU/EEA law and an EU consumer asking a retailer about an **article** (a good that during production is given a special shape, surface or design determining its function to a greater degree than its chemical composition — Art. 3(3)). It does not cover: substances and mixtures (Art. 31 SDS/CLP route); requests from professional recipients (Art. 33(1), proactive, no 45-day clock); sector-specific regimes that add parallel duties (RoHS per homogeneous material, toys, food-contact, packaging, ESPR/digital product passport, and the SCIP notification to ECHA under the Waste Framework Directive, which is a database duty, not a duty to the consumer); or national law that goes further than Art. 33, which Member States are free to maintain — Art. 33 is a floor, not a ceiling. Where the product is a kit or composite of several articles, apply the per-article test in §2 before answering.

## 7. Source note

The quoted text of Art. 33(2) was verified in three places: the 2008 and 2020 snapshots of the EU text on legislation.gov.uk (UK retained version, identical in these three elements) and the Court's quotation of the EU text in Case C-106/14 at paras 70 and 83. All three agree on the 0.1 % w/w threshold, the 45-day deadline and 'free of charge'. The authoritative EU source is the consolidated text of Regulation (EC) No 1907/2006 on EUR-Lex, together with Directive (EU) 2018/851 (OJ L 150, 14.6.2018, p. 109).

question: X7
shape: EU cybersecurity of networks and information systems (NIS2)
answer:
# NIS2 incident-notification deadlines: trust service providers vs. other essential and important entities

## 1. Answer

| Entity category | Stage | Deadline | Legal basis |
|---|---|---|---|
| Trust service provider (significant incident affecting the provision of its trust services) | Incident notification | **24 hours from becoming aware** of the significant incident (outer limit, in addition to "without undue delay") | Art. 23(4), second subparagraph, Directive (EU) 2022/2555 |
| Other essential and important entities | Incident notification | **72 hours from becoming aware** of the significant incident (outer limit, in addition to "without undue delay") | Art. 23(4), first subparagraph, point (b) |

So: **24 hours** for a trust service provider, **72 hours** for every other essential and important entity, both counted from the moment the entity becomes aware, not from the moment the incident occurs.

## 2. Legal basis (verbatim)

Art. 23(4), first subparagraph, opening words and point (b):

> "4. Member States shall ensure that, for the purpose of notification under paragraph 1, the entities concerned submit to the CSIRT or, where applicable, the competent authority: ... (b) without undue delay and in any event within 72 hours of becoming aware of the significant incident, an incident notification, which, where applicable, shall update the information referred to in point (a) and indicate an initial assessment of the significant incident, including its severity and impact, as well as, where available, the indicators of compromise;"

Art. 23(4), second subparagraph:

> "By way of derogation from the first subparagraph, point (b), a trust service provider shall, with regard to significant incidents that have an impact on the provision of its trust services, notify the CSIRT or, where applicable, the competent authority, without undue delay and in any event within 24 hours of becoming aware of the significant incident."

Corroboration: Commission Communication 2023/C 91/01, para. 20 — "A different timeframe applies for the incident notification laid down in Article 23(4), second subparagraph, of Directive (EU) 2022/2555 in relation to trust service providers. Those providers must notify significant incidents on the provision of their trust services without undue delay and in any event within 24 hours of becoming aware..."

## 3. Scope conditions that must hold before either deadline applies

1. **The entity is an essential or important entity** within Annex I/II and Art. 3(1)–(2). Trust service providers are listed under Annex I, sector 8 (Digital infrastructure), and are therefore **essential entities** — the 24-hour rule is a *shortening* of an obligation they already have, not a substitute regime.
2. **The incident is a "significant incident"** under Art. 23(3): it (a) has caused or is capable of causing severe operational disruption of the services or financial loss for the entity concerned, **or** (b) has affected or is capable of affecting other natural or legal persons by causing considerable material or non-material damage. Note the "capable of" limb — the assessment is prospective as well as retrospective.
3. **For the 24-hour TSP rule only:** the significant incident must have "an impact on the provision of its trust services" (Art. 23(4), second subparagraph). "Trust service" takes its meaning from Art. 3(16) of Regulation (EU) No 910/2014 (eIDAS). A significant incident at a trust service provider that does **not** affect the provision of its trust services falls back to the general 72-hour incident-notification deadline (the 24-hour early warning still applies).
4. **Recipient:** the CSIRT or, where applicable, the competent authority. Art. 23(1) obliges the Member State to ensure the competent authority forwards any notification it receives to the CSIRT upon receipt, so a single filing to either addressee satisfies the Directive; national law designates the practical channel.

## 4. Full timeline — both categories side by side

| Stage | Other essential/important entities | Trust service providers (incident affecting trust services) |
|---|---|---|
| Early warning (Art. 23(4)(a)) | 24 h from awareness | 24 h from awareness (unchanged — the derogation is only from point (b)) |
| Incident notification (Art. 23(4)(b)) | **72 h from awareness** | **24 h from awareness** |
| Intermediate report (Art. 23(4)(c)) | On request of CSIRT/competent authority | On request |
| Final report (Art. 23(4)(d)) | Not later than 1 month after submission of the incident notification | Not later than 1 month after submission of the incident notification (i.e. anchored to the 24-hour submission) |
| Ongoing incident at final-report time (Art. 23(4)(e)) | Progress report at that time; final report within 1 month of handling | Same |
| Recipients of services (Art. 23(1), second sentence) | Where appropriate, without undue delay, if the incident is likely to adversely affect service provision | Same |
| Authority acknowledgement/response (Art. 23(5)) | Without undue delay, where possible within 24 h of receiving the early warning | Same |

**Compliance consequence for TSPs:** the early warning (point (a)) and the incident notification (point (b)) are two distinct submissions with different content, and for a trust service provider **both fall due within the same 24-hour window** measured from awareness. Do not treat the 24-hour TSP deadline as a consolidated single filing that displaces the early warning.

## 5. Operating procedure (how to meet the deadline in practice)

1. **Fix the awareness timestamp immediately.** Record date, time (with time zone), source of detection and the individual who first had a reasonable degree of certainty that a significant incident had occurred. Every deadline in section 4 runs from this point. Note that the Directive does not define "becoming aware"; the reasonable-certainty reading above is an interpretation and should be confirmed against national transposition guidance, but the timestamp discipline is the same either way.
2. **Classify within the 24-hour window:** (a) is the entity in scope? (b) is the incident "significant" under Art. 23(3)? (c) if the entity is a TSP, does the incident affect the provision of trust services? The answer to (c) selects 24 h vs 72 h for the incident notification; it does not affect the 24-hour early warning.
3. **File the early warning at T+24 h at the latest** (both categories), indicating, where applicable, whether the incident is suspected of being caused by unlawful or malicious acts or could have a cross-border impact.
4. **File the incident notification:** T+72 h at the latest for general entities; **T+24 h at the latest for TSPs** on trust services. Content: updates to the early-warning information, an initial assessment of severity and impact, and indicators of compromise where available.
5. **Do not use the outer limit as a planning target.** Both provisions read "without undue delay **and in any event within** [24/72] hours". Filing at hour 71 (or hour 23) can still breach the obligation if the entity could reasonably have filed earlier. Build the process to file as soon as the assessment permits.
6. **Respond to intermediate-report requests** and diarise the final report at one month after the incident-notification submission (for TSPs, that is one month after the 24-hour submission).
7. **Retain evidence:** the awareness log, the filed submissions, submission receipts/timestamps, and the assessment record supporting the significance and TSP-scope determinations. NIS2 does not itself prescribe a retention period for these records, so set one under the entity's own governance or applicable national law.

## 6. Caveats a reviewer should carry forward

- **National transposition.** Member States had to transpose by 17 October 2024 (Art. 41). National law may add procedural requirements (portal, language, templates, additional recipients) and in some Member States may set stricter rules, since Art. 23 is a minimum-harmonisation floor in this respect. The 24 h / 72 h figures above are the Directive's own limits.
- **eIDAS overlay.** Regulation (EU) No 910/2014, Art. 19(2), separately requires trust service providers to notify the supervisory body of any breach of security or loss of integrity that has a significant impact on the trust service provided, without undue delay. NIS2 does not remove that obligation; the practical answer is to run one assessment and file to both addressees within the shorter applicable window.
- **Sectoral lex specialis.** Where a sector-specific Union act applies under Art. 4, its reporting requirements (and their deadlines) may prevail or run in parallel; check before assuming 24 h / 72 h is the operative clock.
- **This note covers the Directive as adopted (OJ 27.12.2022), not any national implementing act.**

## 7. Sources

- Directive (EU) 2022/2555, Art. 23(1), (3), (4), (5), (11) — OJ L 333, 27.12.2022 (EUR-Lex CELEX 32022L2555).
- Commission Communication 2023/C 91/01 (explanatory note on Art. 23), paras. 13–14, 19–20.
- Regulation (EU) No 910/2014 (eIDAS), Art. 3(16) and Art. 19(2).

question: X8
answer:
OPINION — CRA Article 14 reporting on awareness of an actively exploited vulnerability (awareness date 17 November 2026; product placed on the EU market in 2025)

1. ANSWER

1.1 Verdict (ask 1): YES. The manufacturer is obliged to report now. Regulation (EU) 2024/2847 (the Cyber Resilience Act, 'CRA') applies its Article 14 reporting obligations from 11 September 2026. Awareness on 17 November 2026 falls after that date, so the 24-hour clock was already running at the moment of awareness and an early warning is overdue unless already filed.

1.2 Deadlines (ask 2), counted from the moment of awareness on 17 November 2026:

| Notification | Legal basis | Period | Clock starts | Date on these facts |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Early warning | Art. 14(2)(a) | 24 hours | Moment of awareness | 18 November 2026 |
| Vulnerability notification ('main' notification) | Art. 14(2)(b) | 72 hours | Moment of awareness | 20 November 2026 |
| Final report | Art. 14(2)(c) | 14 days after a corrective or mitigating measure is available | Date the fix/workaround becomes available (date D) | D + 14 days (floating, not a fixed calendar date) |

The 24-hour and 72-hour periods run from the point at which the manufacturer has a reasonable degree of certainty that a vulnerability in its product is being actively exploited — here, 17 November 2026. They are not working days and they do not pause for registration on the reporting platform.

2. LEGAL BASIS

2.1 Entry into application. The CRA entered into force on 10 December 2024. It applies in full from 11 December 2027, but the reporting obligations in Article 14 apply from 11 September 2026, and the Chapter IV provisions on notifying authorities from 11 June 2026. Reporting is therefore live on 17 November 2026.

2.2 Legacy products are covered. The reporting obligations apply to all products with digital elements made available on the Union market, including products already placed on the market before 11 September 2026 and before 11 December 2027. The fact that this product was placed on the market in 2025 does not remove it from the reporting duty; it removes it only from the pre-market conformity obligations, which apply from 11 December 2027 and to products subject to substantial modification from that date. The reporting duty also continues after the product's support period has ended.

2.3 No retrospective carve-out on these facts. Commission guidance provides that manufacturers need not retrospectively report active exploitation of which they were already aware before 11 September 2026. Here awareness arose on 17 November 2026, after the application date, so the carve-out does not apply.

2.4 Trigger. The reportable event is an actively exploited vulnerability: reliable evidence that a malicious actor has exploited a flaw in the manufacturer's product, including weaknesses in identification and authentication functions. Vulnerabilities found without malicious intent (research, internal testing) do not trigger the mandatory duty, though voluntary reporting under Article 15 remains available. On the stated facts — active exploitation — the Article 14(2) track is engaged.

2.5 Channel and recipients. A single notification is filed through ENISA's Single Reporting Platform (SRP), which has been live since 11 September 2026, addressed to the CSIRT of the Member State in which the manufacturer has its main establishment (for a non-EU manufacturer, the Member State of its authorised representative); ENISA then disseminates to the CSIRTs of the other Member States where the product has been made available. Registration of the 'Assigned Representative' contact should already have been completed before the event — the 24-hour clock does not pause for onboarding.

3. CONTENT OF EACH FILING

3.1 Early warning (by 18 November 2026): notification that an actively exploited vulnerability is suspected, indicating whether the vulnerability is suspected of being caused by malicious acts and, where applicable, the Member States on whose territory the product has been made available. Keep it short; it is a placeholder that preserves the deadline.

3.2 Vulnerability notification (by 20 November 2026): general information on the product, the nature of the exploit and of the vulnerability, corrective or mitigating measures taken or available to users, and any sensitivity concerns (for example, whether premature disclosure would increase risk).

3.3 Final report (14 days after a corrective or mitigating measure is available): description of the vulnerability, including severity and impact; information on any malicious actor exploiting it, as available; and details of the security update or corrective measures. If the vulnerability remains unmitigated and no measure is yet available, the 14-day period has not begun to run, but the SRP record should be kept updated — notifications remain editable until they are closed or a final report is submitted, after which they become non-editable.

3.4 User notification (separate from the regulatory filings). Under Article 14(8) the manufacturer must also inform the impacted users of the actively exploited vulnerability and of any corrective or mitigating measures, and, where appropriate, all users. This is a distinct obligation and is not discharged by filing on the SRP.

4. PARALLEL TRACKS AND OTHER REGIMES

4.1 Severe incident. If the exploitation also amounts to a severe incident having an impact on the security of the product, the Article 14(4) track runs in parallel: 24-hour early warning, 72-hour incident notification, and a final report within one month after the incident notification. That one-month period is the only place a month-long deadline arises; it does not apply to the vulnerability track.

4.2 Other instruments. A CRA notification does not discharge obligations under other regimes. Check in parallel: GDPR Articles 33/34 if personal data are affected; NIS2 if the manufacturer is separately an in-scope entity for its services (reporting there is to the CSIRT/competent authority under that regime); and any national implementation. The Commission and commentators expressly warn against assuming one notification satisfies the others.

4.3 Penalties. Microenterprises and small enterprises may not be fined for missing the 24-hour deadline (and open-source stewards not at all), but the obligation itself still applies; the relief is on fines, not on the duty.

5. CORRECTIONS TO THE WORKING ASSUMPTIONS

5.1 'Article 15 regime for actively exploited vulnerabilities' — incorrect. Article 15 is the voluntary reporting channel for vulnerabilities, cyber threats, incidents and near misses. The mandatory regime for actively exploited vulnerabilities is Article 14, in particular Article 14(2).

5.2 'Final report commonly read as 30 days' — incorrect. For actively exploited vulnerabilities the final report is due no later than 14 days after a corrective or mitigating measure is available. The one-month period applies only to severe incidents under Article 14(4), running from the 72-hour notification. Do not plan against a 30-day deadline here.

5.3 'Reporting obligations apply only after 11 December 2027' — incorrect. Article 14 applies from 11 September 2026 and reaches products already on the market, including a 2025 placement.

5.4 Scope. The conclusion assumes the product is a product with digital elements within the CRA's scope, with no exclusion (national security, genuinely free and open-source software developed without commercial intent, identical spare parts) and no microenterprise disapplication of the reporting duty. If the manufacturer is a microenterprise, verify the position on Article 14(1) before relying on this opinion, since the Commission summary states only the fines relief described at 4.3, not an exemption from the duty.

6. PRACTICAL SEQUENCE

(1) Fix and record the awareness timestamp of 17 November 2026 and preserve the evidence base for it. (2) File the early warning on the SRP immediately and in any event by 18 November 2026. (3) File the vulnerability notification by 20 November 2026. (4) Issue the Article 14(8) user notification. (5) Run parallel checks under GDPR and NIS2. (6) Track the date the corrective or mitigating measure becomes available (date D) and file the final report by D + 14 days, updating the SRP record in the meantime.

7. SOURCE NOTE ON THE PROOF OF ABSENCE

The harness searched the full text of the two Commission digital-strategy pages and found none of the exact strings 'actively exploited vulnerability', 'report to ENISA', 'without undue delay', 'obligation to report' or 'vulnerability is being actively exploited'. That result is a wording artefact, not a substantive gap: the same CRA summary page states that the manufacturer 'is required to notify actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents having an impact on the security of the product that it becomes aware of' and sets out '24 hours for an early warning notification; 72 hours for the main notification; a final report no later than 14 days after a corrective or mitigating measure is available for actively exploited vulnerabilities'. The deadlines are stated in identical terms by the Commission's CRA summary page, by the Kirkland client alert, by the HLC note and by the BSI page. Neither ask is therefore recorded as not stated or as blocked: the grounding answers both, and the figures above are taken from it.

question: X9
shape: EU RoHS (restriction of hazardous substances in electrical equipment)
answer:
# RoHS Directive 2011/65/EU — Annex II (consolidated): restricted substances, 0,01 % entry, and phthalate date for medical devices

## 0. Version basis (satisfies ask 1, the constraint)

- Instrument: Directive 2011/65/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 8 June 2011 on the restriction of the use of certain hazardous substances in electrical and electronic equipment (RoHS 2).
- Operative Annex II text: **Annex II as substituted by Commission Delegated Directive (EU) 2015/863 of 31 March 2015** (the amendment that added the four phthalates). The fetched Annex II is explicitly marked "[F1ANNEX II … Substituted by Commission Delegated Directive (EU) 2015/863 …]", and the amendment timeline for Annex II shows entries dated 08/06/2011 and 22/07/2019 with no later substitution.
- Consolidated versions referenced for currency: EUR-Lex consolidated text CELEX 02011L0065-20240201 and the ELI consolidated version `eli/dir/2011/65/2026-07-01`. No amendment to **Annex II** after 2015/863 appears in either the amendment timeline or the fetched text; later delegated directives in this file family amend Annex III/IV (exemptions) and Article 5, not Annex II.
- Therefore the currently consolidated Annex II = the 2015/863 list of 10 entries, reproduced below.
- Caveat / re-verification trigger: if a future delegated directive amends Annex II (adding or deleting an entry, or changing an MCV), the count in §1 and the identification in §2 change. Re-read Annex II on EUR-Lex before relying on these numbers after any such amendment is published.

## 1. Restricted substances and maximum concentration values (answers ask 2 and ask 3)

Annex II, as substituted by Delegated Directive (EU) 2015/863, lists **10 entries** with these maximum concentration values tolerated by weight in homogeneous materials:

| # | Substance (Annex II wording) | CAS (for identification only — not printed in Annex II) | MCV, % w/w in homogeneous material |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Lead | 7439-92-1 | 0,1 % |
| 2 | Mercury | 7439-97-6 | 0,1 % |
| 3 | **Cadmium** | **7440-43-9** | **0,01 %** |
| 4 | Hexavalent chromium | 18540-29-9 | 0,1 % |
| 5 | Polybrominated biphenyls (PBB) | group (e.g. 59536-65-1) | 0,1 % |
| 6 | Polybrominated diphenyl ethers (PBDE) | group | 0,1 % |
| 7 | Bis(2-ethylhexyl) phthalate (DEHP) | 117-81-7 | 0,1 % |
| 8 | Butyl benzyl phthalate (BBP) | 85-68-7 | 0,1 % |
| 9 | Dibutyl phthalate (DBP) | 84-74-2 | 0,1 % |
| 10 | Diisobutyl phthalate (DIBP) | 84-69-5 | 0,1 % |

**Ask 2 — number of restricted substances: 10.**
Count basis: one count per Annex II entry. Consistency check: 9 entries at 0,1 % + 1 entry at 0,01 % = 10 entries; the fetched text contains exactly ten substance lines.
Nuance to carry into any downstream BOM/declaration work: PBB and PBDE are **substance groups** (209 congeners each in practice), so "10" is the number of *restricted entries*, not the number of distinct chemical congeners that a supplier declaration must cover. A supplier declaration covering "PBB/PBDE" covers the whole group.

**Ask 3 — the entry with a maximum concentration of 0,01 % by weight in homogeneous materials: Cadmium.**
It is the only entry in Annex II with an MCV other than 0,1 %. "0,01 %" is the EU decimal-comma form of 0.01 % w/w = 100 ppm in each homogeneous material. Practical consequence for BOM work: the cadmium threshold is 10× tighter than every other RoHS entry, so any cadmium-bearing material (e.g. cadmium pigments, cadmium-stabilised PVC, cadmium plating, cadmium in certain solders/contacts) must be assessed at the 100 ppm level, not the 1000 ppm level used for the other nine entries.

## 2. Date of application of DEHP, BBP, DBP and DIBP to medical devices (answers ask 4)

The Annex II notes state verbatim:

> "The restriction of DEHP, BBP, DBP and DIBP shall apply to medical devices, including *in vitro* medical devices, and monitoring and control instruments, including industrial monitoring and control instruments, from **22 July 2021**."

> "The restriction of DEHP, BBP, DBP and DIBP shall not apply to cables or spare parts for the repair, the reuse, the updating of functionalities or upgrading of capacity of EEE placed on the market before 22 July 2019, and of medical devices, including *in vitro* medical devices, and monitoring and control instruments, including industrial monitoring and control instruments, placed on the market before 22 July 2021."

> "The restriction of DEHP, BBP and DBP shall not apply to toys which are already subject to the restriction of DEHP, BBP and DBP through entry 51 of Annex XVII to Regulation (EC) No 1907/2006."

**Ask 4 — date: 22 July 2021.**

Date logic, stated explicitly so it can be audited:

- 22 July 2019 — general application date of the four phthalates to EEE in categories other than medical devices / monitoring and control.
- **22 July 2021 — application date to medical devices (including in vitro medical devices) and to monitoring and control instruments (including industrial).** This is the ask-4 answer.
- The trigger is *placing on the market*: the restriction attaches to devices placed on the market **on or after 22 July 2021**. Devices placed on the market before that date are outside the phthalate restriction, and cables or spare parts for their repair/reuse/updating/upgrading remain outside it indefinitely — a grandfathering route that matters for service-spares planning.
- Scope point: the Annex II note treats medical devices and in-vitro medical devices on the **same** 22 July 2021 date for these four phthalates, so no separate IVD date applies here.
- Context (not part of the Annex II note, flag as such): the original six substances reach categories 8 and 9 under the Directive's main applicability provisions, on earlier dates than the phthalates; the 22 July 2021 date in ask 4 is specific to DEHP/BBP/DBP/DIBP.

## 3. Direct answers

1. (Constraint) Annex II of Directive 2011/65/EU as currently consolidated — read as substituted by Delegated Directive (EU) 2015/863, no later Annex II amendment identified.
2. **10 substances (entries)** are restricted in Annex II.
3. **Cadmium** is the substance with a maximum concentration of **0,01 % by weight in homogeneous materials** (all other nine entries are 0,1 %).
4. The restriction on **DEHP, BBP, DBP and DIBP applies to medical devices (including in vitro medical devices) from 22 July 2021** (same date for monitoring and control instruments; general EEE date 22 July 2019; pre-22 July 2021 devices and their cables/spare parts are carved out).

## 4. How to re-verify (procedure)

1. Open EUR-Lex consolidated text of Directive 2011/65/EU (CELEX 02011L0065, latest consolidation date).
2. Go to Annex II; confirm the header still reads "Substituted by Commission Delegated Directive (EU) 2015/863".

question: X10
answer:
Answer: 56 hours.

Legal basis and calculation
- Regulation (EC) No 561/2006, Article 6(2): total driving time in any one week must not exceed 56 hours.
- Article 6(3): total driving time in any two consecutive weeks must not exceed 90 hours.
- Article 4(i): 'week' means the period from Monday 00:00 to Sunday 24:00.

Week 1 actual driving = 30 h.
Week 2 single-week ceiling = 56 h.
Week 2 fortnight-average ceiling = 90 - 30 = 60 h.
Binding ceiling = min(56, 60) = 56 h.

Compliance check at the answer
- Week 2 = 56 h: 56 <= 56 (weekly cap met, exactly at the limit).
- Two-week total = 30 + 56 = 86 h: 86 <= 90 (fortnight cap met, 4 h margin).
- Therefore 56 h is the largest following-week figure that does not exceed either driving-time limit. 57 h would already breach the 56-h weekly cap; 60 h would meet the 90-h fortnight cap but breach the weekly cap; 61 h would breach both.

Why the answer is not 60 h
The 90-hour fortnightly limit alone would leave 60 h, but Article 6(2)'s 56-hour single-week limit is lower and therefore controls. The fortnightly average does not authorise a 60-hour week.

Practical lawfulness
56 h is attainable within the daily driving limits: e.g. 9 + 9 + 9 + 9 + 10 + 10 = 56 h across six driving days, using the two permitted 10-hour extensions. The driver must still take the Article 7 break (45 min after no more than 4.5 h driving, or a 15+30 split) and the required daily/weekly rest under Article 8. Those rules are separate constraints on the schedule; they do not reduce the weekly maximum below 56 h. A reduced weekly rest, if taken, affects rest compensation, not the 56/90 driving ceilings.

Assumptions and limits of the answer
- Standard EU Regulation 561/2006 applies, with no national derogation or sector-specific exception.
- The 30 h is driving time, not duty time, and is the total for the immediately preceding Monday-Sunday week.
- No Article 12 exceptional-circumstances extension is being claimed. Article 12 cannot in any case be used to exceed the 90-hour fortnightly limit, and using it to exceed 56 h would be a derogation from the weekly limit, not compliance with it.
- Only the weekly driving-time limits are being maximised; the actual week must also satisfy daily driving, break and rest rules.
- A week before Week 1 does not change Week 2's ceiling: the 90-hour test pairs Week 1 with Week 2. Any earlier high week would have constrained Week 1, not Week 2 directly.

question: X11
shape: UN vehicle regulation (electric power train, UN R100)
answer:
ISOLATION RESISTANCE REQUIREMENT — UN R100, HV BUS TO ELECTRICAL CHASSIS, 400 V GALVANICALLY CONNECTED AC/DC SYSTEM

1. GOVERNING RULE (structure of the requirement)

UN Regulation No. 100 (electric power train safety) sets the minimum isolation resistance between the high voltage bus and the electrical chassis as a per-volt quantity, scaled by the working voltage of the bus:

  - DC bus:    Ri >= 100 ohm per volt of working voltage
  - AC bus:    Ri >= 500 ohm per volt of working voltage

Where the AC and DC high voltage buses are galvanically connected to each other, the Regulation does not allow the two per-volt figures to be applied bus-by-bus and then averaged or taken separately. Instead it treats them as one high voltage bus, and the AC figure governs the whole system:

  - Default (galvanically connected AC + DC): Ri >= 500 ohm/V of the working voltage of the whole system.
  - Exception: if ALL AC buses are protected by one of the two protective measures listed in the Regulation, the requirement drops to Ri >= 100 ohm/V of the working voltage of the whole system.

The two listed measures are alternative AC-bus protections that reduce the risk of a person contacting a live AC conductor (in substance: additional/ reinforced insulation or an equivalent physical barrier over the AC bus, and a protective arrangement that de-energises or isolates the AC bus on a detected fault). Their exact wording should be spot-checked against the published text, but the point that matters for this calculation is that the Regulation offers them as an either/or, and satisfying either one (for all AC buses) triggers the relaxed 100 ohm/V figure. Nothing in the 05-series text known to date changes the 100 / 500 ohm/V coefficients; those have been stable across R100 series and are consistent with ISO 6469-3.

2. VOLTAGE BASIS

The multiplier is the working voltage of the high voltage bus, defined as the highest voltage between any two live parts of the bus, or between any live part and the chassis, under normal operating conditions — not nominal pack voltage. For this vehicle the declared working voltage of the galvanically connected system is 400 V, and that single figure is used for both cases. Because the buses are galvanically connected, there is no separate AC working voltage to use: the whole-system working voltage is 400 V.

3. CALCULATION

Case (a) — no AC-bus protection, 500 ohm/V applies to the whole system:
  Ri,min = 400 V x 500 ohm/V = 200,000 ohm = 200 kOhm

Case (b) — all AC buses protected by one of the two listed measures, 100 ohm/V applies:
  Ri,min = 400 V x 100 ohm/V = 40,000 ohm = 40 kOhm

4. RESULTS

  (a) AC buses unprotected: minimum isolation resistance = 200 kOhm (200,000 ohm)
  (b) all AC buses protected by one of the two measures: minimum isolation resistance = 40 kOhm (40,000 ohm)

5. CROSS-CHECKS AND NOTES THE APPLICANT SHOULD CARRY INTO THE DESIGN

  - Ordering check: 40 kOhm (relaxed case) < 200 kOhm (default case). The exception correctly relaxes the requirement by a factor of five; no value stated here exceeds a limit stated here.
  - Per-bus reading check: if the rule were (wrongly) applied bus-by-bus, the DC bus would need 40 kOhm and the AC bus 200 kOhm. The galvanically connected system must satisfy the more onerous of these, i.e. 200 kOhm — identical to case (a). The answer is therefore robust to that ambiguity.
  - Voltage sensitivity: the requirement scales linearly with the declared working voltage. If the declared working voltage is raised to the full-charge DC-link value (e.g. 420 V), the figures become 210 kOhm and 42 kOhm respectively. Do not declare 400 V if the bus actually operates above it.
  - Design margin: the figures above are the pass/fail floor at the moment of measurement, not a design target. Insulation resistance falls with temperature, humidity and ageing, and the Annex measurement carries uncertainty, so specify a design target of at least 2x the floor (>= 400 kOhm for case (a), >= 80 kOhm for case (b)) at end of life, wet, hot. Verify at the worst-case corner, not at 23 degrees C dry.
  - Measurement: the Annex procedure measures bus-to-chassis resistance with the vehicle in its normal operating state, contactors closed where the procedure requires, using a voltmeter of known internal resistance with and without an added known resistor R0 between bus and chassis; the derived Ri is compared against the per-volt criterion above. Perform it separately for the DC bus and the AC bus and also for the combined system, and report the combined-system value against the 200 kOhm (or 40 kOhm) criterion.
  - Scope: this is the isolation requirement for the traction high voltage bus. The charging inlet, the REESS internal isolation, and the AC-side (on-board charger / e-machine) isolation are separate line items and are not covered by this figure.
  - Provenance caveat: the coefficients used (500 ohm/V AC, 100 ohm/V DC, and the galvanic-connection promotion clause with its two-measure exception) are the established R100 convention. They should be confirmed verbatim against the published 2026/1695 text before the value is entered into a compliance dossier; the arithmetic above is correct for those coefficients, and the coefficients themselves have not changed in the series history known to date.
