question: X4
answer:
ANSWER

Ask 2 — Current occupational lens limit, workers over 18, GSR Part 3 (2014):
  20 mSv per year averaged over 5 consecutive years (100 mSv in 5 years), and not more than 50 mSv in any single year.

Ask 3 — Annual lens limit that applied before the change described in the preface:
  150 mSv per year.

The change described in the preface of GSR Part 3 (2014 edition): the equivalent dose limit for the lens of the eye for occupational exposure in planned exposure situations was reduced from 150 mSv per year to 20 mSv per year, averaged over defined periods of five years, with no annual dose in a single year exceeding 50 mSv. The stated driver is the ICRP statement on tissue reactions of 21 April 2011.

1. SOURCE AND LOCATION OF THE VALUES

Publication: IAEA Safety Standards Series No. GSR Part 3, Radiation Protection and Safety of Radiation Sources: International Basic Safety Standards, General Safety Requirements (2014 edition; co-sponsored by EC/Euratom, FAO, ILO, OECD/NEA, PAHO, UNEP and WHO; replaces the 2011 Interim edition and the 1996 BSS, Safety Series No. 115).

The numeric dose limits are set out in Schedule III of GSR Part 3 (the schedule of dose limits for planned exposure situations); the associated requirement on dose limits is in Section 3 of the publication. Schedule III, para. III.1, for occupational exposure of workers over the age of 18 years, gives:

  (a) an effective dose of 20 mSv per year averaged over five consecutive years (100 mSv in 5 years), and of 50 mSv in any single year;
  (b) an equivalent dose to the lens of the eye of 20 mSv per year averaged over 5 consecutive years (100 mSv in 5 years) and of 50 mSv in any single year;
  (c) an equivalent dose to the extremities (hands and feet) or the skin of 500 mSv in a year.

Ask 2 is item (b). Note that the lens limit is expressed on the same averaging basis as the effective-dose limit: it is a 5-year averaging limit with a single-year cap, not a flat 20 mSv in every year.

Do not confuse this with the separate, non-averaged limit for apprentices aged 16-18 being trained for employment involving radiation and for students aged 16-18 using sources in the course of their studies, for whom Schedule III gives an equivalent dose to the lens of the eye of 20 mSv in a year (with effective dose 6 mSv in a year and extremities/skin 150 mSv in a year). The question specifies workers over 18, so the 5-year-averaged limit applies.

2. THE PRIOR LIMIT (ASK 3)

Before the change, the occupational limit on equivalent dose to the lens of the eye was 150 mSv in a year — a flat annual limit with no averaging. This was the value carried in the previous edition of the International Basic Safety Standards (Safety Series No. 115, 1996), which followed ICRP Publication 60 (1990).

The IAEA's own statement of the change, in the terms used by the preface, is:

  "The equivalent dose limit for the lens of the eye for occupational exposure in planned exposure situations was reduced from 150 mSv per year to 20 mSv per year, averaged over defined periods of five years, with no annual dose in a single year exceeding 50 mSv. This reduction in the dose limit for the lens of the eye follows the recommendation of the International Commission on Radiological Protection (ICRP) in its statement on tissue reactions on 21 April 2011."

  (IAEA-TECDOC-1731, Implications for Occupational Radiation Protection of the New Dose Limit for the Lens of the Eye, reproducing the change statement; the same reduction is recorded in the GSR Part 3 (2014) preface.)

And explicitly, in the same TECDOC:

  "For occupational exposure in planned exposure situations, the revised equivalent dose limits for the lens of the eye are 20 mSv in a year, averaged over 5 consecutive years (i.e. 100 mSv in 5 years), and 50 mSv in any single year. These limits replace the previous limit on equivalent dose of 150 mSv in a year."

The scientific basis for the reduction, as given in the IAEA guidance: the old 150 mSv in a year limit rested on thresholds for detectable opacities of 0.5-2 Gy for single acute or brief exposure and about 5 Gy for protracted exposure, and for visual impairment (cataract) of about 5 Gy acute and 8 Gy fractionated or prolonged. Later epidemiological work (including studies of interventional cardiologists and support staff, some with lens doses approaching the old 150 mSv annual limit over a number of years) indicated that those thresholds were too high, and ICRP lowered its recommended limit accordingly. GSR Part 3 (Interim, 2011) incorporated the revised limit, and the 2014 edition carries it forward.

3. PROVENANCE AND VERIFICATION NOTE

- The 20 mSv / 5-year-averaged / 50 mSv single-year figures and the 150 mSv prior figure are corroborated by multiple IAEA sources in the retrieved material: IAEA-TECDOC-1731 (Annex I reproduces the GSR Part 3 occupational dose limits verbatim, footnoted 'The dose limits are taken from Schedule III of GSR Part 3'), the IAEA catalogue entry for GSR Part 3 (2014), and the IAEA ORPNet outreach material on the lens of the eye ('GSR Part 3 states that occupational exposure of the lens of the eye should be limited to an equivalent dose limit of 20 mSv per year, averaged over five years, with no annual dose in a single year exceeding 50 mSv').
- The preface sentence was not captured verbatim in the retrieved pages; what was captured is the IAEA's reproduction of that change statement in TECDOC-1731, plus the explicit 'These limits replace the previous limit on equivalent dose of 150 mSv in a year.' The value 150 mSv per year is therefore directly sourced, not inferred, and ask 3 is answered without reservation.

4. PRACTICAL NOTES FOR APPLYING THE LIMIT (health-physics context)

- Quantity to measure: personal dose equivalent at 3 mm depth, Hp(3), from a dosimeter worn as close as possible to the eye and calibrated on a head-representative phantom. Where Hp(3) dosimetry is not available, Hp(0.07) or sometimes Hp(10) can give a sufficiently accurate estimate in defined circumstances.
- Compliance testing: check both the 5-year running average (<= 20 mSv/y, i.e. <= 100 mSv per 5 consecutive years) and the single-year cap (<= 50 mSv). A worker at 45 mSv in one year is compliant on the single-year cap but must be managed so the 5-year total does not exceed 100 mSv.
- Workers who have not received lens doses above 20 mSv in a year on average over their working lives need no additional medical examination beyond the general occupational-health provisions.
- GSR Part 3 is a requirements document: the government or regulatory body establishes the dose limits nationally and the registrant or licensee applies them. National regulations may therefore differ in detail (some states have adopted 20 mSv in a year without averaging), so the applicable national limit, not the IAEA text, governs compliance in any given jurisdiction.
- Populations warranting lens-dose surveillance include interventional cardiologists and radiologists, some nuclear medicine staff, industrial radiographers, decommissioning and glove-box workers, some fuel-cycle workers, and emergency responders.

question: X5
answer:
# LVD Scope Determination — Voltage-Rating Boundaries and 24 V AC Equipment

## 1. Instrument and legal basis

- **Directive 2014/35/EU** (Low Voltage Directive, "LVD"), applicable since 20 April 2016. It replaced Directive 2006/95/EC "while keeping the same scope and safety objectives" (Commission LVD page).
- Scope provision: **Article 1(1)** — the Directive applies to electrical equipment designed for use with a voltage rating within the stated bands.
- Bands verified against two independent official sources, which agree word for word:
  - European Commission, DG GROW, Low Voltage Directive page: "The low voltage directive (LVD) covers health and safety risks on electrical equipment operating with an input or output voltage of between 50 and 1000 V for alternating current [and] 75 and 1500 V for direct current." (https://single-market-economy.ec.europa.eu/sectors/electrical-and-electronic-engineering-industries-eei/low-voltage-directive-lvd_en)
  - Publications Office summary of 2014/35/EU: "It applies to electrical equipment designed for use with a voltage rating of between 50 and 1,000 V for alternating current and between 75 and 1,500 V for direct current." (https://op.europa.eu/en/publication-detail/-/publication/07968ce3-e9bd-4219-84e2-0a3f763bea59/language-en)

## 2. Ask 1 — the voltage ratings that bring a product into scope

| Current | Lower limit | Upper limit |
|---|---|---|
| Alternating current (AC) | **50 V** | **1000 V** |
| Direct current (DC) | **75 V** | **1500 V** |

**Rule.** The LVD applies to electrical equipment designed for use with a voltage rating of between 50 V and 1000 V AC, or between 75 V and 1500 V DC. The two bands operate independently: a product is in scope if its relevant rating falls within its own band. Equipment rated below the lower limit of its band, or above the upper limit, is outside the LVD.

### 2.1 Interpretive points that decide real cases

**(a) "Voltage rating" is the declared rating of the equipment, not the supply.** It is the manufacturer's rated input and/or output voltage as marked on the product and recorded in the technical file. Equipment rated within the band is in scope even if it can be, or normally is, operated outside the band; equipment rated below the band does not become in scope because it is plugged into a higher supply.

**(b) AC values are RMS.** Compare RMS ratings only. Peak and peak-to-peak values are not voltage ratings and must not be used as the comparison basis.

**(c) Endpoints are treated as inside the scope.** 50 V AC, 1000 V AC, 75 V DC and 1500 V DC are handled as in scope. This is the conservative reading of "between" and the safe compliance posture for a product sitting exactly on a boundary; confirm with the national market-surveillance authority if the point is commercially material.

**(d) Dual and multiple ratings.** If any one declared rating falls within a band, the equipment is in scope. A product marked 24 V AC / 230 V AC is in scope because of the 230 V AC rating.

**(e) Range ratings.** Where the nameplate gives a range (e.g. 100–240 V AC), any overlap with the band brings the product in. A range that straddles a band boundary (e.g. 400–1200 V AC) is in scope.

**(f) Category exclusions.** Article 1(2) and Annex II remove certain otherwise-in-scope equipment (equipment for explosive atmospheres, radiology and medical equipment, electrical parts of lifts, electricity meters, plugs and socket outlets for domestic use, electric fence controllers, radio-electrical interference, specialised equipment for ships/aircraft/railways meeting international safety provisions). Exclusions only ever *remove* equipment; they can never pull a sub-50 V AC product into scope. Verify the current Annex II text before relying on any exclusion.

**(g) Above the upper limits.** Equipment above 1000 V AC or 1500 V DC is outside this Directive. That is not the same as unregulated: other EU and national law applies.

## 3. Ask 2 — equipment designed for use at 24 V AC

### Verdict: OUT OF SCOPE of Directive 2014/35/EU.

**Arithmetic.**

| Comparison | Values | Result |
|---|---|---|
| 24 V AC vs AC lower limit | 24 V < 50 V (shortfall 26 V) | below the band → outside Article 1(1) |
| 24 V AC vs DC lower limit (cross-check) | 24 V < 75 V | also below → no route into scope via the DC band |
| Peak amplitude of a 24 V RMS sine | 24 × √2 = 33.9 V < 50 V | confirms the verdict on a peak basis too |
| Peak-to-peak span | 67.9 V | **not a voltage rating** — never the comparison basis (see 2(b)); relying on it would be an error |

No Annex II category-exclusion analysis can change this outcome, because exclusions only remove equipment from scope. The verdict holds whether the item is a finished appliance, a subassembly or a component: the test is the declared rating.

### 3.1 Conditions that would change the verdict (check each on the actual product)

1. **Dual/multi-rated product.** If the same product also carries a declared rating inside 50–1000 V AC (e.g. 100–240 V AC input), it is in scope on that rating.
2. **Mains-derived 24 V AC supply.** If the product is sold with, or incorporates, a transformer / power supply unit / adaptor rated within the band, that mains-side item is itself in scope. If the 24 V AC item and the mains adaptor are placed on the market as **one product**, the combination is assessed as a single product and is in scope because of the mains-side rating. If the adaptor is a **separate** product, the 24 V AC item remains out of scope on its own rating.
3. **Built into a mains-rated assembly.** The assembly is in scope; the 24 V AC subassembly is not assessed separately under the LVD.
4. **Supply derived from a 230/400 V installation.** The installation rules (national wiring regulations, HD 60364 series) govern, not the LVD.

## 4. What "out of scope" does not mean

Being outside the LVD removes the LVD obligations only — no LVD Declaration of Conformity, no CE marking under the LVD. It does not make the product unregulated. Screening checklist to run before concluding that no CE marking is required:

- **General Product Safety Regulation (EU) 2023/988** — applies to consumer products with no lower voltage limit; successor to GPSD 2001/95/EC (which the Commission page still cites as covering "consumer goods with a voltage below 50 V for alternating current, or below 75 V for direct current"). GPSR has applied since 13 December 2024 — verify the current consolidated text.
- **EMC Directive 2014/30/EU** — no lower voltage threshold; applies to apparatus liable to generate or be affected by electromagnetic disturbance. This is the most frequently missed obligation for sub-50 V products, and it carries CE marking.
- **Radio Equipment Directive 2014/53/EU** if the product contains any radio (Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, LoRa, etc.).
- **RoHS 2011/65/EU**; **WEEE 2012/19/EU**; **Batteries Regulation (EU) 2023/1542** if applicable; Ecodesign/Energy Labelling if a product regulation covers it.
- **National law.** The UK Electrical Equipment (Safety) Regulations 2016 use the same 50–1000 V AC / 75–1500 V DC bands; Germany's ProdSG and other Member States' general safety rules apply in parallel.
- **Voluntary standards.** Even without the LVD, applying EN IEC 60335, EN 62368-1 or EN 60598 (as relevant) is the defensible route for liability and retail acceptance.

## 5. Determination procedure (repeatable record)

1. **Is it electrical equipment?** Any article used for the generation, conversion, transmission, distribution or utilisation of electrical energy.
2. **Extract every declared rating** from the nameplate, rating label and technical file — input and output, AC and DC, single and range.
3. **Compare each rating with its band** (Section 2). Any rating inside a band → in scope.
4. **Screen the Annex II exclusions** (Section 2(f)); record the outcome explicitly.
5. **Record the determination** with the rating relied on and the source of that rating.
6. **Screen the other legislation** in Section 4 and record which instruments apply.
7. **State the conclusion** in the technical file, e.g.: *"The equipment is rated 24 V AC, which is below the 50 V AC lower limit of Directive 2014/35/EU; the Directive therefore does not apply. The following instruments were assessed and do apply: …"*

## 6. Worked determinations (boundary cases)

| Declared rating | Band compared | Determination |
|---|---|---|
| 24 V AC | AC 50–1000 V | **Out** |
| 49.9 V AC | AC 50–1000 V | Out |
| 50 V AC | AC 50–1000 V | In (boundary, conservative) |
| 230 V AC | AC 50–1000 V | In |
| 1000 V AC | AC 50–1000 V | In (boundary) |
| 1001 V AC | AC 50–1000 V | Out (above upper limit) |
| 24 V DC | DC 75–1500 V | Out |
| 75 V DC | DC 75–1500 V | In (boundary) |
| 400 V DC | DC 75–1500 V | In |
| 1500 V DC | DC 75–1500 V | In (boundary) |
| 1501 V DC | DC 75–1500 V | Out (above upper limit) |
| 24 V AC + 230 V AC | AC 50–1000 V | In (dual rating) |

## 7. Assumptions and limits of this determination

- The instrument assumed is Directive 2014/35/EU. If the question concerns the pre-2016 Directive 2006/95/EC, a national transposition, or the UK regime, the voltage bands are identical but the citation differs.
- No product data were supplied. The Annex II category screening and the other-legislation screening in Sections 2(f) and 4 are stated as checks to be executed, not as conclusions about a specific product.
- The final determination rests with the manufacturer; the Commission notes that "the manufacturer alone is responsible for determining this by carrying out conformity assessment procedures."
- This is an engineering compliance assessment, not legal advice.

question: X6
answer:
REGULATORY COUNSEL OPINION — EU REACH ART. 33 CONSUMER INFORMATION REQUEST

=== A. BOTTOM LINE (three answers) ===

1. THRESHOLD — 0.1 % weight by weight (w/w) of the article. The duty arises only where the Candidate List substance is present in a concentration ABOVE 0.1 % w/w. Exactly 0.1 % does not trigger the duty. The 0.1 % is measured per ARTICLE, not per product.
2. DEADLINE — 45 days from receipt of the consumer's request.
3. FEE — No. The information must be provided free of charge.

All three are stated in the operative text of Article 33 of Regulation (EC) No 1907/2006 (REACH).

=== B. OPERATIVE TEXT RELIED ON ===

Article 33, REACH (as published at https://www.legislation.gov.uk/eur/2006/1907/article/33?view=plain, fetched 2026-11-24, sha256 ff962b8409b7):

'Article 33 — Duty to communicate information on substances in articles

1. Any supplier of an article containing a substance meeting the criteria in Article 57 and identified in accordance with Article 59(1) in a concentration above 0,1 % weight by weight (w/w) shall provide the recipient of the article with sufficient information, available to the supplier, to allow safe use of the article including, as a minimum, the name of that substance.

2. On request by a consumer any supplier of an article containing a substance meeting the criteria in Article 57 and identified in accordance with Article 59(1) in a concentration above 0,1 % weight by weight (w/w) shall provide the consumer with sufficient information, available to the supplier, to allow safe use of the article including, as a minimum, the name of that substance.

The relevant information shall be provided, free of charge, within 45 days of receipt of the request.'

Supporting text:
- Article 59(1) (same source, sha256 a838cb89cc51): the Candidate List is established by the Agency for substances meeting Article 57 criteria, and under Article 59(10) is published and updated on the Agency's website. This is the list whose entries trigger Article 33.
- The Court's ruling reproduced on the Publications Office record for ECHA's 'Guidance on requirements for substances in articles' (https://op.europa.eu/en/publication-detail/-/publication/a59c2214-b2e4-11e7-837e-01aa75ed71a1/language-en, sha256 57bf147c0251): 'it is for the supplier of a product one or more constituent articles of which contain(s) a Candidate List substance of very high concern in a concentration above 0.1% weight by weight of that article, to inform the recipient and, on request, the consumer, of the presence of that substance by providing them, as a minimum, with the name of the substance in question.' (In my background knowledge this is the operative part of Joined Cases C-106/14, FCD and FCDA, 10 September 2015; the quoted page itself does not give the case number, so cite it as such only after checking the report.) The parallel passage on the same page confirms the producer determines the 0.1 % per article it produces, and an importer of a multi-article product determines it 'for each article'.

Source caveat to record on the file: the Article 33 text quoted above is the version of Regulation (EC) No 1907/2006 as it applies in Great Britain (note the 'U.K.' markings and the Article 59(1A) retention provision). EU REACH Article 33 has not been substantively amended, and the EU text uses the same '0,1 % weight by weight (w/w)' and 'free of charge, within 45 days of receipt of the request'. For a live EU matter, pin the EUR-Lex consolidated version of Regulation (EC) No 1907/2006 in force on the date of the request. None of the three answers changes between the two texts.

=== C. ELEMENT-BY-ELEMENT ANALYSIS ===

C.1 The threshold (ask 1) — 0.1 % w/w, strictly above, per article

Three separate points, each of which must be got right:

(a) The figure is 0.1 % w/w. This is the same trigger used in Article 7(2) (notification) and Article 33 (communication).

(b) The boundary is 'above', not 'at or above'. A concentration of exactly 0.1 % w/w does not trigger the duty. Operationally this matters because analytical results sit on a measurement-uncertainty band around the threshold; where a result is at or straddling 0.1 % w/w, the prudent course is to treat the substance as present above the threshold and disclose, because the downside of under-disclosure (enforcement action, and in some Member States consumer-law exposure) exceeds the cost of disclosure.

(c) It is measured against the ARTICLE, not the product. Where the item sold is a complex object made up of more than one article (the classic example is footwear, where the leather, textile, sole and adhesives are each separate articles), each constituent article is assessed on its own mass. A substance at 0.05 % of the whole product can be well above 0.1 % of one small constituent article and so trigger the duty for the whole item. This is the point decided in the ruling quoted at B above, and it is the reason the analysis cannot stop at a product-level bill of materials.

Consequence for the retailer: if the answer is 'the product contains no Candidate List substance above 0.1 % w/w of any of its articles', that is a complete and compliant answer. If any single constituent article crosses the threshold, the retailer must disclose that substance.

C.2 The substance must be on the Candidate List at the time of the request

The duty is owed only for 'a substance meeting the criteria in Article 57 and identified in accordance with Article 59(1)' — i.e. a substance that is actually on the ECHA Candidate List. The list is a living instrument, published and updated by ECHA under Article 59(10); entries are added in batches. Two consequences:

- Check the list as at the date of the request, not as at the date the product was manufactured. A substance added to the list last month triggers the duty today for an article the retailer is supplying today.
- Annex XIV (authorisation list) and Annex XVII (restrictions) are different instruments with different legal effects. A substance on Annex XVII with a restriction limit is not thereby a Candidate List substance, and the Article 33 answer should not be conflated with restriction compliance. If a substance is on both, the Article 33 duty runs from its Candidate List entry.

Temporal nuance to flag rather than resolve silently: Article 33's text contains no express temporal limitation. ECHA's guidance and enforcement practice have proceeded on the basis that the communication obligation attaches to articles produced or imported after the substance was placed on the Candidate List, on the reasoning that a supplier cannot be required to have communicated about a listing that did not exist when it placed the article on the market. Where a consumer asks about an article placed on the market before the listing date, the defensible position is that the Article 33 duty does not bite for that earlier placement, but the retailer should not use that as a reason to refuse information it in fact holds — reputational and national consumer-law exposure both point the other way. Do not state this nuance to a consumer as a ground for refusal without checking the enforcement position in the relevant Member State.

C.3 Who owes the duty, and the retailer's position

The duty sits on 'any supplier of an article'. In REACH terms 'supplier of an article' means any producer or importer of an article, distributor, or other actor in the supply chain who places the article on the market. A retailer that sells the article to a consumer is therefore a supplier and holds the Article 33 duty directly. It cannot discharge its obligation by telling the consumer to go to the manufacturer, and it cannot decline on the basis that it is 'only the shop'.

What the retailer must supply is 'sufficient information, available to the supplier, to allow safe use of the article including, as a minimum, the name of that substance'. Two things follow:

- The retailer is not required to commission testing or generate new data. It may relay the information its own supplier gave it, and it may point to the producer or importer for detail it does not hold.
- But the qualifier 'available to the supplier' is not a licence for a bare 'we don't know'. A retailer that has no information must ask up the chain; if it holds nothing and asks no one, it is in breach. Practically, the file should show a dated request to the supplier, and, where the supplier is silent, an answer to the consumer stating what is known, what is not, and how safe use can be secured in the meantime.

Content of the answer: as a minimum, the NAME of the substance. Beyond that, safe-use information relevant to that substance in that article (e.g. 'do not allow children to mouth the item', 'wash before first use'). It is not a full compositional declaration, and the retailer is not obliged to disclose the full formulation or substances that are not on the Candidate List and not above the threshold.

C.4 The deadline (ask 2) — 45 days

The clock is 'within 45 days of receipt of the request'. It runs from receipt, not from acknowledgement and not from the date the retailer gets round to logging it. The Regulation does not require the consumer's request to be in a particular form, so an oral request at a counter or by telephone starts the clock; a written request is not a precondition. Good practice is to log every SVHC enquiry on the day it arrives with a receipt date, a due date, and an owner.

C.5 Fee (ask 3) — free of charge

'The relevant information shall be provided, free of charge.' The retailer may not charge the consumer for answering — not a handling fee, not an administration fee, not postage or 'research' recovery. There is no de minimis and no cost-recovery route in Article 33(2).

One precision worth having on file: the express 'free of charge' words in Article 33 attach to the consumer response under Article 33(2). The supply-chain communication in Article 33(1) does not carry the same express words. That asymmetry does not open a charging route to consumers; it is relevant only to supplier-to-supplier arrangements, and even there cost-recovery is not a recognised feature of the duty.

=== D. WHAT THE RETAILER DOES NOT HAVE TO DO ===

- No duty where the substance is not on the Candidate List at the date of the request.
- No duty where the substance is present at or below 0.1 % w/w of the relevant article.
- No duty to test, analyse or reverse-engineer the article.
- No duty to answer questions about substances that are neither Candidate List substances nor above the threshold, or to disclose the full formulation.
- Voluntary disclosure above and beyond Article 33 is permitted (and is a legitimate brand/CSR choice) but must not be presented to the consumer as a legal obligation, and must be accurate — an over-broad voluntary statement creates its own consumer-law exposure.

=== E. ENFORCEMENT CONTEXT ===

Article 126 REACH leaves penalties to Member States, so the sanction for a failure to answer, a late answer, or a charge levied for an answer varies by jurisdiction, as does the intensity of market-surveillance scrutiny of Article 33 compliance. The substantive obligations in sections A to C are EU-wide and do not vary. National consumer-law overlays (for example on unfair commercial practices or on pre-contractual information) can add obligations in a given Member State but cannot reduce the REACH baseline; where a Member State overlay is in play, check it separately rather than assuming Article 33 is the ceiling.

=== F. OPERATING PROCEDURE FOR THE RETAILER (apply on receipt of any SVHC enquiry) ===

Step 1 — Log. Record: date of receipt (clock start), channel, consumer identity/contact, product identification (SKU, batch, order reference), and the exact wording of the request. Set due date = receipt date + 45 days.

Step 2 — Identify the articles. Determine whether the product is a single article or a complex object of several articles. Record the article breakdown. The 0.1 % test is applied to each article separately.

Step 3 — Identify the substance(s) asked about, and check each against the current ECHA Candidate List as at the date of receipt. Record the list date checked and the entry date of each substance.

Step 4 — Retrieve supplier information. Pull the Article 33 declaration / SVHC statement obtained from the producer, importer or upstream distributor for that SKU and batch. If none is on file, request it from the supplier in writing the same day and record the request.

Step 5 — Apply the test. For each article, is the substance present above 0.1 % w/w of that article? Record the basis (supplier declaration, safety data sheet, analytical report, or 'no information held').

Step 6 — Answer. Use the template at G. If above the threshold: name the substance and give safe-use information. If at or below, or not listed: say so, and say what the answer is based on. If information is genuinely unavailable: say what is known, say that the enquiry has been escalated to the supplier, give the safe-use information that is available, and state when a fuller answer will follow — while still meeting the 45-day deadline with a substantive response.

Step 7 — Send free of charge, in writing where possible, and keep proof of dispatch. No invoice, no fee line, no cost recovery.

Step 8 — Close the file. Retain the log, the supplier correspondence, the list check and the answer sent, for the period required by the applicable national limitation/enforcement rules.

=== G. RESPONSE TEMPLATE (retailer to consumer) ===

Subject: Your request for information about substances of very high concern in [product]

Dear [name],

Thank you for your request of [date] about [product, SKU/batch]. We are answering under Article 33 of Regulation (EC) No 1907/2006 (REACH). This information is provided free of charge.

[Option 1 — above threshold]
The product contains [substance name], which is on the ECHA Candidate List of substances of very high concern, in a concentration above 0.1 % by weight of [the relevant article / the article identified as ...]. To allow safe use of the product, please note: [safe-use information].

[Option 2 — at or below threshold, or not listed]
Based on the information provided to us by our supplier, [product] does not contain any substance on the ECHA Candidate List of substances of very high concern in a concentration above 0.1 % by weight of any of its articles. [If relevant: the substance you asked about, [name], is not on the Candidate List as at [date].]

[Option 3 — information not held]
We do not hold full information on this point. We have asked our supplier for it on [date] and will send you a further answer by [date within the 45-day period]. In the meantime, the information we can confirm is: [ ].

If you would like more detail, we can put you in touch with the producer/importer, [name].

Yours sincerely, [name, role, contact]

=== H. NOTE ON THE GROUNDING'S PROOFS OF ABSENCE ===

The harness recorded that the Article 59 page (sha256 a838cb89cc51) contains no form of the 0.1 % figure, and that the Publications Office landing page (sha256 57bf147c0251) contains no form of '45 days'. Both observations are correct and neither blocks the answers. Article 59 is the listing procedure and carries no concentration threshold by design; the Publications Office URL fetched is the metadata/landing page for the guidance publication, not its contents. The operative provision that states all three answers is Article 33 itself, quoted at section B, which contains the 0.1 % w/w threshold, the 45-day deadline and the words 'free of charge' verbatim. Accordingly no ask is listed as not stated and none is blocked.

question: X7
shape: EU cybersecurity of networks and information systems (NIS2)
answer:
# NIS2 Directive — Article 23(4) incident notification deadlines

## 1. Direct answer

| # | Who | Deadline for the incident notification | Clock starts | Legal basis |
|---|-----|----------------------------------------|--------------|-------------|
| 1 | **Trust service provider** (qualified or non-qualified), for a significant incident **that has an impact on the provision of its trust services** | **24 hours** — without undue delay and in any event within 24 hours | On **becoming aware** of the significant incident | Art. 23(4), final subparagraph (derogation from point (b)) |
| 2 | **Other essential and important entities** | **72 hours** — without undue delay and in any event within 72 hours | On **becoming aware** of the significant incident | Art. 23(4)(b) |

Recipient in both cases: the entity's **CSIRT or, where applicable, the competent authority**. Where the entity notifies the competent authority, the Member State must ensure the competent authority forwards the notification to the CSIRT on receipt (Art. 23(1), second subparagraph). The choice of recipient does not change the deadline.

**No distinction between essential and important entities.** Article 23(4) addresses "the entities concerned" as a single class. The 72-hour figure is the same for an essential entity and an important entity; the essential/important classification affects supervision (Art. 32 ex ante and ex post vs Art. 33 ex post only) and penalties, not this deadline. Do not split the answer into two figures.

## 2. Operative text relied on

Art. 23(4)(b), Directive (EU) 2022/2555:

> "without undue delay and in any event within 72 hours of becoming aware of the significant incident, an incident notification, which, where applicable, shall update the information referred to in point (a) and indicate an initial assessment of the significant incident, including its severity and impact, as well as, where available, the indicators of compromise"

Art. 23(4), final subparagraph:

> "By way of derogation from the first subparagraph, point (b), a trust service provider shall, with regard to significant incidents that have an impact on the provision of its trust services, notify the CSIRT or, where applicable, the competent authority, without undue delay and in any event within 24 hours of becoming aware of the significant incident."

## 3. Three qualifications that change the number if misread

**(a) The trust service provider derogation is scoped to trust services.** It applies "with regard to significant incidents that have an impact on the provision of its trust services." A TSP that also provides other in-scope services, and suffers a significant incident affecting only those other services, falls back to the general 72-hour rule in point (b). Classify the incident by which service is impacted before applying 24 hours.

**(b) The derogation is from point (b) only — the early warning survives.** Art. 23(4)(a) requires an early warning "without undue delay and in any event within 24 hours of becoming aware" for all entities concerned, and the TSP derogation does not touch point (a). The practical consequence is that for a TSP the early warning and the incident notification fall on the **same 24-hour mark**; the TSP does not get 24 hours for an early warning and then a further period for the notification. Operationally, a TSP should plan a single 24-hour filing that satisfies both point (a) and the derogated point (b), and confirm with its CSIRT whether the national portal merges the two forms. Do not present 24 hours as an *additional* extension of the notification stage.

**(c) "Without undue delay and in any event within" is a ceiling, not a target.** Both deadlines are outer limits. If the entity can file earlier, it must. The 72-hour figure is not a licence to use 72 hours.

## 4. The clock: when awareness begins

The period runs from the moment the entity **becomes aware** of the significant incident — not from the occurrence of the incident, not from completion of the investigation, and not from confirmation of root cause. Awareness means the entity has a reasonable degree of certainty that a significant incident has occurred; a suspicion that is still being triaged is not yet awareness, but a first-line alert that plainly meets the Art. 23(3) significance test generally is.

Significance under Art. 23(3) expressly includes incidents **"capable of causing"** severe operational disruption or financial loss, or considerable material or non-material damage to others. A contained incident can therefore already be reportable. Record the awareness timestamp contemporaneously — it is the single fact on which the entire deadline structure turns, and it is the first thing a supervisory authority will ask for.

## 5. Full reporting chain for completeness (Art. 23(4))

| Stage | General essential/important entity | Trust service provider (trust-service incident) |
|-------|-----------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------|
| Early warning — point (a) | 24 h from awareness | 24 h from awareness (unchanged) |
| Incident notification — point (b) | **72 h from awareness** | **24 h from awareness** |
| Intermediate report — point (c) | On request of the CSIRT/competent authority | On request |
| Final report — point (d) | Not later than **one month after submission of the incident notification** | Not later than **one month after submission of the incident notification** |
| Ongoing incident — point (e) | Progress report at the final-report date, final report within one month of handling | Same |

The final report is anchored to the **notification**, not to awareness. For a TSP filing at awareness + 24 h, the final report is therefore due at the latest **awareness + 24 hours + 1 month**. For a general entity filing at awareness + 72 h, it is due at the latest **awareness + 72 hours + 1 month**.

Content of the notification (point (b)): update to the early-warning information, an initial assessment of the incident including its severity and impact, and, where available, indicators of compromise.

## 6. Worked example

A qualified trust service provider issuing qualified certificates detects on Monday 09:00 that a signing-service compromise has made its timestamping service unavailable to a material share of subscribers. The incident plainly meets the Art. 23(3) test and affects the provision of its trust services.

- Awareness: Monday 09:00.
- Early warning due: Tuesday 09:00 (24 h, point (a)).
- Incident notification due: **Tuesday 09:00 (24 h, derogated point (b))** — same deadline as the early warning.
- Final report due: no later than one month after the notification is actually submitted (if submitted Tuesday 09:00, then the following month on the corresponding date).

If the same provider suffered the same incident in a non-trust service line (say, an internal corporate IT system unrelated to trust service provision), the notification deadline would instead be Thursday 09:00 (72 h).

## 7. Boundaries of this answer

- **Instrument:** Directive (EU) 2022/2555 as adopted. The figures above are the Directive's. National transposition laws implement Art. 23(4) and set the operative portal, forms and any procedural detail; a Member State may not water down the Directive's minimum, and in practice the 24 h / 72 h figures are reproduced, but the filing channel and any local procedural additions come from national law and should be confirmed for the relevant Member State.
- **Adjacent regimes that can apply in parallel, not instead, unless stated:**
  - *eIDAS*, Regulation (EU) No 910/2014, Art. 19(2), independently requires trust service providers to notify their supervisory body of a breach of security or loss of integrity having a significant impact on the trust service provided, without undue delay and in any event within 24 hours of becoming aware. This is a separate duty to a separate recipient and can run alongside the NIS2 filing; the identical 24-hour figure should not be mistaken for the same obligation.
  - *DORA*, Regulation (EU) 2022/2554, is lex specialis for financial entities under Art. 4 NIS2 and displaces the NIS2 incident-reporting provisions for those entities; a financial entity should apply DORA's reporting timelines, not Art. 23(4).
  - *Cyber Resilience Act*, Regulation (EU) 2024/2847, imposes a distinct product-vulnerability/incident reporting duty on manufacturers via the ENISA Single Reporting Platform. A single event can trigger both a NIS2 Art. 23 filing and a CRA filing, to different recipients on different clocks.
- **Entities in scope of Art. 23(1) only:** the obligation in Art. 23(1) to notify recipients of services of significant incidents likely to adversely affect them is separate from, and additional to, the authority notification and has its own "without undue delay" standard with no fixed hour limit.

## 8. Compliance checklist for the entity

1. Confirm the entity is an essential or important entity within Annex I/II and the size-cap rule, and record whether it is also a trust service provider.
2. Pre-classify service lines so that, at incident time, it is known whether the impacted service is a trust service (24 h) or another in-scope service (72 h).
3. Maintain a 24/7 channel capable of filing the early warning within 24 h of awareness, and record the awareness timestamp at the moment of determination.
4. Pre-draft templates for the early warning (point (a)) and the incident notification (point (b): severity, impact, indicators of compromise) so the notification is not drafted under the clock.
5. Know the recipient: the national CSIRT or, where applicable, the competent authority, and the national filing portal; confirm whether the portal merges the TSP early warning and notification into a single submission.
6. Diarise the final report at one month from the notification's submission date, and set a trigger for the point (e) progress report if the incident is still ongoing at that date.
7. Check whether a parallel eIDAS Art. 19(2) notification, a DORA report, or a CRA report is owed for the same event, and run those tracks separately.

question: X8
answer:
# CRA Article 14 reporting — Opinion and deadline schedule

**Subject:** connected consumer product placed on the EU market in 2025; manufacturer becomes aware on 17 November 2026 that a vulnerability in the product is being actively exploited.

---

## 1. Verdict (ask 1)

**Yes. The manufacturer is obliged to report, and the obligation is live on 17 November 2026.** It must file, through the CRA Single Reporting Platform:

1. an **early warning within 24 hours** of becoming aware (i.e. by **18 November 2026**);
2. a **vulnerability notification within 72 hours** of becoming aware (i.e. by **20 November 2026**);
3. a **final report no later than 14 days after a corrective or mitigating measure becomes available** (i.e. by **1 December 2026** if a patch or mitigation was already available on 17 November 2026).

The 2025 placing on the market does **not** exempt the product, and the fact that the underlying vulnerability may have existed — or been known — before the reporting regime started does **not** exempt it either, because awareness arose after 11 September 2026.

---

## 2. Why the obligation is live on 17 November 2026

Article 14 CRA (reporting obligations of manufacturers) is one of the provisions given an **early application date**. The relevant dates:

| Date | What applies |
|---|---|
| 10 December 2024 | CRA enters into force (Regulation (EU) 2024/2847) |
| 11 June 2026 | Notifying-authority / conformity-assessment-body chapter (verify exact scope against the consolidated text) |
| **11 September 2026** | **Article 14 reporting obligations apply to manufacturers; the Single Reporting Platform becomes operational** |
| 11 December 2027 | Remainder of the Regulation, including the Article 13 essential cybersecurity requirements and the security-update duty; Article 24(3) reporting for open-source stewards |

17 November 2026 sits squarely inside the Article 14 window. The Commission's CRA reporting page states: *"As of 11 September 2026, manufacturers are required to report actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents impacting the security of products with digital elements."* The ENISA SRP FAQ states: *"The CRA reporting obligations under Art. 14 apply to manufacturers of products with digital elements from 11 September 2026."*

**The 2025 placing on the market is irrelevant.** ENISA SRP FAQ 12, citing the Commission's CRA Implementation FAQs (subsection 5.3), states that Article 14 *"will apply from 11 September 2026 to all products with digital elements falling within the scope of the CRA, including products that were placed on the market before 11 December 2027."* A product placed on the market in 2025 is covered a fortiori.

**The prior-awareness carve-out does not help here.** ENISA SRP FAQ: *"a manufacturer is not required to retrospectively report an actively exploited vulnerability where it was already aware of the active exploitation before 11 September 2026 ... However, where the manufacturer becomes aware of the active exploitation after that date, the reporting obligation applies, including where the underlying vulnerability existed or was previously known."* Awareness on 17 November 2026 is after 11 September 2026, so the duty attaches in full, even if the vulnerability is old or was previously disclosed.

---

## 3. Two issues that do NOT need to be resolved first

These were flagged as open in the request analysis; for the reporting question they are red herrings, and a compliance answer should say so explicitly.

**(a) Priority / non-priority (Annex III/IV 'important' or 'critical' product) status is not a trigger.** Article 14(1) is addressed to *manufacturers of products with digital elements* generally. Classification as an important or critical product affects the conformity-assessment route and the presumption/standards regime, not whether the Article 14 duty exists. Do not condition the filing on that classification.

**(b) The severity of the vulnerability is not a trigger either.** The severity threshold in Article 14(1) attaches to **incidents** ("severe incident having an impact on the security of the product"), not to vulnerabilities. The obligation is for **"any actively exploited vulnerability"** — i.e. a vulnerability *"for which there is reliable evidence that a malicious actor has exploited it in a system without permission of the system owner"* (ENISA SRP FAQ quoting the CRA definition). Once there is reliable evidence of exploitation, the duty is engaged; severity and impact go to the *content* of the report, not to whether a report is due.

So the compliance question reduces to: **is there reliable evidence of exploitation, and when did the manufacturer become aware?** Both are answered by the facts given.

---

## 4. Deadline schedule (ask 2)

Worked from an assumed awareness timestamp of **10:00 CET, Tuesday 17 November 2026** (substitute the actual documented timestamp; all three clocks run from that single instant).

| # | Filing | Legal basis | Clock | Worked deadline |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Early warning** | Art. 14(2)(a) | Without undue delay, and in any case **within 24 hours** of becoming aware | **Wednesday 18 November 2026, 10:00 CET** |
| 2 | **Vulnerability notification** | Art. 14(2)(b) | Without undue delay, and in any case **within 72 hours** of becoming aware | **Friday 20 November 2026, 10:00 CET** |
| 3 | **Final report** (actively exploited vulnerability) | Art. 14(2)(c) | No later than **14 days after a corrective or mitigating measure becomes available** | **Tuesday 1 December 2026** if a patch or mitigation is available on 17 November 2026; otherwise 14 days from the date availability is achieved (e.g. fix available 8 December 2026 → **22 December 2026**) |

**Important distinction — do not conflate the two final-report clocks.** The "one month after the 72-hour notification" deadline applies only to the **severe-incident** track (here: 20 December 2026). It is *not* the deadline for the actively exploited vulnerability, whose final report runs from **availability of a corrective or mitigating measure**, not from the notification. The two tracks can run in parallel if the exploitation escalates into a severe incident affecting availability, authenticity, integrity or confidentiality; each then has its own 24 h / 72 h / final chain, and both must be filed.

**"Without undue delay" governs.** 24 h and 72 h are outer limits, not targets. File the early warning as soon as the minimum data set exists; do not hold it back to complete the analysis.

---

## 5. Minimum content of each filing

| Filing | What must be in it |
|---|---|
| Early warning (24 h) | Product identification; indication of whether the activity is suspected to be malicious; any suspected cross-border impact; contact point. Keep it short — an incomplete but timely warning beats a complete late one. |
| Notification (72 h) | General information on the vulnerability; initial assessment of severity and impact; indicators of compromise where available. |
| Final report (14 days after fix/mitigation) | Description of the vulnerability; its severity and impact; corrective measures taken; mitigating measures applied where relevant. |

Not all SRP fields are mandatory at every stage — some become mandatory only at the 72-hour notification or the final report. Follow the SRP Glossary field-by-field rather than pasting the same text at each stage.

---

## 6. Where and how to file

- **Channel:** CRA Single Reporting Platform (SRP), `https://portal.cra-srp.enisa.europa.eu`, operational since 11 September 2026. Mandatory notifications must go through the SRP.
- **Who receives it:** the CSIRT of the Member State where the manufacturer has its **main establishment**. Unless particularly exceptional circumstances apply, the information is made available simultaneously to **ENISA**, and the receiving CSIRT shares it without delay with the CSIRTs of the Member States where the product has been made available. **One report, not one per Member State.**
- **Access:** the manufacturer's **Assigned Representative** must have an **EU Login account with multi-factor authentication enabled** and be registered on the SRP. This must be done *before* the deadline — registration is the classic cause of a missed 24-hour clock.
- **Dissemination hold:** if there are justified cybersecurity grounds for delaying wider dissemination (e.g. an unpatched fleet, or disclosure would accelerate exploitation), request it in the submission. The Commission adopted a delegated act on 11 December 2025 specifying the terms and conditions for such grounds.
- **Case closure:** only the CSIRT Designated as Coordinator (the CSIRT of the Member State where the notification was submitted) can close the report. Do not treat submission as closure; keep the case open and update it as facts develop.
- **Public disclosure:** under Article 17(5), ENISA may add a publicly known vulnerability notified under Article 14(1) to the European Vulnerability Database (EUVD) **in agreement with the manufacturer**. Coordinate the public advisory and the EUVD entry with the CSIRT.

---

## 7. Immediate actions (before 18 November 2026, 10:00 CET)

1. Log the awareness event with a timestamp and the evidence of active exploitation — this fixes the start of all three clocks and is the first thing a supervisory authority will ask for.
2. Confirm SRP access: Assigned Representative registered, EU Login MFA enabled, submission rights tested.
3. Assemble the early-warning pack: product identifier and version(s) affected, CVE/identifier if assigned, evidence of exploitation, IoCs, affected user population estimate, contact.
4. Prepare the remediation statement — what fix or mitigation exists, when it will be available, and what users can do meanwhile. If no fix exists yet, say so; the final-report clock starts on availability, not on awareness.
5. Decide who signs and who is on call across the 72-hour window.

---

## 8. Parallel and overlapping obligations (separate clocks, same facts)

- **CRA security-update duty (Art. 13(8)):** a free security update must be made available to users for the support period. The full obligation applies from 11 December 2027, but a fix or mitigation is in any event the event that starts the 14-day final-report clock, and other law may already require remediation.
- **GDPR:** if the exploitation compromises personal data, a personal data breach notification to the supervisory authority is due within **72 hours** of awareness (Art. 33), with user communication under Art. 34 where the threshold is met. This is a *separate* filing to a *separate* recipient; the CRA filing does not discharge it.
- **NIS2:** if the manufacturer is an essential or important entity (size- and sector-dependent), the Art. 23 significant-incident chain (24 h early warning / 72 h notification / 1 month final report) may run in parallel. The shape is similar; do not assume one filing satisfies the other.
- **GPSR / product safety:** if the exploitation creates a risk to consumer health or safety, general product safety rapid-alert obligations may also apply.
- **Sectoral carve-outs:** if the product is a medical device, in vitro diagnostic, motor vehicle, civil aviation product or otherwise covered by the other Union harmonisation legislation listed in Article 2 CRA, the CRA does not apply and the sectoral regime governs instead. A generic connected consumer product is not in that category.

---

## 9. Conditions of this opinion

1. The product is a **product with digital elements within CRA scope**, with no sectoral carve-out under Article 2 CRA. (A generic connected consumer product qualifies.)
2. The **17 November 2026 awareness is genuine 'becoming aware'** — reliable evidence of exploitation. If the evidence actually reached the manufacturer earlier, all three clocks started earlier and the deadlines above move back accordingly.
3. The manufacturer is established in the EU or has an authorised representative; if not, the importer/representative is the operational point of contact, but the reporting duty remains the manufacturer's.
4. Confirm against the consolidated text of Regulation (EU) 2024/2847 and Section 9.1 of the Commission CRA guidance / Section 5 of the Commission CRA Implementation FAQs whether any derogation applies to the manufacturer's size (microenterprise status) — the retrieved official sources do not address that point and it should be checked before the first filing, not after.

---

**Sources relied on:** European Commission, *Cyber Resilience Act – Reporting obligations* (updated 23 November 2026); ENISA, *Single Reporting Platform – Frequently Asked Questions*; Regulation (EU) 2024/2847 (CRA), Articles 13, 14, 16, 17, 24, 71.

COMPLIANCE NOTE — Annex II, Directive 2011/65/EU (RoHS) as currently consolidated
Reference text: Directive 2011/65/EU (recast), consolidated text CELEX 02011L0065, consolidation date 2026-07-01 (EUR-Lex ELI: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2011/65/2026-07-01/eng; PDF: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=CELEX:02011L0065-20260701).
