# AC-7 (Unsuccessful Logon Attempts), NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 — what the control actually requires for attempts, window and lockout

## 1. Answer

NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, control AC-7, requires **no specific number of consecutive invalid logon attempts, no specific time period, and no specific lockout duration**. All three are deliberately left blank in the control text and are marked as Assignment parameters to be filled in by the organization. The control's requirement is therefore procedural and assessable, not numeric: the organization must *define* these values, and the system must *enforce* them.

Consequently there is no figure to report for any of the three asks. Any specific numbers attributed to AC-7 come either from the implementing organization's own tailoring (its security plan / control implementation statement) or from a different document entirely — not from SP 800-53 Rev. 5.

- Ask 1 (number of attempts): **none stated — organization-defined.**
- Ask 2 (time period): **none stated — organization-defined.**
- Ask 3 (lockout duration): **none stated — organization-defined**, and only applicable at all if the organization selects the time-based lockout option from AC-7b's list.

## 2. Control text, verbatim

From https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/specialpublications/NIST.SP.800-53r5.pdf (fetched 2026-11-24T02:51:50Z, sha256 fc63bcd61715), corroborated word-for-word by the AC-7 page at https://nist-sp-800-53-r5.bsafes.com/docs/3-1-access-control/ac-7-unsuccessful-logon-attamps/ (sha256 f9630cd5ebc4) and by the OSCAL-derived PDF at https://csrc.nist.gov/CSRC/media/Projects/risk-management/800-53%20Downloads/800-53r5/SP_800-53_v5_1-derived-OSCAL.pdf (sha256 9ce01f4d67c9):

> **AC-7 UNSUCCESSFUL LOGON ATTEMPTS**
> **Control:**
> a. Enforce a limit of [Assignment: organization-defined number] consecutive invalid logon attempts by a user during a [Assignment: organization-defined time period]; and
> b. Automatically [Selection (one or more): lock the account or node for an [Assignment: organization-defined time period]; lock the account or node until released by an administrator; delay next logon prompt per [Assignment: organization-defined delay algorithm]; notify system administrator; take other [Assignment: organization-defined action]] when the maximum number of unsuccessful attempts is exceeded.
>
> **Discussion:** The need to limit unsuccessful logon attempts and take subsequent action when the maximum number of attempts is exceeded applies regardless of whether the logon occurs via a local or network connection. Due to the potential for denial of service, automatic lockouts initiated by systems are usually temporary and automatically release after a predetermined, organization-defined time period. If a delay algorithm is selected, organizations may employ different algorithms for different components of the system based on the capabilities of those components.

Note that even the Discussion, where one might expect a suggested figure, uses the phrase "a predetermined, organization-defined time period" — the placeholder is repeated, never resolved to a number.

## 3. Parameter map: each ask against the control text

| Ask | Control element it maps to | SP 800-53 operation type | What Rev. 5 states |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 — number of consecutive invalid logon attempts | AC-7a: "a limit of [Assignment: organization-defined number] consecutive invalid logon attempts by a user" | Assignment | No number. Placeholder only. |
| 2 — time period | AC-7a: "during a [Assignment: organization-defined time period]" | Assignment | No period. Placeholder only. |
| 3 — lockout duration | AC-7b, first selection option: "lock the account or node for an [Assignment: organization-defined time period]" | Selection (one or more) **plus** Assignment | No duration. Placeholder only, and the time-based lockout is only one of five selectable responses. |

**Critical nuance on ask 3.** AC-7b is a *Selection (one or more)*, not a mandate. The five selectable responses are: (i) lock the account or node for an organization-defined time period; (ii) lock the account or node until released by an administrator; (iii) delay the next logon prompt per an organization-defined delay algorithm; (iv) notify the system administrator; (v) take other organization-defined action. An organization that selects only (ii), (iii), (iv) or (v) has **no lockout duration at all**, and is still conformant with AC-7. So ask 3 has no answer even in the organization's own tailoring until the organization has made its AC-7b selection.

## 4. What AC-7 *does* require — the enforceable obligations

Stripped of the placeholders, AC-7 imposes five testable requirements. These are what an assessor actually verifies:

- **R1 — A limit exists and is enforced.** The system must refuse further authentication attempts after the configured maximum of consecutive failures for a given user. The limit must be a real, enforced parameter, not a documented intention.
- **R2 — The counting window is defined and bounded.** Failures are counted within a defined period; the implementation must have a determinate rule for when the counter starts and when it ages out.
- **R3 — The counting is per user and per consecutive failure.** A successful logon resets the counter (implied by "consecutive"). Failures attributed to other users do not count toward this user's limit.
- **R4 — An automated response fires on exceedance.** The response must be automatic and must be at least one of the actions selected under AC-7b.
- **R5 — The parameter values are documented and implemented consistently.** The chosen number, period, selected action and (if applicable) duration must appear in the system security plan / control implementation statement and must match the deployed configuration.

## 5. Why there are no numbers: the Assignment/Selection mechanism

SP 800-53 is a catalogue of controls, not a configuration standard. Bracketed `[Assignment: ...]` and `[Selection: ...]` operations are parameter placeholders; a control with unresolved placeholders is *not* implemented. The organisation resolves each placeholder in its security plan, based on risk tolerance, mission, and the system's exposure. NIST supplies the requirement structure and the assessment method; the organisation supplies the values.

This is confirmed by the baseline assignment: AC-7 appears in the Low, Moderate **and** High baselines (Appendix D, Table D-1, per https://csrc.nist.gov/CSRC/media/Publications/sp/800-53/rev-5/draft/documents/sp800-53r5-draft-baselines-markup.pdf, sha256 bba84ffcac41 — "AC-7 Unsuccessful Logon Attempts AC-7 AC-7 AC-7"). Baselines select *which controls apply*; they do not supply parameter values. SP 800-53B contains no parameter values either.

## 6. Control enhancements — also parameterised, none of them supply a figure

From the same sources (PDF sha256 fc63bcd61715; spreadsheet sha256 1777ed6f839b; AC-7 page sha256 f9630cd5ebc4):

- **AC-7(1) Automatic Account Lock — WITHDRAWN: "[Withdrawn: Incorporated into AC-7.]"** Do not cite AC-7(1) as a separate source of a lockout duration; its content was folded into the base control, and it too carried no number.
- **AC-7(2) Purge or Wipe Mobile Device** — "Purge or wipe information from [Assignment: organization-defined mobile devices] based on [Assignment: organization-defined purging or wiping requirements and techniques] after [Assignment: organization-defined number] consecutive, unsuccessful device logon attempts." Placeholder for the attempt count; no figure.
- **AC-7(3) Biometric Attempt Limiting** — "Limit the number of unsuccessful biometric logon attempts to [Assignment: organization-defined number]." Placeholder; no figure.
- **AC-7(4) Use of Alternate Authentication Factor** — "(a) Allow the use of [Assignment: organization-defined authentication factors] ... and (b) Enforce a limit of [Assignment: organization-defined number] consecutive invalid logon attempts through use of the alternative factors by a user during a [Assignment: organization-defined time period]." Placeholders; no figures.

Every enhancement that touches attempt counting is parameterised in exactly the same way as the base control.

## 7. Misattribution warning

Figures of the form "N attempts within T minutes, locked for D minutes" circulate widely in training material and blog posts and are sometimes attributed to AC-7. They are not in the control. Two independent lines of evidence:

1. **Direct reading.** The full AC-7 text, quoted verbatim in §2 from three separate renderings of Rev. 5, contains only Assignment placeholders at every point where a number, a period or a duration would appear.
2. **Search evidence (proofs of absence, run by the harness over full page text).** The string set {"lockout duration", "account lockout duration", "duration of the lockout", "lockout time", "lockout period"} does **not** occur anywhere in the 492-page Rev. 5 PDF (1,561,656 characters), the 396-page OSCAL-derived PDF (1,287,645 characters), the AC-7 control page (17,836 characters), the control-catalog spreadsheet (1,047,669 characters), the CSRC publication landing page (22,401 characters) or the draft baselines markup (19,808 characters). The string set {"time period", "specified period of time", "period of time", "time interval", "configured time period"} does not occur on the CSRC publication landing page or in the draft baselines markup. The string set {"number of consecutive invalid logon attempts", "consecutive invalid logon attempts", "invalid logon attempts", "unsuccessful logon attempts", "failed logon attempts"} does not occur on the CSRC publication landing page.

   **Precision caveat, stated so the evidence is not over-read:** the absence of the literal phrase "lockout duration" does not mean the control has no concept of duration. It means the concept is expressed as "[Assignment: organization-defined time period]" — an unfilled placeholder. The search proves there is no *stated duration*; it does not and cannot prove there is no *duration field*.

## 8. Where the actual numbers come from

The values AC-7 leaves blank are supplied by, in order of authority for a given system:

1. **Organisational policy and the system security plan / control implementation statement** — the authoritative source for a given system. This is what AC-7 points at when it says "organization-defined".
2. **Tailoring in the authorisation package** — risk analysis, mission need, exposure of the authentication surface, threat model, and denial-of-service considerations (the AC-7 Discussion explicitly raises DoS as the reason automatic lockouts are usually temporary).
3. **Other, separate standards** — e.g. NIST SP 800-63B (digital identity) or CIS Benchmarks — if the organisation chooses to adopt them by reference. These are *not* SP 800-53 and are outside this deliverable; no values from them were verified here and none should be reported as an AC-7 requirement.

## 9. Tailoring procedure: producing the three values AC-7 leaves open

This is the work an organisation must do to close out AC-7. Each step produces a documented artefact.

**Step 1 — Resolve AC-7a, ask 1 (attempt limit).** Choose a maximum consecutive-failure count, N. Inputs: the authentication strength in use (MFA permits a higher N than single-factor); whether AC-7(4) alternate factors are offered; the account lockout's DoS exposure; whether privileged and unprivileged accounts need different values. Record N per account class.

**Step 2 — Resolve AC-7a, ask 2 (counting window).** Choose the period T over which consecutive failures are counted. Decide the reset semantics explicitly: does the counter reset on successful logon only, or also on expiry of T? Record the rule, not just the number, because R2 and R3 are assessed against the rule.

**Step 3 — Resolve AC-7b (selection).** Select one or more of the five options. Selection criteria:
- *Time-based lockout* — simple, self-healing, but a DoS vector against known usernames; the AC-7 Discussion endorses keeping it temporary for exactly this reason.
- *Administrator release* — strongest against brute force, highest help-desk cost and DoS exposure; usually reserved for privileged accounts or high-impact systems.
- *Delay algorithm* — good availability/security balance; the Discussion notes different algorithms may be used for different components according to their capabilities.
- *Notify system administrator* — an alerting control, not a blocking one; normally combined with another option rather than used alone.
- *Other* — must be described concretely enough to be assessed.

**Step 4 — Resolve ask 3 (lockout duration), conditionally.** Only if the time-based lockout option was selected in Step 3, choose the duration D and record it. If it was not selected, record explicitly that no lockout duration exists and name the option(s) chosen instead — this is a complete and conformant answer.

**Step 5 — Check for interactions.** Confirm the chosen N, T and D do not conflict with: AC-7(2) mobile-device wipe threshold (a device-wipe count lower than N would fire first and destroy the device before the account lockout is reached — usually undesirable); AC-7(3) biometric attempt limit (if biometrics are a factor, its limit interacts with N); AC-7(4) alternate-factor path (it exists precisely so a locked-out user can recover without administrator release); AC-9 previous-logon notification; AU-2/AU-6 logging and review; IR-4/IR-5 incident handling for lockout storms.

**Step 6 — Document.** Write the resolved values into the control implementation statement (template in §10).

**Step 7 — Verify against the deployed configuration.** Configuration drift between the SSP statement and the identity provider / OS / application settings is the most common AC-7 finding. Test per §11.

### Tailoring worksheet (fill in; blanks are the point)

| Field | AC-7 reference | Value | Account class | Rationale / risk basis |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Max consecutive invalid attempts | AC-7a | N = ____ | | |
| Counting window | AC-7a | T = ____ | | |
| Counter reset rule | AC-7a (R3) | reset on successful logon / reset on window expiry / both | | |
| Selected response(s) | AC-7b | lock for duration / lock until admin release / delay algorithm / notify admin / other | | |
| Lockout duration (if time-based selected) | AC-7b option 1 | D = ____ | | |
| Delay algorithm (if selected) | AC-7b option 3 | describe | | |
| Alternate factors (if AC-7(4) used) | AC-7(4) | list factors, and their own N′ and T′ | | |

## 10. Control implementation statement template

> **AC-7a.** <System name> enforces a limit of **N** consecutive invalid logon attempts by a user during a **T** period. The failure counter is maintained per user account, is reset on successful authentication, and ages out at the end of the T period.
> **AC-7b.** When the limit is exceeded, <system name> automatically **<selected option(s), with D or the delay algorithm named>**. Enforcement is performed by <mechanism: identity provider / OS policy / application control>, configured at <configuration item reference>.
> **Parameters** are documented in the SSP at <section>, approved by <role>, and reviewed at <frequency>.

## 11. Assessment procedure (how a verifier confirms the values are enforced)

Using the organisation's resolved N, T and D:

1. From a test account, submit N−1 invalid credentials within T; confirm no lockout, no delay and no administrator notification (confirms the limit is not set lower than documented).
2. Submit the Nth invalid credential; confirm the selected AC-7b response fires (confirms R1, R4).
3. If time-based lockout is selected: wait until D has elapsed; confirm the account releases automatically. If administrator-release is selected: confirm release requires an administrator action and that no timed release occurs (confirms R4 and the ask-3 answer).
4. Confirm the attempt counter resets on a successful logon before N is reached (confirms R3).
5. Confirm failures older than T do not count toward the limit (confirms R2).
6. Confirm the lockout event is logged and routed per AU-2/AU-6 (confirms the notify-administrator option, if selected).
7. Diff the deployed configuration against the SSP statement; any mismatch is a finding (confirms R5).

## 12. Answering the question as asked

If the question is *what does AC-7 require*, the answer is: a limit, a window and (optionally) a duration that the organisation itself must define and enforce, with no values fixed by NIST. If the question behind the question is *what values should I configure*, that cannot be answered from SP 800-53 Rev. 5 — it must be answered from the organisation's own policy and risk decision, using the procedure in §9. Producing a number in response to the literal question would be fabrication; the correct engineering output is the parameterised requirement plus the tailoring procedure that resolves it.

# Legal analysis — Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 (machinery): date of application and status of Directive 2006/42/EC as at 17 November 2026

## 1. Question presented

According to the text of Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 **as corrected and in force on 17 November 2026**: (a) from which date does the Regulation apply and Directive 2006/42/EC cease to apply, and (b) is Directive 2006/42/EC still in force today?

## 2. Authority and version control (what 'corrected and in force today' means)

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Basic act | Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 of 14 June 2023 on machinery, OJ L 165, 29.6.2023, p. 1 |
| Entry into force | 19 July 2023 (Art. 54, first para.: 20th day after publication) |
| Correction | Corrigendum, OJ L 169, 4.7.2023, p. 35 (CELEX 32023R1230R(01)) — **operative for this question** |
| Amendments incorporated | Regulation (EU) 2024/2748 (M1, OJ L 2748, 8.11.2024) and Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (M2, OJ L 1744, 24.7.2026) — neither carries an amendment marker on Arts. 51, 52 or 54 |
| Consolidated version current on 17 Nov 2026 | CELEX 02023R1230 — EN — **27.07.2026** — 002.001 (latest consolidated version before today; the next most recent is 29.05.2026) |

The consolidated version of 27.07.2026 is therefore the text that governs. In that text the date-bearing provisions (Arts. 51(2), 52(1), 53(1), 54) carry only the **►C1** marker, i.e. they are as corrected by the 4 July 2023 corrigendum and have not been altered by M1 or M2.

## 3. Operative text as corrected (consolidated version 27.07.2026)

**Article 51(2) — Repeals**
> 'Directive 2006/42/EC is repealed with effect from **►C1 20 January 2027 ◄**.'

**Article 52(1) — Transitional provisions**
> 'Member States shall not impede the making available on the market of products which were placed on the market in conformity with Directive 2006/42/EC before **►C1 20 January 2027 ◄**. However, Chapter VI of this Regulation shall apply, from **►C1 19 July 2023 ◄**, mutatis mutandis to such products instead of Article 11 of that Directive…'

**Article 54 — Entry into force and application**
> 'This Regulation shall enter into force on the twentieth day following that of its publication in the Official Journal of the European Union.' (→ 19 July 2023)
> 'It shall apply from **20 January 2027**.' (second para., as corrected by ►C1)
> 'However, the following Articles shall apply from the following dates: (a) Articles 26 to 42 from **►C1 20 January 2024 ◄**; (b) Article 50(1) from **►C1 20 October 2026 ◄**; (c) Article 6(7) and Articles 48 and 52 from **►C1 19 July 2023 ◄**; (d) Article 6(2) to (6), (8) and (11) and Articles 47 and 53(3) from **►C1 20 July 2024 ◄**.'

**Corrigendum, OJ L 169, 4.7.2023, p. 35 — relevant points**
- Pt 5: Art. 51(2), first subpara.: for '14 January 2027', read '20 January 2027'.
- Pt 6: Art. 52(1), first sentence: for '14 January 2027', read '20 January 2027'.
- Pt 7: Art. 52(1), second sentence: for '13 July 2023', read '19 July 2023'.
- Pt 3: Art. 47(2): for '13 July 2023', read '19 July 2023'.
- Pt 4: Art. 50(2): for '14 October 2026', read '20 October 2026'.
- The same systematic correction of the '14th' to the '20th' is carried into Art. 54 (the ►C1 markers on 20 January 2024, 20 October 2026, 19 July 2023 and 20 July 2024 in the consolidated text), and into Art. 54, second para. ('20 January 2027'). The purpose of the corrigendum is to align every date with the true entry-into-force date of 19 July 2023 (publication 29 June 2023 + 20 days), which the original OJ text had mis-computed as 13/14 July 2023.

**Why the correction matters.** The uncorrected OJ text (L 165, 29.6.2023) — still displayed on the non-consolidated EUR-Lex pages — reads '14 January 2027' in Art. 51(2), Art. 52(1) and Art. 54. A reading based on that text is wrong. The corrected text in force today reads **20 January 2027**. The Commission's own EUR-Lex summary confirms: 'Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 will apply from 20 January 2027' and 'repeals and replaces Directive 2006/42/EC as of 20 January 2027'.

## 4. Answers

**(a) Date from which the Regulation applies and the Directive stops applying: 20 January 2027.**
- Regulation applies in full from **20 January 2027** (Art. 54, second para., as corrected), subject to the earlier partial applications listed above.
- Directive 2006/42/EC is repealed, and therefore ceases to apply, **with effect from 20 January 2027** (Art. 51(2), as corrected). The two dates coincide; there is no gap and no overlap in the general regime.
- Date arithmetic check: 20 January 2027 is exactly 42 months after entry into force (19 July 2023), which is the deferral rationale recited in the preamble ('sufficient time for economic operators to comply … the application of this Regulation should therefore be deferred').

**(b) Is Directive 2006/42/EC still in force on 17 November 2026? Yes.** The repeal in Art. 51(2) takes effect on 20 January 2027; a repeal 'with effect from' a future date does not produce effects before that date. On 17 November 2026 the Directive remains in force and continues to govern machinery placed on the market until 20 January 2027. Two qualifications a client must be told:
1. **Partial displacement already operating.** Since 19 July 2023, Chapter VI of the Regulation (market surveillance / Union safeguard procedure) applies *mutatis mutandis* to products placed on the market under the Directive, in place of Article 11 of the Directive (Art. 52(1), second sentence). The Directive is in force but its safeguard mechanism is already superseded.
2. **Other provisions already live.** Articles 26–42 apply from 20 January 2024 (notified bodies), Art. 50(1) from 20 October 2026 (i.e. already applicable on 17 November 2026), Art. 6(7) and Arts. 48 and 52 from 19 July 2023, and Art. 6(2)–(6), (8), (11), Arts. 47 and 53(3) from 20 July 2024.

**Distinction to be maintained.** 'Entry into force' (19 July 2023), 'applies' (20 January 2027 generally, with staged earlier applications) and 'ceases to apply / repealed' (Directive, 20 January 2027) are three different legal states. The Regulation is in force *and* partially applicable today; the Directive is in force *and* fully applicable today, save for the Chapter VI displacement.

## 5. Transitional consequences (Art. 52) — for completeness

- Products placed on the market in conformity with Directive 2006/42/EC **before 20 January 2027** may continue to be made available on the market; Member States must not impede this (Art. 52(1), first sentence). This is a placing-on-the-market cut-off, not a sell-off deadline for distributors: once lawfully placed on the market before 20 January 2027, further making available (e.g. resale, distribution) is protected.
- EC type-examination certificates and approval decisions issued under Article 12 of the Directive **remain valid until they expire** (Art. 52(2)) — no re-issuance under the Regulation is required on that ground alone.
- References to the repealed Directive are to be read as references to the Regulation, in accordance with the correlation table in Annex XII (Art. 51(2), second subpara.).

## 6. Verification notes / caveats

1. **Superseded figures must not be used.** Any internal document citing '14 January 2027' (from the original OJ text, or from pre-4 July 2023 drafts) should be corrected to 20 January 2027.
2. **Minor error in the EUR-Lex summary page.** The summary states 'Article 50(1) from 20 October 2023'; the operative text (Art. 54(b), as corrected) says **20 October 2026**. The summary is a non-binding abstract ('documentary value only' for consolidated texts); the operative text prevails. No effect on the answer to asks 2 and 3.
3. **Residual risk of a later deferral.** The check is run against the consolidated version of 27 July 2026, which is the version current on 17 November 2026 and which contains no amendment marker later than C1 on Arts. 51, 52 or 54. Any act adopted after 27 July 2026 purporting to defer the application date would not appear in that consolidated version; none is reflected in the EUR-Lex status line ('In force: This act has been changed. Current consolidated version: 27/07/2026'). A last-mile confirmation against the OJ L series for August–November 2026 is prudent before any contract or labelling decision is finalised, but the legal position stated here is the one the corrected text supports.
4. **Territorial/EEA scope** does not affect the dates.

## 7. Bottom line

| Point | Answer |
|---|---|
| Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 applies in full from | **20 January 2027** (Art. 54, 2nd para., as corrected by OJ L 169, 4.7.2023, p. 35) |
| Directive 2006/42/EC ceases to apply / is repealed with effect from | **20 January 2027** (Art. 51(2), as corrected) |
| Directive 2006/42/EC still in force on 17 November 2026? | **Yes** — repeal not yet effective; Chapter VI of the Regulation already applies *mutatis mutandis* in place of its Art. 11 since 19 July 2023 |

## 8. Sources relied on

- Regulation (EU) 2023/1230, consolidated version 02023R1230 — EN — 27.07.2026 (Arts. 51, 52, 53, 54).
- Corrigendum to Regulation (EU) 2023/1230, OJ L 169, 4.7.2023, pp. 35–36, ELI http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2023/1230/corrigendum/2023-07-04/oj.
- EUR-Lex act page and 'Dates' table for CELEX 32023R1230 (entry into force 19/07/2023; partial application 19/07/2023, 20/01/2024, 20/07/2024, 20/10/2026).
- EUR-Lex summary 'Machinery safety requirements — SUMMARY OF: Regulation (EU) 2023/1230' (application from 20 January 2027; repeal and replacement of Directive 2006/42/EC as of 20 January 2027).

question: X2
answer:
REGULATORY DETERMINATION — Legacy class IIa device under MDD 93/42/EEC, certificate kept valid by Art. 120(2) MDR (EU) 2017/745, Art. 120(3c) conditions assumed met.

1. ANSWER

| # | Question | Answer | Legal basis |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2 | Last date on which the legacy device may be placed on the market or put into service | 31 December 2028 | Art. 120(3a)(b) MDR, as inserted by Regulation (EU) 2023/607 |
| 3 | Deadline to lodge a formal application with a notified body | 26 May 2024 | Art. 120(3c)(e) MDR (first limb) |
| 3 | Deadline to have a written agreement signed with the notified body | 26 September 2024 | Art. 120(3c)(e) MDR (second limb) |

Both ask-3 dates are already in the past (grounding fetched 24 November 2026). The question is correctly framed in the past tense ('must it have lodged ... had signed'): these are conditions precedent to the 2028 sell-off, not future planning dates. If either was missed, the 31 December 2028 date is not available at all and the device may only be placed on the market / put into service once a full MDR certificate is issued (or under an Art. 59 derogation).

2. DERIVATION, STEP BY STEP

Step 1 — Is the device inside the transitional regime at all? The certificate was issued under Directive 93/42/EEC and is kept valid by Art. 120(2) MDR. Art. 120(3a) applies to 'devices for which a certificate valid by virtue of paragraph 2 of this Article has been issued in accordance with Directive 90/385/EEC or Directive 93/42/EEC'. Yes.

Step 2 — Which tier? Art. 120(3a) has two tiers:
 (a) 31 December 2027 — all class III devices and class IIb implantable devices, excluding well-established technologies (sutures, staples, dental fillings, dental braces, tooth crowns, screws, wedges, plates, wires, pins, clips, connectors);
 (b) 31 December 2028 — class IIb devices other than those in (a), class IIa devices, and class I devices placed on the market in a sterile condition or with a measuring function.
A class IIa device falls in tier (b). The 2027 date is irrelevant to it. (The same 31 December 2028 date is given for devices that needed no notified body under the MDD but need one under the MDR, e.g. class I re-usable surgical instruments — not this case, but it confirms the outer bound of the regime.)

Step 3 — Conditions attached to that date (Art. 120(3c), as amended by Reg. (EU) 2023/607), which the request tells us to assume are met:
 (a) the device continues to comply with Directive 93/42/EEC;
 (b) there are no significant changes in the design or intended purpose of the device;
 (c) [3c(d)] a QMS conforming to Art. 10(9) MDR is in place no later than 26 May 2024;
 (d) [3c(e)] no later than 26 May 2024 the manufacturer or authorised representative has lodged a formal application with a notified body under Annex VII s.4.3 first subparagraph for the device or a substitute device, and no later than 26 September 2024 the notified body and the manufacturer have signed a written agreement under Annex VII s.4.3 second subparagraph;
 (e) [3c(f)] the notified body responsible for the certificate carries out the appropriate surveillance.
With (a)–(e) satisfied, the device 'may be placed on the market or put into service until' 31 December 2028.

Step 4 — Result: 31 December 2028; application by 26 May 2024; agreement by 26 September 2024.

3. CORRECTION TO THE PROJECT BRIEF — DO NOT USE ITS 2028 FIGURES

The project brief's 'usually relevant' section states that the application must be lodged by 31 May 2028 and the agreement signed by 31 August 2028 (described there as 'extended from the original 26 September 2024'). That is wrong and appears in none of the sources. Art. 120(3c)(e) — quoted verbatim in the grounding from two independent sources — sets 26 May 2024 and 26 September 2024, and Regulation (EU) 2023/607 did not move those two dates; it moved the market-access dates (to 31 Dec 2027 / 31 Dec 2028 / 26 May 2026) and removed the sell-off rule. Any downstream document reproducing '31 May 2028' or '31 August 2028' should be corrected. Sanity check: an application deadline of 31 May 2028 would sit after the 31 December 2028 cut-off only in appearance — it would leave seven months to obtain a certificate, which is not what the legislator enacted and not what any source says.

4. EVIDENCE TRAIL (verbatim from the grounding)

- 31 December 2028, class IIa: '31 December 2028 for other Class IIb devices, Class IIa, Class I devices placed on the market in sterile condition or have a measuring function' — Commission/MDCG confirmation letter template, health.ec.europa.eu/document/download/c56f83df-... (md_confirmation-letter-2023-607-nbcg.docx).
- 31 December 2028, class IIa: 'Devices covered by valid MDD/AIMDD Certificates (as of 20 March 2023) and that are Class IIb devices (excluding Class IIb implantable non-WET), or Class IIa devices, or Class I sterile devices or Class I devices with a measuring function; ... 31 December 2028' — BSI transition-timeline deck, slide table.
- 31 December 2028, class IIa: 'December 31, 2028, for class IIb devices other than those referred to in subparagraph (a) of this paragraph, class IIa devices, and class I devices placed on the market in a sterile condition or with a measuring function.' — Johner Institute, quoting Art. 120(3a)(b).
- 26 May 2024 and 26 September 2024: 'no later than 26 May 2024, the manufacturer or the authorised representative has lodged a formal application with a notified body in accordance with Section 4.3, first subparagraph, of Annex VII ... and, no later than 26 September 2024, the notified body and the manufacturer have signed a written agreement in accordance with Section 4.3, second subparagraph, of Annex VII.' — BSI deck, quoting Art. 120(3c)(e); corroborated by Johner ('no later than September 26, 2024'; 'May 2024 at the latest to a notified body') and by the HPRA page ('the manufacturer or authorised representative has lodged an application for MDR certification with a notified body by 26 May 2024, the manufacturer has signed a written agreement with a notified body by 26 September 2024').
- QMS condition: 'no later than 26 May 2024, the manufacturer has put in place a quality management system in accordance with Article 10(9)' — BSI deck, Art. 120(3c)(d).
- Removal of the sell-off restriction: 'The restrictions ("sell-off rule") have been removed by the amending regulation.' — Johner; HPRA: 'devices already placed on the market can continue to be made available or put into service until the revised expiry of the certificate or until the shelf life of the device.'

5. SCOPE OF THE PROOF OF ABSENCE ON ASK 2 (disclosed, not dispositive)

The harness proof of absence for ask 2 concerns only https://www.hpra.ie/regulation/medical-devices/manufacturers-and-authorised-representatives/mdr-transitional-provisions (27,861 characters): none of '31 December 2028', '31 December 2027', '27 May 2025', '27 May 2024', 'Article 120(2)', 'Article 120(3c)', 'placed on the market or put into service' occurs in that page. That is accurate — the HPRA page states only '2028 for other class IIb, class IIa and Class Is, Im devices' without the day and month, and gives the two 2024 condition dates. Because the proof is page-scoped and three other sources in the same grounding state 31 December 2028 for class IIa verbatim, the ask is answered and is therefore not recorded as not stated. The date does not rest on the HPRA page.

6. NUANCES THAT AFFECT HOW THE DATE IS APPLIED

(a) Placing on the market vs putting into service. Art. 120(3) permits both 'until' 31 December 2028. Because Reg. (EU) 2023/607 deleted the sell-off restriction in Art. 120(4), units lawfully placed on the market on or before 31 December 2028 may continue to be made available to the end user and put into service after that date, for the shelf life of the device. The 31 December 2028 date is therefore the cut-off for new placements, not a recall date.
(b) The certificate's own expiry still bites. 31 December 2028 is the outer limit of the transitional regime, not a substitute for certificate validity; if the Art. 120(2) validity is withdrawn, surrendered or expires earlier without renewal, the grace falls away on that earlier date.
(c) Continuity of the conditions. The 2028 date is available only while every 3c condition is continuously satisfied. Withdrawal of the notified-body application or termination of the written agreement means 3c(e) is no longer met and the transition period is lost from that point (Johner, in German, states exactly this). A significant change in design or intended purpose has the same effect.
(d) The agreement may be signed before 26 September 2024; earlier signature does not shorten the 31 December 2028 date.
(e) Certificate-specific dates are not addressed here because the request does not state the certificate number or expiry; the answer is the statutory outer limit for a general class IIa device, and is not the answer for a class IIa surgically invasive instrument only if a different classification under the MDR moves the device into another tier (it does not: MDR class IIa remains tier (b)).
(f) Law is stated as at the grounding date (24 November 2026). No post-2023/607 amendment to these three dates appears in the grounding; the 31 December 2028 date, and the two 2024 condition dates, should be re-verified against the in-force text of Art. 120 MDR at the moment of reliance, since the transition timeline has been amended once already.

7. WHAT WOULD VOID THIS ANSWER

If any of the following is true, the answer above does not apply and the device needs a full MDR certificate before it is placed on the market or put into service: no formal application lodged by 26 May 2024; no signed written agreement by 26 September 2024; no MDR-compliant QMS by 26 May 2024; significant change in design or intended purpose after the certificate date; certificate not in fact valid by virtue of Art. 120(2); application withdrawn or agreement terminated.

question: X6
answer:
REGULATORY ANSWER — EU REACH Art. 33(2): consumer right to know about Candidate List substances in articles

GOVERNING PROVISION (verbatim, Art. 33 of Regulation (EC) No 1907/2006 as fetched)
Art. 33(2): 'On request by a consumer any supplier of an article containing a substance meeting the criteria in Article 57 and identified in accordance with Article 59(1) in a concentration above 0,1 % weight by weight (w/w) shall provide the consumer with sufficient information, available to the supplier, to allow safe use of the article including, as a minimum, the name of that substance. The relevant information shall be provided, free of charge, within 45 days of receipt of the request.'
Sources: https://www.legislation.gov.uk/eur/2006/1907/article/33/data.xht and https://reachonline.eu/REACH/EN/REACH_EN/article33.html (texts identical on all three points).

ANSWERS
1) Concentration threshold: 0.1 % w/w of the article. The duty to answer arises only where the Candidate List substance is present in the article in a concentration ABOVE 0.1 % weight by weight. Exactly 0.1 % does not trigger the duty ('above 0,1 %'). In practice: 0.1 % w/w = 1 g of the substance per 1 kg of article mass. Calculation: concentration (%) = (mass of substance in the article / mass of the article) x 100.
2) Deadline: 45 days from receipt of the consumer's request. The clock starts on the day the retailer receives the request; 45 calendar days. Worked example: request received 1 March -> answer due by 15 April (30 days remaining in March + 15 days in April). The 45-day clock is flat in the operative text; it is not conditioned on how recently the substance was added to the Candidate List. (Note: the project briefing's premise of a '12-month since listing' variant is NOT supported by the Article 33 text fetched and should not be relied on; no such carve-out appears in Art. 33. If a supplier asserts one, ask for the legal citation.)
3) May the retailer charge? NO. The second subparagraph of Art. 33(2) requires the information to be provided 'free of charge'. No fee, handling charge, administration charge, cost-recovery for supplier enquiries, or pass-through of analytical testing costs may be imposed on the consumer for answering an Art. 33(2) request.

WHO OWES THE DUTY
'Any supplier of an article' — this includes a retailer/distributor that places the article on the market (Art. 3(14) defines distributor as including a retailer). The retailer cannot deflect the request to its own supplier; it may (and normally must) obtain the data via Art. 33(1) supply-chain communication, but the answer is owed by the retailer to the consumer within 45 days regardless. The qualifier 'available to the supplier' limits the depth of the safe-use information, not the obligation to respond or the deadline.

SCOPE CONDITIONS TO CHECK BEFORE APPLYING THE 0.1 % FIGURE
- The object must be an ARTICLE (Art. 3(3): an object which during production is given a special shape, surface or design which determines its function to a greater degree than does its chemical composition). If the product is a substance or mixture as supplied, Art. 33 does not apply — the Safety Data Sheet / CLP regime does, and the 0.1 % article threshold is the wrong test.
- The substance must be on the Candidate List (Art. 59(1)) at the time of the request.
- Concentration is assessed on the article as placed on the market. Per ECHA guidance (Guidance for Suppliers of Articles), where an article is assembled from objects that were themselves articles before assembly, the 0.1 % trigger is applied to each such object; where a substance/mixture (e.g. paint, glue) was added during production, the trigger is applied to the article to which it was added. The headline figure remains 0.1 % w/w; the disputed question is only what 'the article' is.
- The requester must be a consumer. A professional/industrial recipient is covered by Art. 33(1) (no 45-day statutory deadline, no 'free of charge' clause).
- If the substance is not present above 0.1 % w/w, the Art. 33(2) duty to supply the information does not arise; a clear statement that the substance is not present above 0.1 % w/w is the appropriate response and is best given within the same 45 days.

OPERATING PROCEDURE FOR THE RETAILER
1. Log the date of receipt of the request (this starts the 45-day clock) and the identity of the requester (consumer vs professional).
2. Identify the exact article and the substance named; confirm the substance is on the current Candidate List.
3. Obtain the concentration data from the producer/importer/upstream supplier under Art. 33(1); if data is unavailable, state what is available — the obligation is to give information 'available to the supplier', not to generate new data.
4. Compute concentration against the correct article mass (see scope conditions).
5. Reply in writing, free of charge, by day 45, naming the substance and giving sufficient information for safe use; keep a record of the request date, the reply and its date.

CONSEQUENCES OF NON-COMPLIANCE
Member States set penalties for breach of REACH (Art. 126); the level varies by jurisdiction. Charging a fee is itself a breach of the 'free of charge' requirement. Enforcement exposure therefore depends on the Member State of the retailer.

JURISDICTIONAL NOTE
This answer is the EU REACH position. The GB retained version of Art. 33 carries the same 0.1 % / 45 days / free of charge text, so the figures do not change for GB, but the Candidate List (GB vs ECHA) and enforcement differ; for non-EU jurisdictions the answer must be re-derived.

PIN CITED ANSWERS: 0.1 % w/w (Art. 33(2), first subparagraph); 45 days (Art. 33(2), second subparagraph); free of charge — no fee permitted (Art. 33(2), second subparagraph).

question: X7
shape: EU cybersecurity of networks and information systems (NIS2)
answer:
# NIS2 incident notification deadlines

## 1. Direct answer

| Entity / incident | Notification | Deadline | Legal basis |
|---|---|---|---|
| Trust service provider — significant incident that has an impact on the provision of its trust services | Incident notification to the CSIRT or, where applicable, the competent authority | Without undue delay and in any event within **24 hours** of becoming aware of the significant incident | Directive (EU) 2022/2555, Article 23(4), second subparagraph |
| Other essential and important entities | Incident notification to the CSIRT or, where applicable, the competent authority | Without undue delay and in any event within **72 hours** of becoming aware of the significant incident | Directive (EU) 2022/2555, Article 23(4), first subparagraph, point (b) |

In short: **24 hours for a trust service provider whose trust services are affected; 72 hours for other essential and important entities.** Both periods run from the moment the entity becomes aware of the significant incident, and both are outer limits subject to the overriding obligation to notify without undue delay.

## 2. Exact legal text

Article 23(4), first subparagraph, point (b), of Directive (EU) 2022/2555 provides that the entities concerned must submit:

> "without undue delay and in any event within 72 hours of becoming aware of the significant incident, an incident notification, which, where applicable, shall update the information referred to in point (a) and indicate an initial assessment of the significant incident, including its severity and impact, as well as, where available, the indicators of compromise;"

Article 23(4), second subparagraph, provides the trust service provider derogation:

> "By way of derogation from the first subparagraph, point (b), a trust service provider shall, with regard to significant incidents that have an impact on the provision of its trust services, notify the CSIRT or, where applicable, the competent authority, without undue delay and in any event within 24 hours of becoming aware of the significant incident."

Article 23(1) establishes the underlying duty:

> "Each Member State shall ensure that essential and important entities notify, without undue delay, its CSIRT or, where applicable, its competent authority in accordance with paragraph 4 of any incident that has a significant impact on the provision of their services as referred to in paragraph 3 (significant incident)."

## 3. Do not confuse the incident notification with the early warning

The NIS2 reporting regime is staged. The 24-hour trust service provider rule is a derogation only from point (b) — the incident notification — not from point (a), the early warning.

| Stage | All essential and important entities | Trust service providers (trust-service impact) | Legal basis |
|---|---|---|---|
| Early warning | Without undue delay and in any event within **24 hours** of awareness | Without undue delay and in any event within **24 hours** of awareness | Article 23(4)(a) |
| Incident notification | Without undue delay and in any event within **72 hours** of awareness | Without undue delay and in any event within **24 hours** of awareness | Article 23(4)(b) and Article 23(4), second subparagraph |
| Intermediate report | On request of the CSIRT or competent authority | On request of the CSIRT or competent authority | Article 23(4)(c) |
| Final report | Not later than **one month** after submission of the incident notification | Not later than **one month** after submission of the incident notification | Article 23(4)(d) |
| Progress report / final report if incident ongoing | Progress report at the time of the final report; final report within one month of handling the incident | Progress report at the time of the final report; final report within one month of handling the incident | Article 23(4)(e) |

**Practical consequence for trust service providers:** the early warning remains due at 24 hours, and the incident notification is also due at 24 hours. The provider should be prepared to submit both at the 24-hour mark, or to use a combined submission if the national CSIRT or competent authority expressly permits it. Do not treat the 24-hour incident notification as a substitute for the early warning unless the national reporting channel confirms that the two have been combined.

## 4. When the clock starts: "becoming aware"

The clock runs from **becoming aware of the significant incident**, not from the first anomalous log entry, alert, or third-party tip. Under the Commission's guidance and Recital 101 of the Directive, an entity becomes aware when, after an initial assessment, it has a reasonable degree of certainty that a significant incident has occurred. The initial assessment period is therefore critical: the entity should assess suspicious events in a timely manner and record when it reached the threshold of reasonable certainty.

Compliance control: maintain a timestamped incident-decision log showing (a) the first detection, (b) the assessment steps, (c) the moment the entity concluded that a significant incident had occurred, and (d) the moment each notification was submitted. That log is the primary evidence for the start of the 24-hour and 72-hour periods.

## 5. Scope condition for the 24-hour trust service provider rule

The 24-hour rule applies only where both conditions are met:

1. the incident is a **significant incident** within the meaning of Article 23(3); and
2. the significant incident **has an impact on the provision of the trust service provider's trust services**.

If a trust service provider suffers a significant incident that does **not** impact the provision of its trust services, the general 72-hour incident-notification deadline applies. If the incident is not significant, there is no mandatory Article 23 notification, although a voluntary notification may be made.

Trust service providers are listed in Annex I (digital infrastructure) and are in scope as essential or important entities depending on size; Article 23 applies to both essential and important entities.

## 6. Notification route and content

- **Route:** notify the national CSIRT or, where applicable, the competent authority. Where the entity notifies the competent authority, the Member State must ensure that the competent authority forwards the notification to the CSIRT upon receipt.
- **Incident notification content:** the incident notification must update the early warning where applicable and must include an initial assessment of the significant incident, including its severity and impact, and, where available, indicators of compromise.
- **Early warning content:** where applicable, indicate whether the incident is suspected of being caused by unlawful or malicious acts or could have a cross-border impact.

## 7. Worked deadline example

Assume the entity becomes aware of a significant incident at **2026-01-12 10:00 UTC**.

| Entity / stage | Deadline | Illustrative deadline |
|---|---|---|
| Early warning — all entities | 24 hours after awareness | 2026-01-13 10:00 UTC |
| Incident notification — trust service provider (trust-service impact) | 24 hours after awareness | 2026-01-13 10:00 UTC |
| Incident notification — other essential and important entities | 72 hours after awareness | 2026-01-15 10:00 UTC |
| Final report — trust service provider, if incident notification submitted 2026-01-13 10:00 UTC | One month after submission of incident notification | 2026-02-13 10:00 UTC |
| Final report — other essential and important entities, if incident notification submitted 2026-01-15 10:00 UTC | One month after submission of incident notification | 2026-02-15 10:00 UTC |

The example is illustrative. The final report is calculated from the actual submission time of the incident notification, not from the awareness time. Month-end and national public-holiday rules should be confirmed against the applicable national law.

## 8. Compliance procedure and controls

1. **Incident response plan:** embed the 24-hour early warning, 24-hour trust service provider incident notification, and 72-hour general incident notification into the incident response runbook with named owners and backup owners.
2. **Pre-identification:** record the national CSIRT and competent authority contacts, reporting portal, authentication requirements, and any mandated template before an incident occurs.
3. **Pre-approved templates:** maintain draft early-warning and incident-notification templates so that the 24-hour and 72-hour deadlines are not lost to drafting delays.
4. **Trust-service impact assessment:** for trust service providers, include a documented test for whether the incident has an impact on the provision of trust services, because that determines whether the deadline is 24 or 72 hours.
5. **Awareness timestamp:** record the reasonable-certainty determination in writing, with the identity of the decision-maker.
6. **Submission evidence:** retain the submission receipt, the submitted content, and the time of submission for each stage.
7. **Final-report calendar:** automatically create a final-report task one month after the incident notification is submitted; if the incident is still ongoing at that point, create the progress-report and subsequent final-report tasks.
8. **Escalation:** route notification decisions through legal/compliance, the incident response lead, and senior management; include the DPO where personal data is affected.
9. **Testing:** run tabletop exercises that test the 24-hour and 72-hour clocks, including a trust-service provider scenario where the early warning and incident notification fall on the same 24-hour deadline.

## 9. National transposition and sector-specific law

The Directive sets the mandatory outer limits, but the notification channel, form, and practical mechanics are governed by national transposition. Member States may not extend the Directive's outer limits, and national law or CSIRT guidance may require earlier notification or additional content. Check the law and CSIRT guidance of the Member State in which the entity is established or provides services.

Also check Article 4 of the Directive: where sector-specific Union law imposes cybersecurity risk-management or incident-notification requirements that are at least equivalent in effect, the relevant NIS2 provisions may not apply. Trust service providers may also have a separate breach-notification duty to their eIDAS supervisory body; confirm whether the national regime permits a single notification to satisfy both the NIS2 and eIDAS routes. The NIS2 deadline itself remains Article 23(4), second subparagraph: 24 hours.

## 10. Common audit findings to avoid

- Applying the 72-hour incident-notification deadline to a trust service provider's trust-service incident; the correct deadline is 24 hours.
- Omitting the early warning because a 24-hour incident notification was filed; the early warning remains due under Article 23(4)(a).
- Starting the clock at first detection rather than at the documented point of reasonable certainty that a significant incident occurred.
- Calculating the final report from the awareness time rather than from the submission of the incident notification.
- Failing to record the trust-service impact assessment that determines whether the 24-hour or 72-hour rule applies.
- Treating "without undue delay" as permitting use of the full 24 or 72 hours when earlier notification was possible.

## 11. Sources

- Directive (EU) 2022/2555 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 14 December 2022 on measures for a high common level of cybersecurity across the Union (NIS2 Directive), Article 23(4), first subparagraph, point (b), and second subparagraph; Article 23(1), (3) and (4)(a), (c), (d) and (e).
- Commission Guidance on the reporting obligations under Article 23(4) of Directive (EU) 2022/2555 (OJ C 328, 18.9.2023), including the explanation that trust service providers must notify within 24 hours.
- National CSIRT guidance, e.g. Centre for Cybersecurity Belgium, NIS2 Notification Guide v1.3 (August 2025), which states 72 hours generally and 24 hours for trust service providers for the incident notification.

question: X8
answer:
DELIVERABLE — CRA Article 14 reporting duty and deadlines for a connected consumer product placed on the EU market in 2025, with awareness on 17 November 2026.

1. VERDICT ON ASK 1 — YES, THE CRA OBLIGES THE MANUFACTURER TO REPORT NOW.
Basis (all grounded in the fetched sources):
(a) Regulation (EU) 2024/2847 (CRA) entered into force 10 December 2024; main obligations apply from 11 December 2027, but 'reporting obligations set out in Article 14 apply from 11 September 2026' (Commission CRA summary page). The Commission's news article of 11 September 2026 states: 'As of 11 September 2026, manufacturers must report any actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents that have an impact on the security of their products.'
(b) 17 November 2026 is after 11 September 2026. The duty is therefore live on the awareness date.
(c) The 2025 placing-on-the-market date does not exempt the product: 'Reporting obligations apply to all products with digital elements that have been made available on the Union market, including those already placed on the market before 11 December 2027' (Commission CRA summary page); ENISA's SRP FAQ confirms Art. 14 applies 'from 11 September 2026 to all products with digital elements falling within the scope of the CRA, including products that were placed on the market before 11 December 2027'; PwC states the same ('regardless of when sold'). The pre-11 December 2027 'substantial modification' carve-out in the summary applies to the substantive conformity obligations, not to reporting.
(d) The trigger condition is met on the stated assumptions: the manufacturer is the CRA manufacturer, the product is a product with digital elements in scope, and it has become aware of an 'actively exploited vulnerability', defined by ENISA's SRP FAQ as 'a vulnerability for which there is reliable evidence that a malicious actor has exploited it in a system without permission of the system owner'. The reporting clock starts on awareness of the exploitation, not on internal discovery of the bug alone (PwC: 'The 24-hour clock starts when you become aware of active exploitation'; ENISA: 'The reporting process starts when a manufacturer ... becomes aware of an actively exploited vulnerability or severe incident').

Note on the harness's proof of absence for ask 1: it is not used. The proof searched the digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu CRA summary page for the exact strings 'actively exploited vulnerability' (singular), 'obligation to report', 'report to ENISA' and 'without undue delay'. That page does answer the question — it says the manufacturer 'is required to notify actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents ... that it becomes aware of', that Art. 14 reporting obligations apply from 11 September 2026, and that they cover products already on the market. The non-match is a plural/singular and phrase-variant artifact, not a silence. not_stated is therefore empty.

2. DEADLINES (ASK 2) — VALUES AND WORKED DATES FROM T0 = 17 NOVEMBER 2026 (awareness).
Hours are clock hours from awareness (not working hours); the final-report period is calendar days.

Stage 1 — EARLY WARNING: within 24 hours of becoming aware (and without undue delay). Due 18 November 2026, same time of day as awareness.
Content: brief alert, not a full analysis — that the product is suspected of being affected by a malicious act / actively exploited vulnerability, and any suspected cross-border impact.

Stage 2 — VULNERABILITY NOTIFICATION ('main' notification): within 72 hours of becoming aware (and without undue delay). Due 20 November 2026, same time of day as awareness.
Content: general information on the product, the nature of the vulnerability and its active exploitation, initial assessment of severity and impact, and corrective or mitigating measures taken or planned, plus indicators of compromise where available. The 72-hour clock runs from awareness, not from submission of the early warning (ENISA notes its SRP counter currently shows a 48-hour-from-early-warning due date and that this display logic is being corrected — do not plan against the counter).

Stage 3 — FINAL REPORT (actively exploited vulnerability): no later than 14 days after a corrective or mitigating measure (e.g. a patch) becomes available. This clock is event-anchored, not awareness-anchored:
- If a corrective/mitigating measure was already available on 17 November 2026, the final report is due 1 December 2026.
- If the measure becomes available on date D, the final report is due D + 14 calendar days.
Do NOT use '10 working days' (the figure floated in the request's assumptions) — the grounded figure is 14 days after mitigation availability. For completeness, a severe incident (a different trigger from an actively exploited vulnerability) requires the final report within 1 month of the 72-hour notification; that is not the applicable limb here on the stated facts.

3. WHERE TO FILE.
Submit through ENISA's CRA Single Reporting Platform (SRP), selecting as recipient the CSIRT designated as coordinator (CDaC) of the Member State of the manufacturer's main establishment; the notification is submitted to that CSIRT and to ENISA, and the CDaC shares it without delay with the CSIRTs of affected Member States (report-once mechanism). Selecting the wrong CDaC can invalidate the notification and require resubmission. Mandatory notifications must go through the SRP; keep evidence of submission timestamps.

4. EXECUTION CHECKLIST (to be applied on 17 November 2026).
T0: log the exact date/time awareness was established (who knew what, when, source of the reliable evidence of exploitation). This timestamp is the legal start of both the 24 h and 72 h clocks — record it to the minute and in a fixed time zone.
T0 + <=24 h: file the early warning on the SRP; record the SRP acknowledgement.
T0 + <=72 h: file the notification with severity/impact assessment and measures taken/planned.
On availability of a patch or mitigation (or immediately, if one already exists): start the 14-day final-report countdown; diarise D + 14. File the final report covering the vulnerability, severity and impact, root cause, corrective/mitigating measures applied, and any cross-border impact.
Throughout: run parallel-track checks (i) NIS2 or national incident-reporting duties if the manufacturer is also an essential/important entity — these can impose separate, shorter or differently-anchored deadlines and different authorities; (ii) the adjacent CRA duty to inform users/distributors once a corrective or mitigating measure is available; (iii) researcher-coordination and confidentiality handling if disclosure is pending.

5. EXPOSURE.
Late or missing notification is an infringement. Suggested penalties are reported up to EUR 15 million or 2.5% of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher (PwC, secondary source). Microenterprises and small enterprises may not be fined for missing the 24-hour deadline (Commission CRA summary page) — but the obligation itself still applies to them.

6. ASSUMPTIONS CARRIED (state these in any downstream use).
Product is a product with digital elements within CRA scope with no exclusion; the entity is the CRA manufacturer; 17 November 2026 is the awareness date within the CRA meaning (awareness of the vulnerability AND its active exploitation); the vulnerability meets the actively exploited vulnerability definition. If any of these fails, the verdict and the clock start change. The primary legal text of Article 14 of Regulation (EU) 2024/2847 should be cited alongside these sources in any formal filing or board paper; the deadlines above are corroborated by the Commission CRA summary page, the Commission news article of 11 September 2026, the ENISA SRP FAQ and PwC, all fetched 24 November 2026.
