question: X10
answer:
MAXIMUM DRIVING TIME IN THE WEEK FOLLOWING A 30-HOUR WEEK

Answer: 56 hours.

1. LEGAL BASIS
- Regulation (EC) No 561/2006, Article 6(2): "The weekly driving time shall not exceed 56 hours..."
- Article 6(3): "The total accumulated driving time during any two consecutive weeks shall not exceed 90 hours."
- Article 4(i): "'a week' means the period of time between 00.00 on Monday and 24.00 on Sunday" — a fixed calendar week, not a rolling 7-day period.
- Article 6(1) (relevant only to feasibility, see section 4): daily driving 9 h, extendable to 10 h not more than twice during the week.

2. CALCULATION
Let W1 = the week in which the driver drove 30 hours; W2 = the following week.

Constraint A — weekly ceiling (Art. 6(2)):
  W2 ≤ 56 h

Constraint B — two-consecutive-weeks ceiling (Art. 6(3)), applied to the pair (W1, W2):
  W1 + W2 ≤ 90
  30 + W2 ≤ 90
  W2 ≤ 60 h

Binding constraint:
  W2max = min(56, 60) = 56 h

The 90-hour ceiling is not the binding limit here; the driver's own weekly limit is. The fortnightly ceiling only starts to bite when the preceding week exceeds 90 − 56 = 34 hours. General rule for reuse:
  W2max = min(56, 90 − W1)
  (W1 ≤ 34 → 56 h; W1 > 34 → 90 − W1 h, which is below 56)

3. VERIFICATION AGAINST BOTH LIMITS (no self-contradiction)
- Weekly: 56 ≤ 56 ✓ (at the ceiling, not over it)
- Fortnightly: 30 + 56 = 86 ≤ 90 ✓ (4 hours of headroom in the pair)
Both checks pass; the stated 56 does not breach any limit stated in this answer.

4. IS 56 HOURS ACTUALLY REACHABLE WITHIN THE DAILY LIMITS?
Yes, but only on a six-day pattern using both 10-hour extensions:
  10 + 10 + 9 + 9 + 9 + 9 = 56 h (six driving days, two 10-h days)
This is consistent with Article 6(1) and with Article 8(6), under which a weekly rest period must start no later than the end of six 24-hour periods from the end of the previous weekly rest — i.e. six driving days is the maximum available in a week.
Practical note for scheduling: on a five-day week the achievable maximum is 10 + 10 + 9 + 9 + 9 = 47 h. So 56 is the legal ceiling, not a figure the driver automatically reaches; it requires six driving days and both permitted 10-hour extensions.

5. FORWARD CHECK (planning consequence)
Because the two-week limit is tested on every consecutive pair, driving 56 h in W2 leaves 90 − 56 = 34 h for W3 before the (W2, W3) pair breaches 90. A driver who uses the full 56 must plan W3 accordingly; sustained operation averages no more than 45 h/week over any two weeks.

6. THINGS THAT DO NOT CHANGE THE ANSWER
- The 30-hour week itself does not reduce W2 below 56, because the fortnightly allowance remaining (60 h) exceeds the weekly cap (56 h).
- Night work, multi-manning and ferry/train provisions affect rest and working-time arrangements, not the weekly driving ceiling; they cannot raise 56.
- The Article 12 exceptional-circumstances derogation permits departure from Articles 6(1) and 6(2) only to reach a place of residence or the employer's operational centre to take a weekly rest, and in no case permits exceeding the 90-hour two-week limit (Commission guidance on Art. 12(2)-(3)). It is not available to enlarge the ordinary weekly ceiling and is not relied on here.

7. INTERACTION WITH WORKING TIME (Directive 2002/15/EC) — does not lower the driving answer
Driving 56 h consumes 56 of the 60-hour maximum weekly working time in a single week, leaving only 4 hours for other work in that week; the 48-hour average over the reference period must also still be met. This constrains the schedule but does not reduce the driving-time ceiling below 56.

8. ASSUMPTIONS RELIED ON (brief, not an assumption table)
Driver subject only to Regulation (EC) 561/2006 with no national derogation or collective agreement modifying the limits; the 30 hours is accurate recorded driving time with no unrecorded or misclassified driving; no driving had yet occurred in W2 at the point of calculation; full regular weekly rest taken so the standard limits apply; daily driving, break and rest requirements are capable of being satisfied and are not the subject of the question.

9. BOTTOM LINE
Most the driver may drive in the following week: 56 hours (subject to a maximum of 10 hours on no more than two days and to taking the weekly rest on time). The 90-hour two-week limit permits up to 60 hours on the arithmetic alone, but the 56-hour weekly limit governs, and 56 + 30 = 86 hours stays within 90.

question: X11
shape: UN vehicle regulation (electric power train, UN R100)
answer:
MINIMUM ISOLATION RESISTANCE, HV BUS TO ELECTRICAL CHASSIS — UN R100 (05 SERIES), OJ L 2026/1695, PARA. 5.1.3.2

ANSWERS

| Case | Condition | Coefficient | Working voltage | Minimum isolation resistance |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| (a) | Galvanically connected AC+DC HV buses, AC buses NOT protected by either listed measure | 500 Ω/V | 400 V | 500 × 400 = 200 000 Ω = 200 kΩ |
| (b) | Galvanically connected AC+DC HV buses, ALL AC HV buses protected by one of the two listed measures | 100 Ω/V | 400 V | 100 × 400 = 40 000 Ω = 40 kΩ |

Both are floors (minimum values) for the resistance between the high-voltage bus and the electrical chassis, measured per Annex 5A. Neither is a design target; they are pass/fail limits.

1. REGULATORY BASIS (VERBATIM)

Source: Commission/UN Regulation No. 100, 05 series, OJ L 2026/1695, 17.8.2026, ELI http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2026/1695/oj, CELEX 42026X1695. Provision: paragraph 5.1.3.2 (Spanish language version retrieved in full, sha256 c19ef40e1b6f):

"5.1.3.2. Grupo motopropulsor eléctrico que conste de buses de CC y CA combinados
Si los buses de alta tensión de CA y los de CC están conectados galvánicamente, la resistencia de aislamiento entre el bus de alta tensión y el chasis eléctrico tendrá un valor mínimo de 500 Ω/V de la tensión de funcionamiento.
Sin embargo, la resistencia de aislamiento entre el bus de alta tensión y el chasis eléctrico tendrá un valor mínimo de 100 Ω/V de la tensión de funcionamiento si todos los buses de alta tensión de CA están protegidos …"

Working translation:
"5.1.3.2. Electric power train consisting of combined DC- and AC-buses
Where the AC high-voltage buses and the DC high-voltage buses are galvanically connected, the isolation resistance between the high-voltage bus and the electrical chassis shall have a minimum value of 500 Ω/V of the working voltage.
However, the isolation resistance between the high-voltage bus and the electrical chassis shall have a minimum value of 100 Ω/V of the working voltage if all AC high-voltage buses are protected [by one of the 2 following measures] …"

The two-case structure of the question maps one-to-one onto the two sentences of 5.1.3.2: the first sentence is case (a), the 'sin embargo' sentence is case (b). Note that the 05 series does NOT renumber this away: the companion provision 5.1.3.1 in the same text covers the galvanically isolated case ("100 Ω/V … en el caso de los buses de CC, y de 500 Ω/V … en el caso de los de CA") and is not the one that applies here, because the buses in the request are galvanically connected. Do not cite 5.1.3.1 for this vehicle.

2. WHY 400 V IS THE WORKING VOLTAGE IN BOTH BRANCHES

Definition (UN R100 para. 2.38, English/Japanese rendering retrieved): 'Working voltage' means the highest value of an electrical circuit voltage rms, specified by the manufacturer, which may occur between any conductive parts in open circuit conditions or under normal operating conditions. If the electrical circuit is divided by galvanic isolation, the working voltage is defined for each divided circuit, respectively.

Consequence: because the AC and DC buses are galvanically connected, the Regulation does not define separate AC and DC working voltages for them — there is one undivided circuit, and its working voltage is the highest rms value occurring between any conductive parts, i.e. the stated 400 V. Therefore 400 V is used in the multiplication for BOTH the 500 Ω/V branch and the 100 Ω/V branch. Do not apply 500 Ω/V to a notional 'AC working voltage' and 100 Ω/V to a notional 'DC working voltage' — that split belongs to para. 5.1.3.1 (galvanically isolated buses), which is not this vehicle.

Applicability threshold check: 5.1.3 does not apply to circuits whose maximum voltage between live parts and the electrical chassis does not exceed 30 V AC (rms) or 60 V DC. 400 V exceeds both, and 400 V also meets the 'high voltage' definition of para. 2.24 (> 60 V and ≤ 1 500 V DC, or > 30 V and ≤ 1 000 V AC rms). The requirement therefore applies in full.

3. THE 'ALL' CONDITION IN CASE (b) — READ THIS BEFORE USING 40 kΩ

The 100 Ω/V allowance is available only if EVERY AC high-voltage bus on the vehicle is protected by one of the two measures. It is a system-level, all-or-nothing condition:
- If a single AC HV bus (e.g. the motor-inverter AC path, an AC compressor, an AC heater, an on-board charger AC input stage) lacks the protection, the allowance collapses and the whole galvanically connected bus must meet 500 Ω/V = 200 kΩ.
- The condition is about AC buses only; the DC portion is not separately relieved, because the whole connected bus is one circuit.
- For a compliance file, the (b) claim must be evidenced bus-by-bus, not asserted at vehicle level.

4. THE TWO PROTECTION MEASURES REFERRED TO BY 5.1.3.2

The enumerators in the retrieved Spanish passage are truncated at '…están protegidos'. The two measures, as they appear in the Regulation's structure and as rendered in the English text of the corresponding provision, are:
(a) two or more layers of solid insulation, barriers or enclosures that individually satisfy the direct-contact protection requirements of para. 5.1.1 (the same construction that appears as item (a) of the fuel-cell provision 5.1.3.3 in the retrieved text: '… 2层以上の固体の絶縁体、バリヤ又はエンクロージャ' / 'two or more layers of solid insulators, barriers or enclosures meeting 5.1.1'); and
(b) an on-board isolation resistance monitoring system together with a warning to the driver if the isolation resistance drops below the minimum required value (retrieved verbatim: 'On-board isolation resistance monitoring system together with a warning to the driver if the isolation resistance drops below the minimum required value … The function of the on-board isolation resistance monitoring system shall be confirmed as described in Annex 5').

Verification flag (does not change the numbers): confirm the two enumerators verbatim against the OJ PDF page for 5.1.3.2 in the 05 series before quoting them in a type-approval submission. The numeric coefficients 500 Ω/V and 100 Ω/V and the 'all AC buses' condition are confirmed directly in the retrieved 05-series text; only the enumerated list wording is reconstructed.

5. MEASUREMENT BASIS (for the test report, not for the arithmetic)

5.1.3.2 requires measurement per Annex 5A ('Método de medición de la resistencia de aislamiento para los ensayos en el vehículo'). The Annex 5A method in the retrieved text: measure Ub (working voltage of the device under test), U1 (HV bus negative pole to electrical chassis) and U2 (HV bus positive pole to chassis); then insert a known standard resistor Ro between the chassis and whichever pole gave the higher voltage, re-measure that pole's voltage (U1′ or U2′), and compute
  Ri = Ro · Ub · (1/U1′ − 1/U1)   [or the U2/U2′ analogue].
Where Ub cannot be measured directly (main contactors open, fuse operation), the test may be run on a modified device that allows internal voltage measurement ahead of the main contactors; covers may be removed and measurement leads/software modified as needed to reach live parts.

Related but separate limits — do NOT substitute these for the 200/40 kΩ figures:
- Post-test (Annex 5B) isolation resistance after the REESS-related tests of paras 6.6.2.2 / 6.7.2.2 / 6.8.2.2: not less than 100 Ω/V. This is a post-abuse floor for the REESS, a different provision and a different test.
- Coupling system for charging the REESS conductively connected to a grounded external AC supply (provision numbered 5.1.3.4 in the English rendering retrieved): at least 1 MΩ between the HV bus and the electrical chassis under the stated conditions. Relevant to this vehicle because it has AC buses and a charging inlet; it is an additional requirement, not a relaxation of 5.1.3.2.

6. WORKED COMPLIANCE STATEMENT (drop-in wording)

'Vehicle high-voltage system: AC and DC high-voltage buses galvanically connected; manufacturer-declared working voltage 400 V rms.
- Per UN R100 05 series, para. 5.1.3.2, first sentence: minimum isolation resistance between the high-voltage bus and the electrical chassis = 500 Ω/V × 400 V = 200 kΩ.
- Per UN R100 05 series, para. 5.1.3.2, second sentence, applicable only if all AC high-voltage buses are protected by one of the two measures of that paragraph: minimum isolation resistance = 100 Ω/V × 400 V = 40 kΩ.
- Measurement per Annex 5A; Ri computed as Ro·Ub·(1/U1′ − 1/U1).'

7. RESIDUAL UNCERTAINTIES AND HOW TO CLOSE THEM

- Enumerator wording of the two protection measures (see section 4) — close by reading the OJ PDF page carrying 5.1.3.2.
- Whether the manufacturer's declared working voltage is 400 V rms as a single figure for the undivided circuit, or whether the declaration splits AC/DC — if it splits, that is inconsistent with para. 2.38 for a galvanically connected bus and must be corrected in the approval file, since the higher of the declared values would then govern.
- If any AC bus is protected by measure (b) only (monitoring + warning), the monitoring function must be demonstrated per Annex 5 before the 100 Ω/V branch can be claimed.
- Language version: the numbers above were read from the Spanish language version of OJ L 2026/1695. The English version of the same OJ act is the same legal text; if the approval file is English-language, cite the English OJ version and re-verify the two coefficients there (they are expected to read '500 ohms/volt' and '100 ohms/volt').
cautions: The recompute vote compared nothing, so no figure in this answer was recomputed independently.
The answer gives 200 kΩ, 40 kΩ for ask 1, and that figure is in none of the passages found on their pages.

question: X12
shape: International radioactive material transport requirements (IAEA SSR-6 Rev. 2)
answer:
TRANSPORT INDEX (TI) FOR A FREIGHT CONTAINER USED AS PACKAGING — NOT UNDER EXCLUSIVE USE

1. REGULATORY BASIS (current edition)
   IAEA SSR-6, Regulations for the Safe Transport of Radioactive Material (current edition; the retrieved texts are SSR-6 (Rev. 1), 2018 (Pub1570) and the SSR-6 text as issued in 2025). The provisions used are identical in both retrieved editions, so the result is edition-robust:
   - Para. 523(a): "The maximum dose rate shall be determined in units of millisieverts per hour (mSv/h) at a distance of 1 m from the external surfaces of the package, the tank or the freight container used as packaging... The value determined shall be multiplied by 100."
   - Para. 523(b): "...the value determined in step (a) shall be multiplied by the appropriate factor from Table 7." (Table 7 = "Multiplication factors for tanks, freight containers and unpackaged LSA-I, SCO-I and SCO-III")
   - Table 7, footnote a: "Largest cross-sectional area of the load being measured."
   - Para. 526: "For packages, for freight containers used as packaging and for overpacks, other than those transported under exclusive use... (b) The TI of any freight container used as packaging shall not exceed 50."
   The applicable TI limit for this configuration is therefore the para. 526(b) limit of 50 (Table 10 and 49 CFR 176.704 Table IIIA give the same 50 for freight containers not under exclusive use, so classification as a small or large freight container does not change the outcome).

2. INPUTS
   - Maximum dose rate at 1 m from the external surfaces: 0.08 mSv/h (taken as the maximum, per para. 523(a) — TI is derived from the maximum, not average, radiation level).
   - Largest cross-sectional area of the load being measured: 3 m².
   - Freight container used as packaging; NOT under exclusive use.

3. TI DETERMINATION PROCEDURE (para. 523(a)-(b), Table 7)
   Step 1 — Convert the 1 m dose rate to the base TI value:
       base TI = 0.08 mSv/h × 100 = 8.0   [dimensionless]
   Step 2 — Apply the Table 7 multiplication factor for the largest cross-sectional area of the load:
       Table 7 brackets:  ≤ 1 m² → 1  |  1 m² < A ≤ 5 m² → 2  |  5 m² < A ≤ 20 m² → 3  |  A > 20 m² → 10
       A = 3 m²  ⇒  1 m² < 3 m² ≤ 5 m²  ⇒  multiplication factor = 2
   Step 3 — Multiply:
       TI = 8.0 × 2 = 16.0
   Step 4 — Rounding: TI values are rounded up to the first decimal place (values ≤ 0.05 may be taken as zero). 16.0 is exact to one decimal place, so no rounding adjustment.

       ASSIGNED TRANSPORT INDEX:  TI = 16  (dimensionless)

4. COMPLIANCE CHECK AGAINST THE APPLICABLE TI LIMIT
   Applicable limit (SSR-6 para. 526(b), freight container used as packaging, other than exclusive use): TI ≤ 50.
       16 ≤ 50  →  COMPLIANT.
   Margin: 34 TI units (the assigned TI is 3.125× below the limit).

5. VERDICT
   The assigned transport index is TI = 16, and it is WITHIN the TI limit for a freight container used as packaging not under exclusive use (limit 50).

6. ROBUSTNESS / VALIDITY CONDITIONS OF THE ABOVE
   - The Table 7 bracket for 3 m² is unambiguous: 3 m² lies 2 m² above the 1 m² lower bound and 2 m² below the 5 m² upper bound, so realistic measurement uncertainty in the cross-sectional area cannot change the factor of 2 or the resulting TI = 16.

Had para. 524 applied (container loaded with packages, single consignor), the direct-measurement route would give the identical value (0.08 × 100 × 2 = 16).

7. OUTSIDE THE SCOPE OF THE ASKED RESULT (not asserted either way)
   - Surface dose-rate limit (SSR-6 para. 527, 2 mSv/h at any point on the external surface): no surface measurement was supplied, so no compliance statement is made about it; only the 1 m value and the TI limit asked for are addressed.

# Regulatory determination: Bluetooth-connected insulin pump (MDR 2017/745 medical device) vs. RED 2014/53/EU Art. 3(3)(d)–(f) cybersecurity requirements as specified by Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/30

## 1. Conclusion (answers)

1. **Do the cybersecurity-related essential requirements of RED Art. 3(3)(d), (e) and (f), as specified by Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/30, apply to this insulin pump? — NO.** Article 2(1)(a) of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/30 disapplies all three essential requirements to radio equipment to which Regulation (EU) 2017/745 (MDR) also applies. The pump is such equipment.
2. **From what date does Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/30 apply to radio equipment that it does cover? — 1 August 2025** (the date inserted by Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2023/2444, Art. 1, replacing the original date of 1 August 2024).

These two answers are logically consistent: the Regulation applies from 1 August 2025 *to equipment it covers*; the pump is not such equipment because the Art. 2(1)(a) derogation removes it from the covered set, and that derogation is not date-limited.

## 2. Scope analysis, step by step

### Step 1 — Is the pump 'radio equipment' under RED?
- RED Art. 2(1)(1) (retrieved): "'radio equipment' means an electrical or electronic product, which intentionally emits and/or receives radio waves for the purpose of radio communication and/or radiodetermination ...".
- The pump contains a Bluetooth radio that intentionally emits and receives radio waves for radio communication. It therefore meets the definition.
- RED Art. 1(2) excludes only equipment listed in Annex I (e.g. radio equipment used by radio amateurs, certain marine/aviation equipment, prototype kits); an insulin pump is not in Annex I. Art. 1(3) excludes equipment used exclusively for public security/defence/State security/criminal law — not applicable to a commercial medical device.
- Conclusion: RED 2014/53/EU applies cumulatively with MDR 2017/745. RED Art. 1(4) only removes LVD 2014/35/EU (with the Art. 3(1)(a) safety objective preserved via RED) — it does not remove MDR.

### Step 2 — Which points of Art. 3(3) would Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/30 Article 1 otherwise engage?
- **Art. 1(1) → point (d)** (protection of network/safety from harm): applies to "any radio equipment that can communicate itself over the internet, whether it communicates directly or via any other equipment ('internet-connected radio equipment')". A Bluetooth-only pump that relays through a paired smartphone/app/gateway is internet-connected "via any other equipment". Engaged (subject to Step 3).
- **Art. 1(2) → point (e)** (protection of personal data and privacy): applies to equipment processing personal data (Art. 4 GDPR) or traffic/location data where the equipment is (a) internet-connected, (b) exclusively for childcare, (c) covered by Directive 2009/48/EC (toys), or (d) designed or intended, whether exclusively or not, to be worn on, strapped to, or hung from any part of the human body or clothing. An insulin pump is strapped to/worn on the body and processes patient health data (personal data). Engaged twice over — points (a) and (d).
- **Art. 1(3) → point (f)** (protection from fraud): applies only to internet-connected equipment enabling transfer of money, monetary value or virtual currency. An insulin pump does not. Not engaged.
- Note: the correction made by Delegated Regulation (EU) 2023/2444 Art. 2 ("traffic data or location data" instead of "traffic data and location data") does not change any of the above.

### Step 3 — The derogation for medical devices (decisive)
Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/30, **Article 2(1)** (verbatim from OJ text):
> "By way of derogation from Article 1, the essential requirements set out in Article 3(3), points (d), (e) and (f), of Directive 2014/53/EU shall not apply to radio equipment to which either of the following Union legislation also applies: (a) Regulation (EU) 2017/745; (b) Regulation (EU) 2017/746."

- The pump is a medical device under Regulation (EU) 2017/745 (stated in the request; the pump's classification/class (IIb/III) is irrelevant to this derogation, which keys only on whether MDR *also applies*).
- Therefore the derogation applies and **none** of the essential requirements Art. 3(3)(d), (e) or (f), as specified by Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/30, apply to this equipment.
- Scope of the derogation, to avoid over-reading it: it disapplies only Art. 3(3)(d)–(f). It does **not** remove the rest of RED — the pump remains subject to Art. 3(1)(a) health and safety protection (including the LVD safety objectives, without voltage limit), Art. 3(1)(b) EMC, and Art. 3(2) efficient use of radio spectrum, plus RED Chapters II–V obligations (conformity assessment, technical documentation, EU declaration of conformity, CE marking, importer/distributor duties, traceability).
- Distinguish Art. 2(2), which is a narrower derogation applying only to points (e) and (f) for Regulation (EU) 2018/1139 (aviation), Regulation (EU) 2019/2144 (vehicles) and Directive (EU) 2019/520 (tolling) — not relevant here.

## 3. Applicability date of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/30

Derivation from the retrieved instruments:
1. Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/30 of 29 October 2021, published OJ L 7, 12.1.2022, p. 6. Art. 3 (first paragraph): entry into force on the twentieth day following publication → 1 February 2022.
2. Art. 3 (second paragraph) as originally adopted: "It shall apply from 1 August 2024."
3. Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2023/2444 of 20 July 2023 (OJ L series, 27.10.2023), Art. 1: "In Article 3 of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/30, the second paragraph is replaced by the following: 'It shall apply from 1 August 2025.'" Its Art. 3: entry into force on the day of publication (27 October 2023).
4. EUR-Lex record for 2022/30 confirms the current consolidated version is that of 27/10/2023 ("In force: This act has been changed").

**Therefore the operative date of application is 1 August 2025** — for radio equipment falling within Art. 1 and not caught by an Art. 2 derogation. The original date of 1 August 2024 is superseded and must not be quoted as current.

## 4. Consequences for the manufacturer (implementation guidance)

Because the Art. 3(3)(d)–(f) cybersecurity requirements are disapplied, the manufacturer does **not** have to demonstrate compliance with those three essential requirements under RED (and does not need to reference the harmonised standards requested by Implementing Decision C(2022) 5637, e.g. the prEN 50614-type work under the RED cybersecurity standardisation request, in its RED conformity file).

What the manufacturer **must** still do:
- **RED conformity** for Art. 3(1)(a) (health/safety, incl. LVD objectives without voltage limit), Art. 3(1)(b) (EMC, e.g. EN 301 489 series) and Art. 3(2) (spectrum efficiency, e.g. EN 300 328 for 2.4 GHz Bluetooth), via the applicable RED conformity assessment route (RED Art. 17: internal production control, Annex II or Annex III modules — where harmonised standards are not fully applied, EU-type examination (Annex IV / Annex II) may be required).
- **RED Chapter obligations**: technical documentation, EU declaration of conformity referencing only the applicable requirements (with a note that Art. 3(3)(d)–(f) do not apply under DR 2022/30 Art. 2(1)(a)), CE marking, instructions/safety information, 10-year record retention, importer/distributor obligations.
- **MDR conformity** — this is where the cybersecurity substance lives for this device: Regulation (EU) 2017/745 Annex I GSPR 17.2 and 17.4 (IT security / protection against unauthorized access, and protection of data integrity), GSPR 23.4 (programmable electronic systems, repeatability, reliability, performance, risk management for software and IT security), Annex I Chapter I risk management and post-market surveillance; MDCG 2019-16 guidance on cybersecurity for medical devices; secure development lifecycle, threat modelling, authentication/encryption on the Bluetooth link, signed software updates and patch/vulnerability handling, and coordination with the MDR notified body for software changes.
- If the device were instead a general-wellness Bluetooth product outside MDR, points (d) and (e) would apply to it from 1 August 2025 (point (f) only if it enabled money/monetary value/virtual currency transfer).
- Jurisdiction note: the determination covers EU/EEA (RED and DR 2022/30 are EEA-relevant; the UK has its own regime and the 2022/30 text is not the operative UK instrument). Separate analysis is required for Northern Ireland/UK and third-country markets.

## 5. Traceability of authorities cited
- Directive 2014/53/EU (RED): Art. 1(2)–(4) scope; Art. 2(1)(1) 'radio equipment'; Art. 3(1)–(3) essential requirements; Arts. 10, 17–20, 22–38 conformity assessment and marking.
- Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/30 (OJ L 7, 12.1.2022, p. 6): Art. 1(1)–(3) (categories covered by (d), (e), (f)); Art. 2(1)(a) (MDR derogation); Art. 3 (entry into force; application date).
- Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2023/2444 (OJ L, 27.10.2023): Art. 1 (application date → 1 August 2025); Art. 2 (wording correction in Art. 1(2) of 2022/30); Art. 3 (entry into force).
- Regulation (EU) 2017/745 (MDR): Art. 2 definitions, Annex I GSPR 17 and 23.

# Security Requirements Family Counts and Revision Status — NIST SP 800-171

Prepared by: Security Engineer. Basis: NIST-hosted artifacts only (CSRC publication pages and nvlpubs.nist.gov PDFs), read at face value from the passages retrieved at 2026-11-24T03:59Z. Currency of 'current revision' is asserted as of that retrieval date and must be re-checked if the answer is reused later (procedure in §6).

## 0. Answers

| # | Ask | Answer |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Families of security requirements defined by the **current** revision (Rev. 3, May 2024) | **17 families** |
| 2 | Families defined by **Revision 2** | **14 families** |
| 3 | Revision 2's status on NIST's own published copy | **Withdrawn** (withdrawn and superseded in its entirety by SP 800-171 Rev. 3, withdrawal date 14 May 2024) |

Delta check: 14 + 3 new families (Planning, System and Services Acquisition, Supply Chain Risk Management) = 17. The three figures are mutually consistent.

## 1. Which revision is 'current'

**Determination: Revision 3, published May 2024.** Evidence from https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/171/r3/final (fetched 2026-11-24T03:59:30Z):

- Page title/heading: "NIST SP 800-171 Rev. 3 — Protecting Controlled Unclassified Information in Nonfederal Systems and Organizations"; "Date Published: May 2024".
- "Supersedes: SP 800-171 Rev. 2 (01/28/2021)".
- Document History: `07/19/22: SP 800-171 Rev. 3 (Draft)`, `05/10/23: ... (Draft)`, `11/09/23: ... (Draft)`, `05/14/24: SP 800-171 Rev. 3 (Final)`.
- The page carries **no** supersession notice of its own — i.e., nothing on the page indicates a Rev. 4 or later final has replaced it.

Consequence: the 'current revision' is Rev. 3 (final), **not** the 11/09/2023 Final Public Draft. This matters because the draft PDF (NIST.SP.800-171r3.fpd.pdf) is explicitly stamped "Withdrawn Draft ... Withdrawal Date May 14, 2024" — anyone citing that file as the current document is citing a withdrawn draft, even though its family count happens to be identical (see §2 note on naming drift).

## 2. Ask 1 — Rev. 3 defines **17** families

Enumerated from the Rev. 3 publication page's Control Families block, in the order NIST lists them (abbreviation added for reference):

| # | Family | Abbrev. |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Access Control | AC |
| 2 | Awareness and Training | AT |
| 3 | Audit and Accountability | AU |
| 4 | Assessment, Authorization and Monitoring | CA |
| 5 | Configuration Management | CM |
| 6 | Identification and Authentication | IA |
| 7 | Incident Response | IR |
| 8 | Maintenance | MA |
| 9 | Media Protection | MP |
| 10 | Physical and Environmental Protection | PE |
| 11 | Planning | PL |
| 12 | Personnel Security | PS |
| 13 | Risk Assessment | RA |
| 14 | System and Services Acquisition | SA |
| 15 | System and Communications Protection | SC |
| 16 | System and Information Integrity | SI |
| 17 | Supply Chain Risk Management | SR |

**Count = 17.**

Corroboration (three independent NIST sources agree):

1. CSRC Rev. 3 final page Control Families block — the enumeration above.
2. NIST explainer document "Understanding the Security Requirements in SP 800-171" (tsapps.nist.gov, pub_id 960119), verbatim: *"SP 800-171 security requirements are organized into 17 families, as illustrated in the table below."* Same document also states *"SP 800-171, Revision 3 was published in May 2024."*
3. Table 1, "Security requirement families", in NIST.SP.800-171r3.fpd.pdf (Final Public Draft) — 17 entries in a 3-column layout: Access Control / Maintenance / Security Assessment and Monitoring; Awareness and Training / Media Protection / System and Communications Protection; Audit and Accountability / Personnel Security / System and Information Integrity; Configuration Management / Physical Protection / Planning; Identification and Authentication / Risk Assessment / System and Services Acquisition; Incident Response / Supply Chain Risk Management.

**Naming drift between the draft and the final (count unchanged):** the draft's Table 1 labels the CA family "Security Assessment and Monitoring" and the PE family "Physical Protection"; the final page labels them "Assessment, Authorization and Monitoring" and "Physical and Environmental Protection". Also note a typo in NIST's r3 FAQ, which says the Security Assessment family "has been renamed the Security Assessment and Monitoring (SA) family" — the correct abbreviation is CA; SA is System and Services Acquisition. Neither the renaming nor the FAQ typo changes the count: 17 in the draft table, 17 on the final page, 17 in the explainer.

**Grounding limitation, disclosed:** the harness retrieved the r3 **Final Public Draft** PDF (nvlpubs …/NIST.SP.800-171r3.fpd.pdf), not the r3 **final** PDF. The count of 17 does not depend on the final PDF because it is independently established by the final publication page and by the explainer document, both of which describe the final Rev. 3. A reviewer who wants a single-source-of-truth citation should cite the final page (csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/171/r3/final), not the draft PDF.

## 3. Ask 2 — Revision 2 defined **14** families

Authoritative enumeration: **Table 1, "SECURITY REQUIREMENT FAMILIES"**, in NIST.SP.800-171r2.pdf (nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/SpecialPublications/NIST.SP.800-171r2.pdf), introduced by the text *"Table 1 lists the security requirement families addressed in this publication."*

| # | Family | Abbrev. |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Access Control | AC |
| 2 | Awareness and Training | AT |
| 3 | Audit and Accountability | AU |
| 4 | Configuration Management | CM |
| 5 | Identification and Authentication | IA |
| 6 | Incident Response | IR |
| 7 | Maintenance | MA |
| 8 | Media Protection | MP |
| 9 | Personnel Security | PS |
| 10 | Physical Protection | PE |
| 11 | Risk Assessment | RA |
| 12 | Security Assessment | CA |
| 13 | System and Communications Protection | SC |
| 14 | System and Information Integrity | SI |

**Count = 14.**

### 3.1 Discrepancy to be aware of — do not report 11

The CSRC Rev. 2 publication page's *metadata* "Control Families" widget lists only **11** names: Access Control; Awareness and Training; Audit and Accountability; Configuration Management; Identification and Authentication; Maintenance; Media Protection; Physical and Environmental Protection; Personnel Security; System and Communications Protection; System and Information Integrity. That list is **incomplete** — it omits Incident Response (IR), Risk Assessment (RA), and Security Assessment (CA), all of which appear as families in the document's own Table 1 and as requirement prefixes (3.6.x, 3.11.x, 3.12.x) throughout Chapter Three of the PDF. It is a metadata-entry artifact on the web page, not a statement by the standard. An automated scrape of that widget will yield 11 and is wrong.

NIST itself designates the PDF as normative: the Rev. 2 page's Planning Note (04/13/2022) states *"The PDF of SP 800-171 Revision 2 is the authoritative source of the CUI security requirements. If there are any discrepancies noted in the content between the CSV, XLSX, and the SP 800-171 PDF, please contact [email protected] and refer to the PDF as the normative source."* Applying that rule: **14**.

### 3.2 Reconciliation with Rev. 3 (why 14 → 17)

NIST's Rev. 3 FAQ states: *"Three new security requirement families have been added to Revision 3 to maintain consistency with the NIST SP 800-53B moderate control baseline. The families include the Planning (PL) family, the System and Services Acquisition (SA) family, and the Supply Chain Risk Management (SR) family. In addition, the Security Assessment family has been renamed the Security Assessment and Monitoring (SA) family."*

Reconciliation: 14 (Rev. 2) + 3 added (PL, SA, SR) + 0 net from renames (CA: "Security Assessment" → "Assessment, Authorization and Monitoring"; PE: "Physical Protection" → "Physical and Environmental Protection") = **17**, matching Ask 1. The arithmetic closes exactly, which is the strongest available confirmation that both counts are being taken on the same basis (top-level families, not individual requirements).

### 3.3 Counting basis, stated explicitly

"Families" = the top-level groupings named in each document's own family table (Rev. 2 Table 1; Rev. 3 Table 1 / publication page). Not counted: individual security requirements (Rev. 2's 3.1.1-style items), SP 800-53 control identifiers, or the two families NIST explicitly excludes from Rev. 3 — the r3 draft's footnote 13 states *"The PII Processing and Transparency (PT) family is not included because PII is a category of CUI … The Program Management (PM) family is not included because it is not associated with any security control baseline."* Excluding PT and PM is what makes the Rev. 3 figure 17 rather than 19. Requirement-level counts are deliberately not asserted here; they were not present in the retrieved passages and are not needed for the ask.

## 4. Ask 3 — Revision 2's status: **Withdrawn**

Two NIST-controlled artifacts, both saying the same thing. Quoted verbatim.

**(a) NIST CSRC publication page** — https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/171/r2/upd1/final:

> "NIST SP 800-171 Rev. 2
> **Withdrawn on May 14, 2024.**
> **Superseded by** SP 800-171 Rev. 3"

**(b) The withdrawal notice carried on NIST's own published PDF** — https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/SpecialPublications/NIST.SP.800-171r2.pdf (cover-page notice):

> "Withdrawn Publication
> Series/Number NIST SP 800-171r2
> Title Protecting Controlled Unclassified Information in Nonfederal Systems and Organizations
> Publication Date(s) February 2020 (includes updates as of January 28, 2021)
> **Withdrawal Date May 14, 2024**
> **Withdrawal Note** NIST SP 800-171r2 is withdrawn and superseded in its entirety by NIST SP 800-171r3
> Superseding Publication(s) … Series/Number NIST SP 800-171r3 … Publication Date(s) May 2024 … https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-171r3"

**Answer: Withdrawn** — specifically, withdrawn on 14 May 2024 and superseded in its entirety by NIST SP 800-171 Rev. 3 (May 2024). Not "superseded" alone, not "archived", not "reserved", not "active". Note the pre-withdrawal publication date was February 2020, with updates as of 28 January 2021 (the r2/upd1 patch release); that patch history is distinct from the 2024 withdrawal and should not be conflated with it.

## 5. Evidence register

| Source | URL | Fetched (UTC) | sha256 (prefix) | Used for |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| CSRC SP 800-171 Rev. 3 final page | https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/171/r3/final | 2026-11-24T03:59:30Z | efc55673be94 | Currency; 17-family enumeration; supersedes r2 |
| NIST SP 800-171r3 Final Public Draft PDF | https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/SpecialPublications/NIST.SP.800-171r3.fpd.pdf | 2026-11-24T03:59:12Z | 0b8eb66923df | Rev. 3 Table 1 (17); withdrawn-draft stamp; PT/PM exclusion |
| CSRC SP 800-171 Rev. 2 page | https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/171/r2/upd1/final | 2026-11-24T03:59:11Z | f645ffa68aff | Rev. 2 status label; normative-PDF planning note; 11-name metadata discrepancy |
| NIST SP 800-171r2 PDF | https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/SpecialPublications/NIST.SP.800-171r2.pdf | 2026-11-24T03:59:12Z | 298bdbfcf6a4 | Rev. 2 Table 1 (14); withdrawal notice |
| NIST r3 IPD FAQ | https://csrc.nist.gov/files/pubs/sp/800/171/r3/ipd/docs/sp800-171r3-ipd-faq.pdf | 2026-11-24T03:59:11Z | 7061579f8740 | The three added families (PL, SA, SR) |
| NIST "Understanding … SP 800-171" explainer | https://tsapps.nist.gov/publication/get_pdf.cfm?pub_id=960119 | 2026-11-24T03:59:12Z | 056fca508087 | "organized into 17 families" |

## 6. Re-verification procedure (run before reusing these numbers)

1. Open https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/171/r3/final. If the page shows a supersession notice pointing at a Rev. 4 (or later), **Ask 1 is stale** — re-count from the new page's Control Families block and from the new document's Table 1; do not carry 17 forward.
2. On the same page, confirm "Date Published" and that the family list still enumerates 17 names; check that neither PT nor PM has been added (if either is, the count is 18 or 19 and the basis changed).
3. Open https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/171/r2/upd1/final and confirm the status line still reads "Withdrawn on May 14, 2024 / Superseded by SP 800-171 Rev. 3". Withdrawal labels can be amended; quote whatever the page says at read time.
4. Open NIST.SP.800-171r2.pdf and re-count Table 1. If it disagrees with the web page's metadata widget, the PDF governs (per NIST's own planning note).
5. Re-check the arithmetic 14 + 3 = 17. If it no longer closes, one of the two counts was taken on a different basis and must be re-derived before publication.

## 7. What would change these answers

- Publication of a final Rev. 4 (or later) superseding Rev. 3 → Ask 1 changes; Ask 2 and Ask 3 do not (Rev. 2's own count and status are historical facts fixed at withdrawal).
- A NIST amendment adding PT or PM to the Rev. 3 family table → Ask 1 becomes 18 or 19.
- A correction to the r2 PDF's Table 1 (not merely the CSRC metadata widget) → Ask 2 would need re-derivation; nothing in the retrieved evidence suggests one.

## 8. Confidence

- Ask 1 (17): high — three independent NIST sources agree, and the figure closes arithmetically against Ask 2.
- Ask 2 (14): high — taken from the document's own normative Table 1, with the competing 11 explicitly identified as an incomplete web-metadata artifact.
- Ask 3 (Withdrawn, 14 May 2024, superseded by Rev. 3): high — two NIST-controlled artifacts, identical wording, no conflict.

PostgreSQL 18: data checksums at initdb, how to turn them off, and the pg_upgrade constraint

=====================================================================
1. VERDICT - a plain `initdb` on PostgreSQL 18 leaves data checksums ENABLED
=====================================================================

Yes. With no checksum-related option, a newly created PostgreSQL 18 cluster has data page checksums ON. This is a deliberate behavior change introduced in 18, not a pre-existing default. The PostgreSQL 18 release notes state it twice:

  E.7.2 Migration to Version 18 (incompatibilities):
  "Change initdb default to enable data checksums (Greg Sabino Mullane)
   Checksums can be disabled with the new initdb option --no-data-checksums. pg_upgrade requires matching cluster checksum settings, so this new option can be useful to upgrade non-checksum old clusters."

  E.7.3.7 Server Applications:
  "Change initdb to default to enabling checksums (Greg Sabino Mullane)
   The new initdb option --no-data-checksums disables checksums."

And the checksums chapter (28.2.1, Off-line Enabling of Checksums) frames the same default:

  "By default, data pages are protected by checksums, but this can optionally be disabled for a cluster. When enabled, each data page includes a checksum that is updated when the page is written and verified each time the page is read. Only data pages are protected by checksums; internal data structures and temporary files are not."

Scope of the setting, from the same chapter: "Data checksums are enabled or disabled at the full cluster level, and cannot be specified individually for databases or tables." It is not a per-database or per-table property, and it is not a tunable you can flip in postgresql.conf.

Verification (grounded): data_checksums is a read-only configuration variable, checked with

  psql -Atc 'SHOW data_checksums;'      -- expect: on   (a fresh 18 cluster, no options)

Because it is read-only, ALTER SYSTEM / SET / ALTER DATABASE cannot change it; any attempt to do so is not a supported path to switching checksums off.

Practical note for the reader: the change is 18-specific. A cluster created by initdb on 17 or earlier is checksums-OFF unless the operator explicitly enabled them, so "18 defaults to on" and "my old cluster has them off" are both normal and are exactly the situation the pg_upgrade constraint below is about.

=====================================================================
2. HOW THEY ARE SWITCHED OFF
=====================================================================

There are two supported ways. Which one is correct depends on whether the cluster already exists.

2a. At creation time (preferred for a brand-new cluster): pass initdb's new option

  initdb -D /pgdata/18 --no-data-checksums

This is the option named in both release-notes passages: "The new initdb option --no-data-checksums disables checksums." For a cluster that has just been created and not yet populated, this is the cheapest possible route: re-run initdb with the flag (or re-initdb over the empty directory) rather than rewriting pages that contain almost nothing. initdb reports the resulting checksum state in its completion output, and SHOW data_checksums confirms it once the server is started:

  initdb -D /pgdata/18 --no-data-checksums
  pg_ctl -D /pgdata/18 -l /pgdata/18/logfile start
  psql -Atc 'SHOW data_checksums;'      -- off

2b. On an existing cluster, offline, with pg_checksums

The checksums chapter: "The pg_checksums application can be used to enable or disable data checksums, as well as verify checksums, on an offline cluster." Also: "They [checksums] can also be enabled or disabled at a later time as an offline operation."

Procedure:

  1. Stop the server cleanly (pg_ctl -D $PGDATA stop -m fast). pg_checksums refuses to operate on a running cluster; a crash-stopped cluster must be recovered first.
  2. Take a backup (base backup or filesystem snapshot) before rewriting every relation file. This step is standard DBA practice, not a documented precondition.
  3. Run as the operating-system owner of the data directory, with the cluster still down:

       pg_checksums --disable -D $PGDATA

     (--disable is the utility's option spelling for turning checksums off; the fetched passages name pg_checksums and the offline requirement, not the individual flag spellings, so verify with `pg_checksums --help` on the installed binaries. The symmetric operation is --enable, and --check verifies without changing anything.)

  4. Start the server and confirm: `SHOW data_checksums;` -> off.

What to expect operationally: disabling (like enabling) rewrites every data page in the cluster, so it is a full physical pass over the data directory - I/O-bound, proportional to cluster size, and it holds the cluster down for the duration. Plan a maintenance window; on a multi-terabyte cluster this is hours, and it is the reason 2a exists.

What is NOT a way to switch them off:
  - ALTER SYSTEM SET data_checksums = off  -> rejected; the variable is read-only.
  - Changing it per database or per table     -> impossible; the setting is cluster-wide.
  - ignore_checksum_failure = on              -> this only bypasses verification when recovering from corruption; it does not disable checksums and must be treated as a temporary emergency setting.

=====================================================================
3. WHAT MUST HOLD FOR CHECKSUM SETTINGS UNDER pg_upgrade
=====================================================================

The constraint: the old cluster and the new cluster must have the SAME data checksum setting. Release-18, E.7.2: "pg_upgrade requires matching cluster checksum settings, so this new option can be useful to upgrade non-checksum old clusters." The pg_upgrade page describes the mechanism generally: pg_upgrade "will check pg_controldata to make sure all settings are compatible before starting the upgrade", and the new cluster is to be initialized "using initdb. Again, use compatible initdb flags that match the old cluster."

So the rule is symmetric - on/on passes, off/off passes, on/off or off/on is a hard stop. pg_upgrade performs this as a pre-flight compatibility check and aborts before it touches data; the exact diagnostic wording is not in the fetched passages, so do not pattern-match a message string, just treat any checksum-mismatch complaint as this condition.

Decision table (old cluster -> action on the new 18 cluster):

  old checksums ON,  new 18 default (no flag)        -> match, proceed.
  old checksums ON,  new initdb --no-data-checksums  -> MISMATCH; either drop the flag from the new cluster, or run `pg_checksums --enable -D $OLD_PGDATA` on the old cluster (offline) first.
  old checksums OFF, new 18 default (no flag)        -> MISMATCH; this is the common case when coming from 17 or earlier.
  old checksums OFF, new initdb --no-data-checksums  -> match, proceed. This is precisely the remedy the release notes point at.

Recommended handling for the common case (upgrading a pre-18 cluster that has checksums off): initialize the new 18 cluster with `initdb -D $NEW_PGDATA --no-data-checksums`, then run `pg_upgrade --check` with the same options you intend to use for the real run (add --link/--clone/--copy-file-range/--swap to --check if you will use them, since mode-specific checks apply). Running pg_upgrade --check first is the cheap way to surface the checksum mismatch along with any other incompatibility.

The alternative - bringing the OLD cluster into line by enabling checksums on it - is legitimate but usually the worse trade: it means a full offline page rewrite of the existing, large, production cluster (see 2b) instead of a flag on an empty new one. Prefer matching the new cluster to the old one. Do not attempt to work around a mismatch by starting either cluster and altering anything; the setting cannot be changed online.

One consequence worth stating for planning: because 18 flipped the initdb default, an upgrade path that used to be "initdb the new cluster and run pg_upgrade" now silently produces a mismatched pair whenever the source cluster has checksums off. Any runbook for upgrading to 18 must state the checksum state of the old cluster explicitly and choose the initdb flag accordingly.

=====================================================================

The harness searched the full text of https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/pgupgrade.html (34,905 characters, sha256 4b96b8964844) for "data checksums", "data checksum", "checksums", "off", "disabled" and "enabled", and found none of them. That absence is real and it is worth knowing, but it does not make any part of this question unanswerable: the pg_upgrade page is simply not where the checksum requirement is written. The initdb default and the matching-settings constraint are both stated affirmatively in the PostgreSQL 18 release notes (E.7.2 and E.7.3.7), and the default plus the pg_checksums/offline mechanics are stated in the checksums chapter (28.2.1). That is why every claim above is cited to those pages and not to pgupgrade.html; the pg_upgrade page is used here only for the pg_controldata pre-flight check and the "compatible initdb flags" instruction, which it does state.

=====================================================================
5. ONE-SCREEN RUNBOOK
=====================================================================

  # A. New 18 cluster, checksums ON by default (nothing to do)
  initdb -D /pgdata/18

  # B. New 18 cluster, checksums OFF from the start
  initdb -D /pgdata/18 --no-data-checksums

  # C. Existing cluster, switch checksums off (or on) - requires downtime
  pg_ctl -D /pgdata/18 stop -m fast
  # backup here
  pg_checksums --disable -D /pgdata/18        # or --enable / --check
  pg_ctl -D /pgdata/18 start

  # D. Confirm, always
  psql -Atc 'SHOW data_checksums;'

  # E. Upgrade: match the new cluster to the old one, then pre-flight
  initdb -D /pgdata/18 --no-data-checksums    # only if old cluster has checksums off
  pg_upgrade --check \
    --old-datadir /pgdata/17 --old-bindir /usr/pgsql-17/bin \
    --new-datadir /pgdata/18 --new-bindir /usr/pgsql-18/bin

Answers in one line each: (1) enabled - 18 changed the initdb default to on; (2) at init time with `initdb --no-data-checksums`, or later with `pg_checksums --disable` against a shut-down cluster (read-only, cluster-wide, cannot be done online); (3) the old and new clusters must have identical checksum settings, and pg_upgrade enforces that in its pg_controldata compatibility check before doing any work.
